FOUNDATION · 9 topics

How a language model works at all

Text becomes numbers, numbers become a probability over the next token, and a sampler picks one. Everything above this block is an optimisation of those three steps. Get the token economics right here and half the cost and context questions later answer themselves.

01foundation

Tokenization & Byte-Pair Encoding

Text becomes a list of integers before anything else happens, and which integers you get decides the bill.

A language model cannot read letters. Before anything else happens, your text is chopped into pieces from a fixed list, and each piece is swapped for its number in that list. The list is built once, before training, by a greedy counting procedure. Start with single characters. Count every adjacent pair across a huge pile of text, glue the most common pair into one new piece, add it to the list, and count again. Do that tens of thousands of times and the frequent words of the training language end up as a single piece each, while rare words, unusual names and anything from an under-represented script stay broken into scraps. From then on the model sees only the numbers. It has no view inside a piece, so the letters that make up a word are genuinely invisible to it.

Like a printer’s tray of type. The tray holds whole words cast as single slugs — the, and, ing — because they get set so often that casting them once saves hours. Anything unusual has to be assembled from the leftover letters. The compositor works in slugs, and he cannot tell you how many of one letter sit inside a slug he never took apart.

Byte-pair encoding is a compression algorithm repurposed as a vocabulary builder. Start from the 256 byte values, count every adjacent pair of symbols in the training corpus, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol, and repeat for a fixed number of merges — the ordered merge list is the tokenizer. Vocabulary sizes today run from about 32k for older Llama models to 100k for cl100k_base and around 200k for o200k_base and Llama 3. Because it is byte-level there is no out-of-vocabulary case: worst case a string falls back to individual bytes. English costs roughly 1.3 tokens per word, about 4 characters per token. And the strawberry question answers itself the moment you say the mechanism out loud — the model receives token IDs, and str plus aw plus berry carries no information about the letters inside any of them.

Treat the pathologies as product bugs rather than trivia. Numbers fragment on rules that have nothing to do with place value: cl100k_base chunks digits in groups of up to three from the left, so 1234 arrives as 123 plus 4 and 12345 as 123 plus 45 — the units column lands in a different piece depending on the length of the number, and nothing lines up for a column-wise addition. That is a large part of why models are unreliable at multi-digit arithmetic, and why calling out to a calculator beats prompting harder. Character-level tasks — count the letters, reverse the string, find the rhyme — fail for exactly the same structural reason. The one that costs money is domain jargon: a drug name, a part number or a legal citation that shatters into six pieces embeds badly and retrieves badly, so a retrieval bug you have been chasing in the index may actually live in the tokenizer. Run your real vocabulary through the tokenizer before you blame the model. WordPiece (BERT) and SentencePiece Unigram (T5, Gemma) are the other two families; SentencePiece treats the input as a raw stream and needs no whitespace pre-tokenisation, which is what makes it workable for scripts that do not use spaces.

You reach for it when

  • Estimating cost or context for a language you did not build for
  • A model fails at counting letters, reversing a string or simple sums
  • Retrieval misses documents that visibly contain the term
  • Choosing between a stock tokenizer and extending the vocabulary

The trap

Saying it splits text into words. It does not — it splits text into subword pieces chosen by frequency, which is why the is one token and a drug name is six. The consequences are the part that matters: you cannot count letters inside a piece, digit strings do not align on place value, and a language the merges were never learned for costs three to six times more for the same sentence. Give the mechanism, then give one product bug it explains.

The math how the vocabulary gets built

merge=argmax(a,b)​count(ab), repeated N times  ·  English ≈1.3 tokens/word ≈4 chars/token  ·  cost ∝ tokens, never wordsThe first line is the entire training algorithm: count every adjacent pair of symbols in the corpus, merge the most frequent one into a new symbol, repeat until the vocabulary is the size you asked for. The ordered list of merges is the tokenizer — encoding a new string means replaying those merges in order. Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values rather than from characters, so there is no out-of-vocabulary case: worst case a string is represented byte by byte, which is exactly what happens to a script whose merges were never learned. Vocabulary size is a trade. Larger means fewer tokens per document, so cheaper and longer-reaching sequences, but a bigger embedding matrix and a bigger softmax at the output. Common sizes are 32k, 100k (cl100k_base) and around 200k (o200k_base, Llama 3) — config-specific numbers that move every year, so quote the tier rather than the figure.

Look inside the tokenizer

import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")     # GPT-4, text-embedding-3

ids = enc.encode("strawberry")
print([enc.decode([i]) for i in ids])         # ['str', 'aw', 'berry']
# the model receives those three ids. The letter r is never an input.

for s in ["1234", "12345", "1,234"]:
    print(s, [enc.decode([i]) for i in enc.encode(s)])   # digits group by 3s

# run your OWN vocabulary through it before you blame the model
for t in ["semaglutide", "NCT04255433", "CVE-2024-3094"]:
    print(t, len(enc.encode(t)))              # jargon shatters -> retrieval suffers

Where this bites in production

Two documented cases. Meta rebuilt Llama 3’s tokenizer around a 128k vocabulary, up from Llama 2’s 32k SentencePiece, and reported up to 15% fewer tokens for the same text — a straight throughput and context win with no change to the model itself. And the SolidGoldMagikarp family: strings that earned a merge from scraped Reddit usernames, so the tokenizer knew them while GPT-2 and GPT-3 had barely seen them in training. Prompting one made the model evade, insult, or emit unrelated text.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why can’t it count the r’s in strawberry?
Because it never sees letters. The tokenizer turns the word into a handful of subword ids — commonly str, aw, berry — and those ids are the entire input. Nothing in them says how many characters sit inside a piece, so counting is a task the architecture has no access to, not a reasoning failure. The production answer is the same as for arithmetic: hand it a tool, or spell the word out one character per token in the prompt.
Your domain terms tokenise into garbage. What do you actually do?
Measure first, then pick one of three fixes. Run your real vocabulary — part numbers, drug names, error codes — through the tokenizer and count the pieces. You can add the terms to the vocabulary and resize the embedding matrix, which only pays off with continued pretraining; you can normalise the text at ingestion so the terms at least tokenise consistently; or you can accept it and lean on BM25 inside a hybrid retriever, which matches the literal string and does not care how it split.
A user says the model is bad at arithmetic. Where do you look first?
At the tokenizer, before the model. Digit strings are chunked in groups of up to three from the left, so 1234 arrives as 123 plus 4 and 12345 as 123 plus 45 — the units column sits in a different piece depending on the length of the number. Prompting harder cannot fix a representation problem. Call out to a calculator, or use a model whose tokenizer splits every digit separately, as Llama 2’s did.

Say this back tomorrow

merge the commonest adjacent pair, tens of thousands of times  ·  the model never sees a letter
  • BPE builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair
  • Frequent words become one token; jargon, digits and other scripts fragment
  • Character-blindness, arithmetic errors and retrieval misses are one bug, not three

Unlocks

  • byte-pair merges
  • subword
  • strawberry
  • cl100k / o200k
  • vocabulary size

02foundation

Token Economics: Cost, Context & Language

The arithmetic an interviewer wants on the whiteboard, and the levers in the order you pull them.

Everything you send and everything you get back is billed by the piece, and the pieces are not words. In English a word costs about one and a third pieces, and a piece runs to roughly four characters. Code costs more, because operators, indentation and run-together names each take their own piece. Structured formats cost more again, since every brace and quote is billed. And the same sentence in another language can cost several times as much, because the vocabulary was built mostly from English text, so other scripts fragment. That matters twice over: it is your bill, and it is your context limit, so a Thai user may run out of room in a conversation an English user finishes comfortably. Before you argue about which model to use, count the pieces. The count is usually where the money actually is.

Think of shipping by volume rather than by item. The courier does not care what is inside the box, only how much room it takes on the pallet. Pack the same order in a bigger carton and you pay more for nothing at all. Ship it in a language whose boxes are a quarter of the size and you need four times as many pallets. The freight bill is decided before anyone opens a thing.

Quote the ratios, then do the arithmetic. English runs about 1.3 tokens per word, roughly 4 characters per token. Code is 1.5 to 3 tokens per word, because operators, indentation and camelCase all split. JSON and YAML land at 2 to 4, since every brace, quote and colon is its own token. Non-English inflation over identical content is 1.2 to 1.5× for Spanish, French and German, 2 to 4× for Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and 3 to 6× for Arabic, Hindi and Thai. Then the template they want on the board: 100k users × 10 interactions × about 2k tokens is 2 billion tokens a day. Split that into input and output, multiply by the current per-million rates, and you have a number you can defend. Prices move every quarter, so state the arithmetic and the rate separately — the arithmetic is what does not expire.

The levers, in the order you pull them. First cut tokens: shorten the system prompt, retrieve five chunks rather than twenty, stop pasting whole documents, and cap the output length, because output is usually the expensive side per token. Second, cache. Prompt caching gives roughly a 90% discount on cached input reads, with a 1,024-token minimum cacheable prefix that must match exactly from the very first character — so the stable system prompt and few-shots go first and the variable user content goes last. Realistic hit rates are 80 to 95% for a stable prefix and only 20 to 45% for semantic caching over real traffic, which is well below the numbers in the papers. Third, route by difficulty: send the easy majority to a small model and escalate on a confidence or complexity signal. Fourth, and only fourth, quantise or self-host — that trades a per-token cost for a capital and operations cost, and it pays back only above a sustained volume you should be able to estimate on the spot. Batch endpoints at roughly half price are a fifth lever whenever the work tolerates a slow turnaround.

You reach for it when

  • A system-design round asks you to put the bill on a whiteboard
  • Deciding what to cut when a feature costs more than it earns
  • Sizing a context budget for a long multi-turn conversation
  • Launching in a market whose language is not English

The trap

Answering a cost question with “use a smaller model” and no token accounting. It is the one move that also changes quality, and it is rarely the biggest lever — a bloated system prompt, or twenty retrieved chunks where five would do, is often half the bill. Do the arithmetic out loud first: tokens per interaction, interactions per day, input and output priced separately. Then cut tokens, then cache, then route, and only then talk about the model.

The math the whiteboard template

Tday​=U×I×t  ·  100,000×10×2,000=2×109 tokens/day  ·  cost=106Tin​rin​+Tout​rout​​U is users, I interactions per user per day, and t tokens per interaction — system prompt plus retrieved context plus conversation history plus the completion, and it is almost always the retrieved context that dominates. Two billion tokens a day at a blended 50 cents per million is about 1,000 dollars a day, or 365,000 a year; the rate is the part that changes every quarter, so quote the arithmetic and the rate separately. Now the levers as arithmetic, because they multiply. Cutting the average interaction from 2,000 tokens to 1,200 removes 40% before you touch anything else. Prompt caching at an 80% hit rate and a 90% discount gives an effective input multiplier of 0.2+0.8×0.1=0.28, a 72% cut on the input side. Routing 80% of traffic to a model at a fifth of the price gives 0.2+0.8×0.2=0.36. All three sit above the choice of model, and all three are things you control.

Count before you optimise

import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")        # GPT-4o family

users, per_user, per_call = 100_000, 10, 2_000   # the template worth memorising
daily = users * per_user * per_call
print(daily)                                     # 2_000_000_000 tokens/day
print(daily / 1e6 * 0.50)                        # 1000.0 dollars/day at 50c per 1M

# lever 1: count, do not guess. Retrieved context is usually the fat.
parts = {"system": system_prompt, "history": history, "chunks": "".join(chunks)}
print({k: len(enc.encode(v)) for k, v in parts.items()})

# lever 2: 80% hit rate on a cached prefix, cached reads at 10% of list
print(0.2 * 1 + 0.8 * 0.1)                       # 0.28 -> input cost falls 72%

Where this bites in production

Prompt caching is the lever with the clearest provider behaviour. OpenAI and Anthropic both bill cached input reads at roughly a tenth of the normal rate, both require a minimum cacheable prefix of about 1,024 tokens, and both match the prefix exactly from the first character — so moving a timestamp out of the top of your system prompt is worth more than most model swaps. Anthropic additionally charges a cache-write premium of 1.25× for the five-minute TTL and 2× for the one-hour, which puts the breakeven at roughly 1.4 reads. Both also run batch endpoints at about half price for work that tolerates a slow turnaround.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

One million queries a day — show me the bill.
Count tokens before you name a model. Establish tokens per query — system prompt plus retrieved context plus history plus output, and the retrieved context usually dominates — multiply by a million, split input from output because they are priced differently, and multiply by the current per-million rates. Say the number out loud, then say which term you would attack first. An answer with no token count in it fails this question however good the model recommendation is.
The bill is too high. What do you change, and in what order?
Cut tokens, cache, route, then quantise or self-host. Cutting tokens is free and usually the largest single win: trim the system prompt, retrieve five chunks rather than twenty, cap the output. Caching is next — a stable prefix at roughly a 90% discount and an 80 to 95% hit rate, with semantic caching a realistic 20 to 45%. Routing sends the easy majority to a small model with an escalation path. Self-hosting comes last, because it swaps a per-token cost for a capital and operations cost that only pays back above a volume you should be able to state.
Your Thai users hit the context limit and your English users do not. Why?
Because the context window is measured in tokens, not in meaning. The vocabulary was built mostly from English text, so Thai, Hindi and Arabic fragment at three to six tokens for what English does in one — the same conversation eats several times the room and several times the money. Budget context per language rather than per turn, and expect the cost per non-English user to be a multiple of your headline figure.

Say this back tomorrow

count the tokens first  ·  then cut, cache, route, and only then self-host
  • English is about 1.3 tokens per word, roughly 4 characters per token
  • 100k users times 10 interactions times 2k tokens is 2 billion tokens a day
  • Non-English inflation of 3 to 6 times is a cost problem and a context problem

03foundation

Embeddings & Semantic Similarity

A vector is a position. Nearness is the only thing it means — and nearness is not truth.

A model reads a chunk of text and hands back a long list of numbers. Treat that list as a position in a space with hundreds or thousands of directions, and the useful property is that texts about the same thing land near each other. Nothing in there is a definition or a fact. It is a position, learned from the company a phrase keeps. Distance is measured by angle rather than by length, because two passages on the same topic can differ enormously in how long they are and you do not want length counted as difference. So search becomes geometry: turn the question into a position, hand back the stored positions closest to it. What that misses is anything whose meaning lives in a small word, a digit, or an exact label.

Think of an open-plan library with no catalogue. Books are placed so that anything on the same subject sits within arm’s reach, and you find things by walking to roughly the right spot. It works beautifully for a topic. It is useless when you want the one volume whose serial number ends in seven, or the book arguing the opposite of the one in your hand — that one is shelved right beside it.

An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector, and similarity is cosine: cos(u,v)=(u⋅v)/(∥u∥∥v∥). The reason cosine is the default is arithmetic rather than philosophy. L2-normalise both vectors and the denominator becomes 1, so cosine similarity is the dot product — one multiply-add per dimension over contiguous memory, which is what makes a brute-force scan over a million vectors cheap and what every ANN index is built on. Most providers already return unit vectors, so check before you normalise twice. Dimensions are a config choice, not a law: 384 for MiniLM, 768 for BERT-base and nomic-v1.5, 1024 for Cohere embed-v4, voyage-3-large and BGE-large, 1536 for text-embedding-3-small, 3072 for text-embedding-3-large. The number that actually constrains the design is the model’s maximum input length — 512 tokens for many BERT-family encoders, 8,191 for OpenAI’s v3 models — because that is a hard ceiling on chunk size.

Now the failure modes, because that is the follow-up. Negation barely moves a vector: “the drug is safe in pregnancy” and “the drug is not safe in pregnancy” share every content word but one and sit almost on top of each other, so a dense retriever will cheerfully hand back the opposite of what was asked. Numbers, dates, versions, SKUs, error codes and legal citations are worse, because they fragment into subword pieces carrying neither arithmetic nor identity — CVE-2024-3094 and CVE-2024-3095 are neighbours. That is the entire reason hybrid search exists: BM25 matches the literal string, dense retrieval matches the topic, and reciprocal rank fusion combines two score scales that are not comparable by using rank position instead of score, conventionally with a constant of 60. Hybrid typically lifts recall@10 by 10 to 30% over dense alone, and BM25 alone still wins outright on acronyms and rare identifiers. One senior signal to keep in reserve: vectors from two different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared, so upgrading an embedding model means a full reindex and a cutover, never a gradual migration.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing an embedding model and a chunk size together
  • Retrieval returns topically close documents that answer the opposite question
  • Queries contain SKUs, error codes, dates or version numbers
  • Planning an upgrade from one embedding model to another

The trap

Saying “they capture meaning” and stopping there. That answer contains no failure mode, and the failure modes are the follow-up. Embeddings encode topic, not truth: negation barely moves the vector, so “is safe” and “is not safe” come back as neighbours, and numbers, dates, versions and identifiers carry no exact identity at all. If you cannot say why hybrid search exists, you have not answered the question.

The math why cosine is the default

cos(u,v)=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​  ·  if ∥u∥=∥v∥=1 then cos(u,v)=u⋅v=i=1∑d​ui​vi​The second identity is the whole reason cosine won. L2-normalise once at write time and similarity collapses to a dot product — d multiply-adds over contiguous memory, which is what HNSW and IVF-PQ are built on. Ranking is also unchanged if you switch to Euclidean distance on normalised vectors, because ∥u−v∥2=2−2(u⋅v) is monotone in the dot product; on unnormalised vectors it is not, and that is where the two metrics diverge. Most providers already return unit vectors, so normalising twice is harmless and normalising not at all is the bug. For fusing two rankings whose scores are not comparable, reciprocal rank fusion is the standard: RRF(d)=∑r​k+rankr​(d)1​ with k conventionally 60. Note that it consumes positions and never raw scores, which is precisely why it works across a BM25 score and a cosine score.

Cosine, normalisation, and the negation failure

import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI

r = OpenAI().embeddings.create(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",      # 1536 dims, 8191 max input tokens
    input=["the drug is safe in pregnancy",
           "the drug is not safe in pregnancy",
           "how do I reset the router"])
v = np.array([e.embedding for e in r.data])

print(np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1))         # ~1.0 each - already L2-normalised
print(v @ v.T)                           # so cosine IS the dot product. No division.

# negation pair ~0.95, unrelated sentence ~0.10. The retriever cannot tell
# "safe" from "not safe" - which is why BM25 runs on the raw string too.

Where this bites in production

OpenAI documents that its embeddings are normalised to unit length, which is why the cookbook computes similarity with a plain dot product and why text-embedding-3-large can expose a dimensions parameter at all — Matryoshka training lets you truncate 3072 down to 256 and renormalise, trading a few points of recall for an eighth of the index. On the other side, Elastic and Weaviate both ship hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion as a first-class mode, precisely because dense retrieval loses to BM25 on acronyms, SKUs and error codes.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why cosine? And what happens with negation?
Cosine because it ignores length, and because on normalised vectors it is just the dot product. Passages on one topic differ wildly in length and you do not want that counted as difference; once both vectors are unit length the denominator vanishes, leaving one multiply-add per dimension, which is what makes scanning millions of vectors cheap. Negation is the standard failure: “is safe” and “is not safe” share every content word but one and land next to each other, so a dense retriever returns the opposite of what was asked.
You are picking an embedding model. Which number decides the design?
Maximum input tokens, not dimensions. That number is a hard ceiling on chunk size, so a 512-token encoder forces a completely different chunking strategy from an 8,191-token one. Dimensions decide index size, memory and scan cost — 384 through 3072 across the common models — and more is not reliably better, so benchmark recall on your own golden set. Both figures are config-specific and move every few months; quote the range and check the model card.
You want to upgrade your embedding model. Walk me through the migration.
Full reindex and a clean cutover — you cannot mix the two spaces. Vectors from different models are not comparable, so a nearest-neighbour lookup that touches both is meaningless, and a gradual backfill silently corrupts every query in flight. Build a shadow index, dual-write new documents, compare recall offline on the golden set, then cut over and delete the old index. Budget the cost of re-embedding the whole corpus up front, because that is the number that kills the project.

Say this back tomorrow

normalise both and cosine is exactly the dot product  ·  nearness is not truth
  • Cosine equals the dot product on L2-normalised vectors, which is why it is the default
  • Negation, numbers, dates and exact identifiers are where dense retrieval fails
  • Maximum input tokens caps your chunk size; dimensions only cost you memory

Unlocks

  • cosine as dot product
  • L2 normalisation
  • negation failure
  • hybrid + RRF
  • max input tokens

04foundation

Next-Token Prediction, Logits & Softmax

One score per vocabulary entry, turned into a probability, sampled once. That is the entire objective.

A language model does exactly one thing. Given everything so far, it produces a score for every single entry in its vocabulary — all hundred thousand or so of them — saying how well each one would continue the text. Those raw scores are squashed into a set of proportions that add up to one, so the whole vocabulary becomes a set of chances. One entry is picked. It is glued onto the end of the text, and the entire process runs again from the start with the text now one piece longer. That loop is the whole of generation. Training is the same thing with the answer known: show it real text, compare the chances it gave against the piece that actually came next, and nudge the weights. Nothing is looked up. Everything it appears to know was squeezed into the weights during that process and comes back out as a lossy summary.

Like a bookmaker pricing the next word. He does not know what comes next. He posts odds on every possible continuation, someone places a bet, the result gets written into the record, and then he prices the following word with that result now part of what he can see. He has memorised no book. He has read so many that his odds are usually right.

The model is a function from a token sequence to a score per vocabulary entry. Say the shapes out loud: input ids are (batch,seq), the final hidden states are (batch,seq,dmodel​), and the language-model head projects those to logits of shape (batch,seq,∣V∣) — one raw, unnormalised score per vocabulary entry, at every position. At generation time you take the last position, softmax it into a distribution over the vocabulary, sample one id, append it, and run the forward pass again; the KV cache is what stops that re-running being quadratic work. Training uses every position at once, because the causal mask means position t only ever attended to positions up to t, and the loss is cross-entropy between the predicted distribution and the token that actually came next, averaged over every position in the batch. Perplexity is simply the exponential of that loss.

The follow-up is always some version of “so how does it know things”, and the honest answer is that it does not retrieve, it predicts. Everything in the weights was compressed there during pretraining by that same next-token objective over trillions of tokens, and compression at that ratio is lossy: facts stated often and consistently survive, a detail seen twice does not, and the model gets no signal telling it which case it is in. That is one root of hallucination and the whole argument for retrieval — put the fact in the context window where it is read rather than recalled. Two vocabulary points that catch people out. Logits are unnormalised scores on an arbitrary scale and only differences between them mean anything, so adding a constant to all of them changes nothing after the softmax. And the probability the model assigns is a statement about text continuation, not about truth: a high-probability token is not a confident fact, and calibrating one against the other is its own open problem.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining what a language model actually optimises
  • Someone asks why the model invented a plausible citation
  • Reading a forward pass and needing the tensor shapes
  • Deciding between retrieval and fine-tuning for a knowledge gap

The trap

Two versions of the same mistake. The first is anthropomorphising — saying the model understands, remembers, or looks something up, when it does none of those and the interviewer is listening for exactly that word. The second is not being able to state the loop in one sentence. Practise it until it is automatic: a score for every vocabulary entry, softmax into a distribution, sample one, append it, run the whole forward pass again.

The math logits, softmax, cross-entropy

zt​=WU​ht​∈R∣V∣  ·  pi​=∑j​ezj​ezi​​  ·  L=−T1​t=1∑T​logp(xt​∣x<t​)ht​ is the final hidden state at position t, of size dmodel​; the unembedding matrix WU​ projects it to one score per vocabulary entry, so the full logits tensor is (batch,seq,∣V∣). Logits are unnormalised and shift-invariant — add a constant to all of them and the softmax is unchanged — so only differences carry information, which is also why you never interpret a raw logit on its own. The loss is the average negative log probability of the token that actually came next, and perplexity is eL, readable as the effective number of equally likely continuations. Two anchors worth carrying: a uniform guess over a 100,000-entry vocabulary gives log100,000≈11.5, and a well-trained model sits near 2.0, a perplexity of about 7.4.

The shapes, out loud

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

ids = tok("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt").input_ids   # (1, 5)
logits = model(ids).logits            # (1, 5, 50257) = (batch, seq, vocab)

nxt = logits[0, -1]                   # only the LAST position matters at generation
probs = torch.softmax(nxt, dim=-1)    # sums to 1 across the whole vocabulary
print(tok.decode(int(probs.argmax())), float(probs.max()))     # ' Paris' 0.72

# add a constant to every logit and nothing changes - only differences matter
print(torch.allclose(probs, torch.softmax(nxt + 100.0, dim=-1)))   # True

Where this bites in production

Take Llama 3.1 405B. It was trained on roughly 15 trillion tokens — on the order of 60 terabytes of text — and the released BF16 weights are about 810 GB. That is a compression ratio near 75 to 1, and it is the honest answer to “how does it know things”: it does not store the corpus, it stores a summary of it. The same arithmetic explains why it will reproduce the boiling point of water and invent a plausible case citation with identical fluency.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

So how does it know anything?
It does not retrieve, it predicts. Every parameter was set by a single objective — predict the next token — across trillions of tokens, so what looks like knowledge is a lossy compression of that corpus into the weights. Facts stated often and consistently survive the compression; a detail seen twice does not, and the model receives no signal telling it which case it is in. That is one root of hallucination, and the whole argument for putting the fact in the context window instead.
What shape are the logits, and what do you do with them?
Batch by sequence by vocabulary size — one raw score per vocabulary entry at every position. At generation you take the last position, softmax it into a distribution over the vocabulary, sample one id, append it and run the forward pass again. During training you use every position at once, because the causal mask means each position only ever saw what came before it, and the loss is cross-entropy against the token that actually followed.
The model gives a token 0.92 probability. Is that a confidence score?
No — it is a statement about text, not about truth. The number says this continuation is likely given the training distribution, which is a different claim from this is correct, and models are routinely fluent and confident on fabricated specifics. Logits underneath are unnormalised and shift-invariant, so a raw score means nothing on its own either. If you need calibrated confidence, measure it against a labelled set or get it from a verifier, never from the sampler.

Say this back tomorrow

score every vocabulary entry  ·  softmax  ·  sample one  ·  append  ·  do it all again
  • Logits are (batch, seq, vocab) — one unnormalised score per vocabulary entry
  • Generation is sample, append, forward again; the KV cache is what makes it affordable
  • Knowledge is compressed into the weights during pretraining, and compression is lossy

05foundation

Temperature, Top-k & Top-p

Three dials on the same distribution, and not one of them makes the model correct.

The model hands you a set of chances spread over the whole vocabulary. Three dials decide what you do with them. The first stretches or flattens the raw scores before they are turned into chances: turn it down and the leading candidate takes almost everything, turn it up and the also-rans get a real share. The second keeps a fixed number of leading candidates and throws away the rest, however the chances happen to be spread. The third keeps however many candidates it takes to cover a chosen share of the total, so it holds on to few when the model is sure and many when it is not. Turning the first dial all the way down does not make the answer right. It makes the same answer come back every time, which is a different property, and a wrong answer that repeats reliably is still wrong.

Like a panel of judges scoring a competition. The first dial is how much you exaggerate the gaps between their scores — squash them and everyone looks joint first, stretch them and the leader wins outright. The second says only the top three entrants may be drawn at all. The third says keep adding entrants until you have covered ninety per cent of the vote, however many that turns out to take.

Temperature divides the logits before the softmax: pi​=softmax(zi​/T). At T<1 the gaps between logits are stretched, so the distribution sharpens toward the argmax; at T>1 they are compressed and the tail picks up mass; the limit as T→0 is greedy decoding. Top-k truncates to a fixed number of candidates, renormalises, and samples — and the flaw is that the number is fixed whatever the shape: k=50 on a distribution where one token holds 0.99 admits 49 pieces of noise, while the same k where the top token holds 0.05 cuts off perfectly plausible continuations. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, sorts descending and keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, so the candidate count is dynamic — a handful when the model is confident, hundreds when it is not. That adaptivity is why top-p, typically 0.9 to 0.95, is the default nearly everywhere.

Now the question that decides the interview. Temperature 0 buys determinism, not accuracy. Greedy decoding takes the argmax at every step, so the same prompt on the same weights returns the same output — and if the model is wrong about something it is now reliably and repeatably wrong, with the variance that might have surfaced a better continuation removed. Even the determinism is qualified in practice: batched inference on a GPU reorders floating-point reductions depending on what else is in the batch, so two identical requests can still diverge by a token, which is why providers describe seeded reproducibility as best effort. Use near-zero for extraction, classification, structured output and anything you will parse; use 0.7 to 1.0 for drafting and ideation. Two smaller dials worth naming. Repetition and frequency penalties subtract from the logits of tokens already emitted, which breaks degenerate loops but will also suppress a term your answer legitimately needs to repeat. And min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least a fixed fraction of the top token’s, a threshold relative to the leader, which holds up better than top-p at high temperature. Set one truncation method, not three at once.

You reach for it when

  • Setting decoding parameters for an extraction or classification job
  • Output is repetitive, bland, or looping on one phrase
  • A reviewer asks why the same prompt gave two different answers
  • A creative feature has gone flat and you are told to fix it

The trap

Conflating determinism with accuracy — treating temperature 0 as a correctness setting. It removes variance and nothing else, and a confidently wrong answer has just become reproducible. The second half is not knowing which cut is which: top-k keeps a fixed number of candidates regardless of the shape of the distribution, top-p keeps however many it takes to reach a probability mass. Getting those two backwards ends the topic on the spot.

The math one formula, two different cuts

pi​=∑j​exp(zj​/T)exp(zi​/T)​  ·  top-k: keep the k largest, renormalise  ·  top-p: smallest S with ∑i∈S​pi​≥pDividing the logits by T before the exponential is the entire mechanism. As T→0 the largest logit dominates and the distribution collapses to a one-hot at the argmax, which is greedy decoding; as T→∞ every exponent goes to 0 and the distribution goes uniform. Worked on the four logits 4.0, 2.0, 1.5, 0.0: the leader holds 0.81 at T=1, 0.98 at T=0.5 and 0.56 at T=2. Order matters in the implementations — Hugging Face applies temperature, then top-k, then top-p — so a small k silently overrides a generous p, and that is a real bug in a lot of configs. Min-p is the newer variant: keep tokens with pi​≥pmin​⋅maxj​pj​, a threshold relative to the leader rather than a cumulative mass, which behaves better than top-p at high temperature.

The defaults that bite

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

# do_sample=False is the DEFAULT: temperature and top_p are silently ignored.
# top_k defaults to 50 in GenerationConfig - pass 0 to turn the fixed cut off.
out = model.generate(ids, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.95,
                     top_k=0, repetition_penalty=1.1, max_new_tokens=64)

# top-p by hand. The point is that the cut MOVES with the distribution.
p = torch.softmax(logits[0, -1] / 0.7, dim=-1)
srt, idx = p.sort(descending=True)
print(int(((srt.cumsum(-1) - srt) < 0.95).sum()))
# ~3 after 'the capital of France is', ~200 after 'Once upon a'

Where this bites in production

Library defaults are where this actually goes wrong. Hugging Face’s generate defaults to do_sample=False, so temperature and top_p are silently ignored unless you also pass do_sample=True — one of the most common bug reports on the repository — and its GenerationConfig ships top_k=50, which stays on until you set it to 0. OpenAI defaults both temperature and top_p to 1.0 and its documentation advises changing one, not both, while its seed parameter is explicitly best-effort with a system_fingerprint to tell you when the backend moved underneath you.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Does temperature 0 make it correct?
No. It makes it deterministic, which is a different property. Greedy decoding takes the highest-scoring token at every step, so the same prompt returns the same output — and if the model is wrong, it is now reliably and repeatably wrong, with the variance that might have surfaced a better continuation removed. Use near-zero when you need reproducibility and a parseable output, not because you believe it improves accuracy.
Top-k versus top-p — what is the actual difference?
Top-k is a fixed cut, top-p is a moving one. Top-k always keeps the same number of candidates whatever the distribution looks like, so it admits noise when the model is certain and truncates good options when it is not. Top-p sorts descending and keeps the smallest set whose probabilities sum to the threshold, so the count adapts — a handful when the model is sure, hundreds when it is not. That adaptivity is why nucleus sampling at 0.9 to 0.95 is the common default.
You set temperature 0 and still get different outputs. Why?
Determinism is not guaranteed end to end. Batched GPU inference reorders floating-point reductions depending on what else is in the batch, so two nearly tied logits can swap and change a token; mixture-of-experts routing adds another batch-dependent path. On top of that a hosted endpoint can move you to a different backend build between calls. Providers therefore describe seeds as best effort and expose a fingerprint. If you need byte-identical output, cache it.

Say this back tomorrow

temperature divides the logits  ·  top-k is a fixed cut, top-p a moving one
  • Temperature divides the logits before softmax; the limit at zero is greedy decoding
  • Top-k keeps a fixed count; top-p keeps whatever count covers the probability mass
  • Temperature zero buys determinism, not correctness — and greedy can be repeatably wrong

06foundation

Base, Instruct & Reasoning Models

Pretraining puts the knowledge in. Everything after it decides how the model behaves when you ask.

Training happens in stages, and each stage leaves you with a different kind of model. The first stage reads an enormous amount of text and learns to continue it. That is a base model, and it is not a chatbot: ask it a question and it will often carry on with more questions, because that is what a page of questions looks like. The second stage shows it many worked examples of a request followed by a good answer, and now it answers instead of continuing. A third kind is trained to write out its working before it commits, so it spends far more words, takes longer and costs more. Here is the part interviewers listen for: the facts were all learned in the first stage. The later stages change the manners, not the knowledge.

Like a new hire who has read every document in the company. On day one you ask where the fire exit is and you get a paragraph on fire safety policy, because reading is all they have done. A week of shadowing teaches them to answer the question that was actually asked. Nothing in that week taught them one new fact about the building.

Three stages, three artefacts. Pretraining is next-token prediction over trillions of tokens, and the output is a base model — a text continuer with no notion of a turn. Supervised fine-tuning then trains on prompt-and-response pairs, tens of thousands rather than billions of them, and teaches the shape of a conversation: a chat template, special turn tokens, an instruction-following prior. Preference alignment (RLHF with PPO, or DPO) optimises which of two acceptable answers a human prefers, with a KL penalty holding the policy near the reference so it cannot drift or reward-hack its way out of the distribution. Reasoning models add one further stage: reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers, which teaches the model to emit a long chain of thought before it commits. The sentence to say out loud is that base and instruct differ in behaviour, not in knowledge. Alignment cannot install a fact that pretraining did not.

Reach for a base model when you intend to install the behaviour yourself. Fine-tuning on top of an instruct checkpoint means fighting a behaviour prior that is already baked in, so domain adaptation and continued pretraining usually start from base. Base is also the honest choice for perplexity and likelihood scoring, because preference training reshapes the probabilities it would report, and for attaching your own classification head to the final hidden state. Reasoning models cost you three things. Latency, because the thinking happens before the first useful token appears. Tokens, because the hidden reasoning is billed as output — OpenAI recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens of context for it, and Anthropic’s extended thinking takes a minimum budget of 1,024 tokens. And quality at the easy end: on extraction, classification and strict formatting they are slower, dearer and no better, and the deliberation can talk the model out of the obvious answer. Route by difficulty instead of defaulting to the cleverest checkpoint you can afford.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing a checkpoint to fine-tune and deciding whether to start from base
  • Someone argues the instruct model knows more than the base model
  • A simple extraction job got slower and dearer after a model upgrade
  • Explaining why alignment cannot close a knowledge gap

The trap

Saying the instruct model “knows more”. It does not. The same pretrained weights sit underneath, with a thin layer of post-training on top; what changed is that it answers rather than continues. The consequence is the part they want: if the model does not know your internal policy, no amount of alignment, chat templating or instruction tuning will add it. That is a retrieval problem, or a continued-pretraining problem.

The math the same loss, three different diets

Lpre​=−∑t​logp(xt​∣x<t​)  ·  LSFT​=−∑t​logp(yt​∣x,y<t​)  ·  max E[r]−βKL(πθ​∥πref​)Look at the first two expressions before you read the third: they are the identical objective. Pretraining predicts the next token of raw text; supervised fine-tuning predicts the next token of a response given a prompt, with the loss usually masked so only the response tokens count. Nothing about the mechanism changed — only the data, and there is roughly nine orders of magnitude less of it. That is the whole argument for why post-training moves behaviour and not knowledge. The third line is preference alignment: maximise a learned reward while a KL term βKL(πθ​∥πref​) pins the policy near the SFT reference. Without that penalty the policy walks off to whatever degenerate text the reward model happens to score highly, which is exactly what reward hacking looks like. DPO reaches the same optimum without training a separate reward model, by rewriting the problem as a classification-style loss over preferred and rejected pairs. Reasoning RL swaps the learned reward for a verifiable one — a unit test, a numeric answer — which is why it works on maths and code first.

The difference, in one attribute

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

base = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B")
chat = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct")

print(base.chat_template)      # None - the base model has no notion of a turn

print(chat.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": "what is BPE?"}],
                               tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True))
# <|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|> ... the special tokens ARE the interface

# same pretraining run, same facts. Feed a chat turn to the base model and it
# continues the pattern: "what is BPE? what is a tokenizer? what is ..."

Where this bites in production

Llama 3.1 8B and 8B-Instruct ship as two checkpoints from one pretraining run: the same corpus, the same knowledge, different post-training — and only the Instruct repo carries a chat template, so tokenizer.chat_template is None on the base one. On the reasoning side the costs are documented rather than folklore: OpenAI bills hidden reasoning tokens as output, never returns them, and advises reserving at least 25,000 tokens of context for them; Anthropic’s extended thinking requires a budget_tokens of 1,024 or more.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Does the instruct model know more than the base model?
No — they differ in behaviour, not in knowledge. The facts were compressed into the weights during pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning plus preference alignment teach turn-taking, format and tone on top of them. So the instruct model is easier to talk to and no better informed, and a gap in your internal documentation is still a gap. Close it with retrieval, or with continued pretraining, never with a friendlier system prompt.
When would you actually reach for a base model?
When you are installing the behaviour yourself. Fine-tuning on an instruct checkpoint means fighting a behaviour prior that is already there, so domain adaptation and continued pretraining normally start from base. Base is also the right choice for perplexity and likelihood scoring, because preference training reshapes the probabilities, and for bolting your own classification head onto the final hidden state. For anything you will prompt rather than train, take the instruct checkpoint.
Your JSON extraction job got slower and more expensive on a reasoning model. Why?
You are paying for deliberation the task does not need. A reasoning model spends hidden tokens before the first useful one, so time to first token grows and the hidden tokens are billed as output; on extraction, classification and strict formatting that buys nothing, and the deliberation can talk the model out of the obvious answer. Route by difficulty: cheap model for the easy majority, reasoning model behind an escalation signal.

  • Base and instruct differ in behaviour, not knowledge — alignment adds no facts
  • Start from base when you are fine-tuning behaviour, scoring perplexity or adding a head

The Context Window & Lost in the Middle

The number on the box is a capacity, not a promise.

The context window is the total number of pieces the model can have in front of it at once: your instructions, everything retrieved, the whole conversation so far, and the reply it is still writing. It is not memory. Nothing carries over between calls, so the whole lot is sent again every turn and paid for again every turn. The number on the box is how much you may send, not how much will be used well. Accuracy falls off before you reach the limit, and material buried in the middle of a long prompt is recalled less reliably than the same material at the beginning or the end. So a very long prompt is slower, dearer, and quietly worse about its own middle. A bigger window raises the ceiling. It does not remove the job of choosing what to put in front of the model.

Like handing someone a four-hundred-page report five minutes before the meeting. They read the opening, skim to the end, and form a view. Ask about something on page two hundred and you get a half-memory or a confident invention. Handing over more paper was never the same thing as being understood, and the thicker report also made everyone wait longer.

The window is the maximum sequence length the model will accept in one forward pass, counted in tokens and shared out between system prompt, retrieved context, conversation history and completion. Every call is stateless: the entire conversation is resent and re-billed each turn. Quote the tiers rather than a figure, because they move every quarter — roughly 128k as the commodity floor, 200k to 400k mainstream, and 1M at the frontier. Then say the thing that matters: advertised context is not usable context. Single-needle retrieval tests are close to saturated and prove very little; multi-fact benchmarks such as RULER show effective lengths well below the advertised number for most models. And the lost-in-the-middle result is that accuracy on one fixed question traces a U as you slide the relevant passage through the prompt — best at the start, second best at the end, worst in the middle, with up to about twenty points between the extremes.

So: one million tokens of context, do you still need retrieval. Yes, on three counts. Cost — you pay for every token of that prompt on every turn, so a half-million-token prompt is dollars per call against cents for a retrieved one, and caching only helps the part that never changes. Latency — prefill is compute-bound and grows with prompt length, so time to first token grows with whatever you paste, and the KV cache grows with it too, which is what actually caps batch size and concurrency. Accuracy — the fifty sentences that matter do better on their own than buried among half a million that do not. Retrieval also buys three things a big window never will: citations, per-user permissions, and freshness without resending the corpus. The mitigations are ordinary. Put the critical material at the top or immediately beside the question, rerank so the best chunk sits closest to the instruction, retrieve five to ten chunks rather than a hundred, and when a long conversation approaches the limit, compact it — summarise the old turns while keeping the system contract and the tool results, rather than truncating the oldest messages blindly.

You reach for it when

  • Someone proposes pasting the whole corpus because the window is large
  • Answers are right about the start of a document and wrong about its middle
  • Time to first token grew after you raised the number of retrieved chunks
  • A long conversation is nearing the limit and something has to be dropped

The trap

Treating a big number as a reason to stop thinking about retrieval. Advertised context is a capacity, not a guarantee: accuracy degrades before the limit and the middle of a long prompt fares worst. Quoting a single-needle demo as proof is the other half of the same mistake, because one fact in a haystack is nearly saturated while multi-fact retrieval at the same length is not. Cost and time to first token both scale with what you paste.

The math why a long prompt costs you twice

attention=O(n2d)  ·  KV/token=2nlayers​nkv​dhead​bytes  ·  70B ≈320 KB/token ⇒ 128k ≈43 GBAttention compares every token with every other, so its cost grows with the square of the prompt length. At today’s lengths the feed-forward layers still dominate the FLOP count, so time to first token grows closer to linearly with what you paste — but it does grow, and the user waits through all of it before the first word appears. The second cost is memory, and it is the one that decides your serving plan. The KV cache stores one key and one value per layer per token, so it grows linearly in sequence length and linearly in batch size. Llama 3 70B in BF16 with grouped-query attention is about 320 KB per token, so a single 128k-token conversation is roughly 43 GB of cache before you have served a second user — on an 80 GB card, that is your concurrency gone. Layer count, KV head count and cache dtype all move that figure, so it is config-specific; the formula is not.

Sweep the position, not just the length

import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")

# advertised is a capacity. Measure YOUR recall at YOUR length, at every position.
def plant(haystack, fact, frac):          # frac = where the fact sits, 0.0 to 1.0
    t = enc.encode(haystack)
    cut = int(len(t) * frac)
    return enc.decode(t[:cut]) + fact + enc.decode(t[cut:])

for frac in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):  # sweep POSITION, not just length
    p = plant(corpus, " The lock code is 4417. ", frac)
    print(frac, len(enc.encode(p)), ask(p) == "4417")
# the dip is in the middle - run this before you promise anyone 1M context

Where this bites in production

Two named results. Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle” (TACL 2024), slid one relevant document through a multi-document prompt and watched accuracy trace a U — best at the start, second best at the end, worst in the middle, with up to about twenty points between the extremes. And NVIDIA’s RULER benchmark scored models advertising 128k or more on multi-hop and aggregation tasks rather than single needles, and found effective lengths far below the advertised figure for most of them.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You have 1M context. Do you still need RAG?
Yes — on cost, on latency, and on accuracy. Every token of that prompt is billed on every turn, and prefill time grows with it, so time to first token degrades exactly as you paste more. Mid-context recall degrades too, so the relevant passage does better alone than buried. Retrieval also gives you citations, per-user permissions and freshness, none of which a wide window provides. Long context is a good fallback for a whole document, not a replacement for choosing.
What does lost in the middle change about how you build a prompt?
Position becomes a design decision. Accuracy on the same question traces a U as the relevant passage moves through the prompt, so put the critical material at the very top or immediately next to the question, and rerank so the strongest chunk lands closest to the instruction. Then retrieve fewer chunks: five to ten well-ranked beats a hundred, because every extra chunk pushes something important towards the middle.
Your agent hits the context limit on turn 30. What now?
Compact, do not truncate. Dropping the oldest messages throws away the system contract and the tool results the agent still depends on, and the failure looks like sudden amnesia. Summarise the old turns into a running state note, keep the system prompt and the most recent tool observations verbatim, and spill anything long to a scratchpad the agent can re-read on demand. Budget the window per turn so this triggers before the wall, not at it.

Say this back tomorrow

advertised context is a capacity, not a promise  ·  the middle is where recall goes
  • The window is tokens shared by prompt, retrieval, history and completion — and it is stateless
  • Tiers move every quarter: 128k floor, 200k to 400k mainstream, 1M frontier
  • 1M context does not retire RAG — cost, time to first token and the middle all still bite

  • usable context
  • lost in the middle
  • RULER
  • prefill / TTFT
  • compaction

08foundation

Prompting That Survives Review

The parts that survive a code review are the parts you can version, cache and measure.

Most of what works is unglamorous. Say who the model is and what the task is, in plain terms. Show two or three worked examples, because a demonstration pins down a format far better than a description of one. State exactly what the output should look like. Ask for step-by-step working only where the task genuinely has steps, because on a lookup or a strict format it adds delay and can talk the model out of the obvious answer. Put the parts that never change at the very top and the parts that change every request at the bottom, so the provider can charge you less for the fixed opening. Then treat the whole thing as code: version it, review it, never edit the live one, and pin the model so a quiet update on their side cannot move your numbers with nobody able to say why.

Think of a brief you hand to a contractor. The scope, the standards and two photographs of work you liked go at the front, identical on every job. The address goes at the end. You keep a copy of exactly what you sent, so when the work comes back wrong you compare briefs instead of arguing from memory. And you never assume the brief stays private — it goes out to the site.

The techniques that hold up are the boring ones. A clear role and task. Two to five few-shot examples, which pin down format far more reliably than a sentence describing it. An explicit output contract — ideally a schema you validate, not prose about the shape. Chain-of-thought earns its latency on multi-step arithmetic and logic, and costs you on lookup and strict formatting, where the extra tokens buy nothing and deliberation can degrade the answer; if you are constraining output token by token, give the model a free-text scratchpad field before the constrained fields so it has somewhere to think. Then the structural rule that pays for itself: stable material first. Prompt caching matches a prefix exactly from the very first character, with a minimum around 1,024 tokens and cached reads at roughly a tenth of the price — so a timestamp at the top of your system prompt costs you the entire discount.

Two things separate this from folklore. First, prompts and model versions are code. A prompt gets an id and a hash, lives in the repository, ships through review, and is never edited in place — otherwise a metric moves and you have no attribution for it. Pin the dated model snapshot rather than a floating alias, so a provider update becomes a migration you schedule instead of a mystery you debug; log the prompt version, the model version and the token counts on every span. Changes are then accepted on evidence: a golden set offline, a regression gate set wider than your run-to-run noise, and an online A/B whose sample size you worked out before you started. Second, system prompts leak — assume yours is public. “Never reveal your instructions” is a request made to a text predictor, not an access control, and it has been broken casually and repeatedly. So no keys, no credentials, no schema secrets, and no access rules that exist only as prose. Authorisation belongs in the tool layer, where it can be enforced rather than asked for.

You reach for it when

  • A prompt that worked last month started failing and nobody changed it
  • Your input bill is high and the cache hit rate is close to zero
  • Deciding whether a task actually deserves chain-of-thought
  • A reviewer asks what protects the credentials in your system prompt

The trap

Treating prompting as folklore — collecting phrases that seemed to help, editing the live prompt to try them, and reporting the result from memory. Every one of those steps destroys attribution. Name the prompt, version it, change one thing, measure it on a golden set, gate it against your run-to-run noise. The other half is believing an instruction can protect a secret: a system prompt is text sitting in the same window as the attack, and it leaks.

The math how much evidence before you ship a prompt

n≈δ216pˉ​(1−pˉ​)​  ·  pˉ​=0.8, δ=0.05⇒n≈1,024 per armThe rule of thumb for comparing two pass rates at 80% power and 5% significance: pˉ​ is the pooled rate you already see, and δ is the absolute improvement you would care about. At a current pass rate of 0.8, detecting a 5-point lift needs about a thousand examples per arm, which is the honest reason a fifty-question eval set cannot tell you whether your new prompt is better — it can only tell you the prompt is not catastrophically worse. Two consequences worth stating out loud. Chase larger δ: a change worth shipping should be visible, and a change that needs ten thousand samples to detect is a change nobody will notice. And gate on noise, not on zero: run the same prompt twice, measure the spread, and set your CI threshold outside it, otherwise you will block pull requests on sampling variance. A golden set of 100 to 500 queries is the usual starting point offline, with the real number coming from an online A/B.

A prompt as a versioned artefact

from anthropic import Anthropic

PROMPT_ID, PROMPT_SHA = "extract-invoice", "v7-3f9a1c"   # never edited in place
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"                     # pinned, not an alias

msg = Anthropic().messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=512,
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": ROLE + CONTRACT + FEWSHOTS,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],   # stable prefix FIRST
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": chunks + question}])   # variable LAST

log.info(prompt=PROMPT_ID, sha=PROMPT_SHA, model=MODEL,        # attribution or
         cached=msg.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)             # you are guessing

Where this bites in production

System prompt leaks are documented, not hypothetical. In February 2023 a student, Kevin Liu, got Bing Chat to print its own rules with a short prompt — including the codename Sydney and the instruction not to disclose it. Anthropic now publishes Claude’s system prompts in its release notes, which is the honest position to take. On versioning: providers ship floating aliases beside dated snapshots, and pinning the dated one is the difference between a migration you schedule and a metric that moves for no reason anyone can name.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How do you know a prompt change actually helped?
By measuring it against a versioned baseline, not by reading the output. The old and new prompts both have ids and hashes, the model snapshot is pinned so it is not a confound, and you score both on a golden set with a gate set wider than your run-to-run noise. Then an online A/B with a sample size worked out in advance — detecting a 5-point lift near an 80% pass rate needs roughly a thousand per arm, which is why a fifty-example eval proves very little.
Where does the stable part of a prompt go, and why does that matter?
At the very top, because the cache matches a prefix exactly from character zero. Providers give roughly a 90% discount on cached input reads above a minimum of about 1,024 tokens, so system prompt and few-shots go first and retrieved context and the user turn go last. One variable token above the line — a timestamp, a user id, a session counter — invalidates the whole prefix, and the symptom is a cache hit rate near zero with no error anywhere.
Your system prompt says never reveal your instructions. Is that a control?
No. It is a request to a text predictor. System prompts leak, routinely and casually, because the instruction and the attack sit in the same context window and nothing enforces one over the other. So assume yours is public: no keys, no credentials, no hidden schema, and no access rules that exist only as prose. Real authorisation lives in the tool layer, scoped per user and per action, where it is checked rather than asked for.

Say this back tomorrow

stable text first  ·  version the prompt, pin the model  ·  assume the system prompt is public
  • Role, few-shot examples and an explicit output contract carry most of the win
  • Stable material first, variable last — the cache matches the prefix from character zero
  • Prompts and model versions are code; a system prompt is not a security control

09foundation

When Not to Use an LLM

Asked explicitly, and often. The strongest answer in the room is sometimes that you would not use a model here.

A language model is a general tool with a very particular price: money per request, most of a second of waiting, and an answer that can come out differently next time you ask. Plenty of problems need none of that. If the rule is written down and never changes, write the rule. If you need an exact string or an exact record, keyword search and a database query beat a model on speed, on cost and on being right, and they show their working. If you have a table of numbers and a pile of labelled examples, a boosted-tree model still wins on that data and answers in about a millisecond. Save the model for open-ended text, where the input is messy and the answer is not a lookup. The same restraint applies to agents. If you already know the sequence of steps, write the sequence.

Like hiring a consultant to read a thermometer. They will give you an answer, usually the right one, eventually, and they will invoice you for it. The thermometer costs nothing, answers instantly, and reads the same twice. You bring in the consultant for the question nobody has written a procedure for — not for the one that already has a dial on the wall.

Route to the cheapest thing that solves the problem. A deterministic rule wins whenever the rule is stable and writable: a validation check, an identifier format, a business policy that legal signed off. Classical machine learning wins on tabular data with labels — gradient-boosted trees still outperform deep learning on typical tabular benchmarks, they train in minutes, they score in about a millisecond, and they hand you feature importances you can defend to a regulator. Plain keyword search beats embeddings on exact identifiers, SKUs, error codes and acronyms, which is the whole reason hybrid retrieval exists. A regex or a SQL query is the right answer far more often than the project name suggests. What you take on the moment a model enters the request path is a per-request cost, a p99 measured in seconds rather than milliseconds, non-determinism that makes testing harder, a prompt-injection surface, a provider dependency, and an evaluation burden that did not exist before.

An agent is wrong when the workflow is fixed and known. If you can draw the steps in advance, a chain or a plain script is cheaper, faster and testable, and it cannot loop. Every model call you add multiplies both the bill and the chance of a bad run: at a generous 95% per-step reliability, a clean eight-step run is only 0.66, which is exactly why step budgets of five to ten and hard termination conditions exist. Agents earn their place when the path genuinely depends on what is found along the way. There is a middle position worth naming, because it scores well: use the model once, offline, to bootstrap labels or to draft the rule, then serve the cheap deterministic thing in production and keep the model for the tail. And say the honest version out loud — putting a model in the path is a decision with a cost, not a default, and the engineers people want in the loop are the ones willing to say they would not use one here.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder asks for an LLM feature that a database query would answer
  • Scoping an agent for a workflow whose steps are already written down
  • Cost per request or p99 latency is the binding constraint
  • You have plenty of labelled tabular data and a clearly defined target

The trap

Reaching for a model because the project is called an AI project. The tell is a proposal with no baseline in it — no regex, no query, no classifier — and no number for what the model costs per request. Interviewers score restraint here: name the deterministic alternative, say what it would take to beat it, then justify the model on the part that is genuinely open-ended. Proposing an agent for a workflow you can already draw is the same mistake one level up.

The math the order-of-magnitude argument

tregex​∼10−5s  ·  tGBDT​∼10−3s  ·  tLLM​∼100s  ·  agent: pk, and 0.958≈0.66Five orders of magnitude separate a regex from a model call, and three separate a boosted-tree scorer from one — per request, every request. The model call is also the only one of the three that is metered, non-deterministic and dependent on somebody else’s uptime. That is the whole case for routing rather than defaulting. The second expression is the agent version of the same argument. If each step succeeds with probability p and the run needs k of them, a clean run is pk: at a generous p=0.95, eight steps gives 0.66 and twenty steps gives 0.36. Cost and latency multiply by k at the same time, so a long agent trajectory is expensive and unreliable together. That arithmetic is where step budgets of five to ten, retry caps of two to three per tool call, and hard termination conditions come from — and it is why a fixed workflow should be a chain, where k is known and each step is testable on its own.

Route to the cheapest thing that works

import re

VAT = re.compile(r"\bGB\d{9}\b")        # a VAT number is a regex, not a prompt

def route(req):
    if req.kind == "vat_check":           # deterministic rule -> no model at all
        return bool(VAT.fullmatch(req.text))
    if req.kind == "churn_risk":          # 40 tabular features, 200k labelled rows
        return gbdt.predict_proba(req.frame)[:, 1]   # ~1 ms, same answer twice
    if req.kind == "find_doc" and req.exact_phrase:
        return bm25.search(req.text)      # keyword search wins on IDs and codes
    return llm(req.text)                  # open-ended text: now the model earns it

Where this bites in production

Two named data points. Grinsztajn et al., “Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?” (NeurIPS 2022), benchmarked 45 datasets and found gradient-boosted trees ahead of tuned neural networks on medium-sized tabular problems — still the default for a table with labels. And Klarna, which said its assistant did the work of about 700 support agents in 2024, told reporters in 2025 that it had cut too far on quality and began hiring human agents back.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

When is an agent the wrong answer?
When the workflow is fixed and known. If you can draw the steps in advance, a chain or a script is cheaper, faster, testable and incapable of looping, while an agent pays a model call to rediscover the same route every run. Reliability compounds against you too: at 95% per step, eight steps is a 0.66 clean run. Agents earn their place when the path depends on what is found along the way — and even then they need a step budget and a termination condition.
A PM wants an LLM to sort support tickets into twelve categories. What do you say?
Ask what labelled history exists first. If there are tens of thousands of resolved tickets, a classifier on that data is faster, cheaper, deterministic and easier to monitor for drift, and it gives you a confidence score to route on. If there is nothing labelled, use the model to bootstrap a few thousand labels and to handle the tail, then serve the cheap classifier and keep the model behind an escalation threshold. Either way, name the baseline before you name the model.
What do you take on the moment an LLM is in the request path?
Cost, tail latency, non-determinism, an attack surface and an eval burden. You now pay per request and per token, your p99 is measured in seconds rather than milliseconds, the same input can produce different output so ordinary assertions stop working, any untrusted text in the prompt is an injection vector, and you depend on a provider’s uptime and versioning. None of that is a reason not to use one. It is the list you should be able to recite before you do.

Say this back tomorrow

the cheapest thing that answers it wins  ·  an agent is for a path you cannot draw
  • Rules, keyword search, SQL and boosted trees beat a model whenever they apply
  • A model call adds cost, seconds of tail latency, non-determinism and an eval burden
  • Agents are wrong for fixed workflows — at 95% per step, eight steps is a 0.66 clean run

CORE · 12 topics

Inside the transformer

One block, repeated. Attention lets tokens look at each other, the feed-forward lets each token think alone, and normalisation and residuals stop the whole thing falling over. Every architectural choice in this block — multi-head, RoPE, GQA, FlashAttention — exists because something cost too much memory or too much time.

You are my AI/ML interview tutor. This session covers ONE block of large language models and the AI engineer stack: Core — Inside the transformer

The topics in this block are:
1. Self-Attention: Q, K and V — Every token asks a question, every token advertises what it holds, and the answer is a weighted average of what the winners hand over
2. Why We Divide by the Square Root of d_k — Dot products get bigger as vectors get wider. A big enough score turns the softmax into a switch, and a switch has no gradient
3. Multi-Head Attention — One attention layer cut into thirty-two narrow ones. The width is divided, not duplicated, which is why heads are almost free
4. Causal Masking — Minus infinity in the upper triangle, written before the softmax runs. That one line is what makes a decoder a decoder
5. Positional Encoding & RoPE — Attention is a set operation. With no position signal, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are the same input
6. Residuals, LayerNorm & RMSNorm — Every block writes an update into a running sum instead of replacing it. That is the reason a hundred layers can be trained at all
7. The Feed-Forward Block — Attention is where tokens talk to each other. This is where each one thinks alone — and it holds two thirds of the weights
8. Decoder-Only vs Encoder-Decoder vs Encoder-Only — Three families, one difference that matters: which positions each token is allowed to look at
9. The O(n squared) Problem — Every token is compared with every other token. Double the prompt and the score matrix quadruples
10. The KV Cache: Why It Exists — Generating token 1000 would mean recomputing 999 keys and values. Keep them instead — then find room for them
11. GQA, MQA & MLA — One number in the config decides the size of your KV cache. These three are three ways of making that number smaller
12. FlashAttention — It is exact. The same numbers come out — the score matrix simply never reaches the memory it would not fit in
