10core

Self-Attention: Q, K and V

Every token asks a question, every token advertises what it holds, and the answer is a weighted average of what the winners hand over.

Every token in the sentence does three things at once. It writes down what it is looking for. It writes down what it has to offer. And it writes down what it would hand over if somebody picked it. Then every token compares its own question against every other token’s advertisement, one pair at a time, and gets a score for each. Those scores are turned into a set of shares that add up to one, so a token spends its whole attention budget across the sentence. Finally the token collects the hand-over notes of all the others, mixes them in exactly those proportions, and that blend becomes its new representation. That is the entire operation. Nothing is fetched from outside and nothing is looked up. Every token simply rewrites itself as a blend of the tokens it decided to listen to.

Like a room of people holding up two cards each. One card says what you need. The other says what you can supply. You read every supply card in the room, decide how much each one matters to your need, and take a little from each person in proportion. You leave the room still yourself, but coloured by everyone you chose to listen to.

Attention is a soft lookup. Each token’s vector is projected three times: Q=XWQ​, K=XWK​, V=XWV​. With X of shape (B,n,dmodel​) and each projection (dmodel​,dk​), you get Q, K and V of shape (B,n,dk​). Then say the expression out loud: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V. The term QK⊤ is (B,n,n) — every query dotted with every key, one score per ordered pair of positions. The softmax runs along the last axis, so each row becomes a distribution over the sequence that sums to 1. Multiplying by V gives an output of (B,n,dk​): each position is now a convex combination of every value vector. Both consequences fall out of the shapes. That (n,n) matrix is why compute is O(n2d) and naive memory is O(n2), and the divisor in the denominator is the next card.

Three separate projections rather than one is the part people skip past. If a token used its raw embedding as both query and key, its score against itself would be its own squared norm and attention would collapse towards the identity. Separate learned matrices let the question a token asks be a different object from the answer it advertises, and let the payload it hands over be different again. That asymmetry is why QK⊤ is not symmetric: the score from its to cat is not the score from cat to its. Two follow-ups sit directly behind this one. The KV cache exists because at generation time the K and V of every earlier token never change, so you store them rather than recompute them — and there is no Q cache, because the query is only ever for the token you are producing right now. And FlashAttention never materialises the (n,n) matrix at all: it tiles the computation through SRAM so the identical numbers come out in O(n) memory. Exact, not approximate, which is a question people get wrong.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining a transformer block from first principles
  • Working out why a longer context costs so much more
  • Reading attention shapes in a from-scratch PyTorch implementation
  • Someone asks what the KV cache is actually caching

The trap

Saying it lets the model focus on the important words. That is true of any weighting scheme and contains no mechanism at all. An interviewer is listening for three specific things: the expression softmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V, the fact that the score matrix is n by n so compute is quadratic in sequence length, and some account of why the denominator is there. Miss all three and the topic ends.

The math one line, then say the shapes

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V  ·  Q,K,V∈Rn×dk​  ·  QK⊤∈Rn×nRead it right to left and the mechanism is obvious. X is (n,dmodel​) for one sequence. Three learned matrices project it: Q=XWQ​, K=XWK​, V=XWV​, each W of shape (dmodel​,dk​). Then QK⊤ holds one score for every ordered pair of positions, so it is (n,n) — quadratic in sequence length, which is the entire cost story of the transformer and the reason long context is a research area rather than a config change. The softmax runs row-wise, so row i becomes a probability distribution over which positions token i will read from. Multiplying by V replaces token i with a convex combination of value vectors, giving (n,dk​) — the same shape you started with, which is exactly what lets you stack the block eighty times. Note the asymmetry: WQ​ and WK​ are different matrices, so the score from i to j is not the score from j to i.

The four lines that are the transformer

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

B, n, d_k = 1, 6, 64                       # batch, tokens, head dimension
Q, K, V = (torch.randn(B, n, d_k) for _ in range(3))

scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)           # (B, n, n) every query vs every key
scores = scores / d_k ** 0.5               # the scaling. The next card is why.
W = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)              # rows sum to 1 -> a distribution
out = W @ V                                # (B, n, d_k) same shape as the input

print(W.shape, float(W[0, 0].sum()))       # torch.Size([1, 6, 6]) 1.0
print(torch.allclose(out, F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)))   # True
# that (n, n) matrix is the cost story: build it and memory is O(n^2)

Where this bites in production

Take the shapes seriously and the memory problem is obvious. A 128k-token prompt gives a score matrix of 128,000 squared — about 16 billion entries, roughly 33 GB in BF16, for one head in one layer. Llama 3 70B has 64 query heads in each of 80 layers. Nobody has ever had that memory. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is why it runs at all: it tiles the computation through on-chip SRAM and never writes the matrix to HBM.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Say the attention expression out loud, with the shapes.
Softmax of Q times K transpose, over the square root of the head dimension, times V. With one sequence, Q, K and V are each (n,dk​); QK⊤ is (n,n), one score per ordered pair; the softmax runs along the rows so each sums to 1; multiplying by V returns (n,dk​). Saying the output shape matters, because it is the same shape as the input, and that is what lets the block be stacked.
Why three separate projections instead of using the embedding directly?
Because the question a token asks and the answer it advertises must be able to differ. With one shared vector the score of a token against itself is its own squared norm, so attention drifts towards the identity and learns nothing interesting. Separate WQ​ and WK​ also make the score matrix asymmetric, which is what lets its attend hard to cat without cat attending back. WV​ is separate again so the payload is not forced to be the address.
The score matrix is n by n. What does that actually cost at 128k tokens?
About 33 GB per head per layer if you ever materialise it. 128,000 squared is roughly 16 billion entries, two bytes each in BF16 — and a 70B model has 64 query heads across 80 layers. That is why compute is O(n2d) and why doubling context quadruples the attention work. FlashAttention avoids the memory cost by tiling and never writing the matrix out; it is exact, not an approximation.

Say this back tomorrow

query dot key, scale, softmax, weighted sum of values  ·  the score matrix is n by n
  • Every token emits a query, a key and a value from three separate learned projections
  • Softmax of QK-transpose over root d_k, times V — rows sum to one, so the output is a blend
  • The n by n score matrix is why compute is quadratic and long context is expensive

Unlocks

  • query, key, value
  • scaled dot product
  • softmax rows
  • O(n^2) cost
  • KV cache

Why We Divide by the Square Root of d_k

Dot products get bigger as vectors get wider. A big enough score turns the softmax into a switch, and a switch has no gradient.

A score is made by pairing two lists of numbers, multiplying them position by position, and adding everything up. The longer the lists, the more terms you add, so the totals spread further from zero. A head working in sixty-four directions produces scores in a much narrower band than one working in a hundred and twenty-eight. That matters because of what happens next. The step that turns scores into shares is exponential, so it exaggerates gaps. Feed it modest gaps and it hands out a sensible spread. Feed it huge gaps and the leader takes essentially everything while the rest get nothing. Once that happens the layer has nothing left to learn from: nudging a score no longer changes the shares, so no correction flows back into the weights that produced it. Dividing every score by the square root of the head width undoes the growth and keeps the gaps in the range where learning still works.

Like a microphone with the gain turned up. In a quiet room you hear every voice in proportion. Add more speakers and the total signal climbs, and past some point the preamp clips: the loudest voice becomes the only voice and everything else is silence. Turning the gain down in step with the number of speakers keeps the mix audible. That is all the divisor does.

Take q and k with independent entries of mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product q⋅k=∑i=1dk​​qi​ki​ is a sum of dk​ independent terms of variance 1, so it has mean 0 and variance dk​ — standard deviation dk​​. At dk​=64 that is 8; at dk​=128 it is about 11.3. Logits spread that wide are extreme for a softmax, which exponentiates differences: a gap of 10 is a ratio of about 22,000 to 1. The distribution collapses towards one-hot, and the softmax Jacobian is pi​(δij​−pj​), which goes to zero as any pi​ approaches 0 or 1. No gradient reaches WQ​ or WK​ and the layer stops learning. Dividing by dk​​ restores unit variance at any head size, which is why the same recipe works at dk​=64 and at dk​=128.

Work it for a real config. Llama 3 70B uses dmodel​=8192 with 64 query heads, so dk​=128 and the divisor is 128​≈11.31. Take four standardised scores, 1.3, 0.4, −0.4 and −1.3. Multiply them by 11.31 and softmax the result: the leader holds 0.99996 and the other three positions share about four parts in a hundred thousand between them. Divide by 11.31 first and the same four scores give 0.60, 0.24, 0.11 and 0.04 — a distribution the model can actually move. Two things worth adding out loud. It is a fixed constant read off the config, not a learned parameter, and most kernels fold it into the query projection so it costs nothing at runtime. And the argument generalises: anywhere an exponential meets a sum whose length you control, somebody has to divide. That is the same reasoning behind initialisation scales and behind the 1/T in sampling temperature, though the two are not the same object — one is fixed by the architecture, the other is a knob you turn at inference.

You reach for it when

  • An interviewer asks the follow-up to self-attention
  • Writing an attention kernel or a from-scratch implementation
  • Attention weights collapse onto one position and training stalls
  • Explaining why a bigger head needs no new recipe

The trap

Knowing that you divide, but not what breaks if you do not. The failure is specific and you should be able to name it in one breath: the variance of a dot product grows with dk​, so the logits spread out, so the softmax saturates towards one-hot, so its derivative p(1−p) goes to zero, so no gradient reaches the query and key projections and the layer stops learning. “It keeps the numbers stable” is not that answer.

The math the variance argument in one line

Var(q⋅k)=∑i=1dk​​Var(qi​ki​)=dk​  ·  sd=dk​​  ·  Var(dk​​q⋅k​)=1Assume the entries of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. Each product qi​ki​ then has mean 0 and variance 1, and the dot product is a sum of dk​ of them, so its variance is dk​ and its standard deviation is dk​​ — 8 at dk​=64, about 11.3 at dk​=128. Dividing by dk​​ returns it to 1 for any head size, which is the whole point: one recipe, every config. The damage shows up on the backward pass. The softmax Jacobian is ∂pi​/∂zj​=pi​(δij​−pj​), so as any pi​ approaches 0 or 1 every term collapses and the gradient through the attention weights vanishes. Worked numerically at dk​=128: the standardised scores 1.3,0.4,−0.4,−1.3 scaled up give a leader probability of 0.99996, and p(1−p) at that point is about 4×10−5. There is almost nothing left to learn from.

Watch the variance grow, then kill the gradient

import math
import torch

d_k = 128                                   # Llama 3 70B head dimension
q, k = torch.randn(4096, d_k), torch.randn(4096, d_k)
raw = (q * k).sum(-1)                       # one dot product per row
print(float(raw.std()), math.sqrt(d_k))     # ~11.3, 11.31 -> variance IS d_k

z = torch.tensor([1.3, 0.4, -0.4, -1.3])    # four standardised scores
print(torch.softmax(z * math.sqrt(d_k), -1))   # [1.0000, 0.0000, 0, 0]  dead
print(torch.softmax(z, -1))                    # [0.60, 0.24, 0.11, 0.04] alive

p = torch.softmax(z * math.sqrt(d_k), -1)
print(float((p * (1 - p)).max()))           # ~4e-05 : the gradient that is left

Where this bites in production

The 2017 paper states it in a footnote and gives exactly this argument: for large head dimensions the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients. The libraries agree with the footnote. PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention exposes a scale argument that defaults to one over the square root of the head size, and Hugging Face attention modules carry a self.scaling constant folded in before the softmax. Nobody learns this factor.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What actually breaks if you leave the division out?
The softmax saturates and the gradient dies. Dot product variance grows with dk​, so at head dimension 128 the logits have a standard deviation near 11.3; exponentiate gaps that size and one position takes essentially all the mass. The softmax derivative pi​(δij​−pj​) goes to zero at a one-hot distribution, so no signal reaches WQ​ or WK​ and the attention layer never learns which positions matter. It is a training failure, not a numerical-overflow one.
Where does the square root come from, specifically?
From the variance of a sum, not from anything about attention. A dot product of two vectors with independent unit-variance entries is a sum of dk​ terms each of variance 1, so the sum has variance dk​ and standard deviation dk​​. You divide by the standard deviation to return the scores to unit variance. That is also why it is dk​​, the per-head dimension, and never dmodel​​.
Is this the same thing as sampling temperature?
Same algebra, completely different object. Both divide logits before a softmax, but the attention divisor is a constant fixed by the head size, applied inside every layer at training and inference alike, and it exists to keep gradients alive. Temperature is a knob you set per request at generation time, applied once to the output logits, and it changes only how you sample. Calling the divisor a temperature in an interview reads as not knowing which one is learned.

Say this back tomorrow

the variance of a dot product is d_k  ·  divide by root d_k or the softmax becomes a switch
  • A dot product of d_k unit-variance terms has variance d_k, so its spread grows as root d_k
  • Large logits saturate the softmax, and a saturated softmax has a near-zero derivative
  • The divisor is a fixed constant from the config — not learned, and not a temperature

Unlocks

  • variance grows with d_k
  • softmax saturation
  • vanishing gradient
  • root d_k
  • scale default

Multi-Head Attention

One attention layer cut into thirty-two narrow ones. The width is divided, not duplicated, which is why heads are almost free.

One round of attention produces one set of weights, and one set of weights can express only one kind of relationship at a time. So the layer is cut into parallel slices. The model’s working width is divided into equal strips — divided, not copied — and each strip runs the whole attention operation on its own narrow slice. Because the strips are narrower in exactly the proportion that there are more of them, the total work barely changes. Each strip is then free to learn a different job. One ends up tracking the word immediately before. One tracks which noun a pronoun refers to. One watches that every bracket closes. When they have finished, their outputs are laid end to end to rebuild the full width, and one final learned mixing step lets the strips talk to each other.

Like a panel of specialists reading the same page. One checks the grammar, one follows who she refers to, one watches that every bracket closes. They are not each reading the whole page in full detail; the page has been split between them. At the end their notes are stapled together and one editor blends the lot into a single reading.

Take Llama 3 8B: dmodel​=4096 with h=32 heads, so dk​=dmodel​/h=128. You do not run 32 full-width attentions. You project once to (B,n,4096), reshape to (B,n,32,128) and transpose to (B,32,n,128), so each head sees a 128-dimensional slice of the stream. Scaled dot-product attention runs per head, giving (B,32,n,128). You transpose back, concatenate the heads into (B,n,4096), and apply one more learned matrix WO​ of shape (4096,4096). That last projection is not decoration — without it the heads never mix and the block is 32 independent channels. The parameter count is 4dmodel2​ whatever h is, and that is the answer to why not one big head: extra heads cost you nothing, and one head can only place one distribution over the sequence per position.

Say plainly what a head is not. It is not a separate model, it has no layers of its own, and it does not see the whole embedding — it sees dmodel​/h dimensions of it. Changing h at fixed dmodel​ changes the shape of the subspaces, not the amount of compute, so “more heads means more accuracy” is not a claim about capacity at all. There is a real trade, and it runs the other way: at fixed width, more heads means each head is thinner, and past some point a 32-dimensional head cannot represent much. Head width has stayed near 64 to 128 across a decade of models for that reason. The evidence for specialisation is worth naming, because it is what makes the argument concrete: previous-token heads, duplicate-token heads and induction heads are identifiable in trained models, and most heads can be pruned at inference with very little loss, which says a small number are doing the work. One thread to keep in reserve: grouped-query attention does not reduce the number of query heads. It reduces how many distinct K and V heads those queries share, and it exists purely to shrink the KV cache.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining a transformer block and being asked why more than one head
  • Debugging a shape mismatch in a from-scratch attention implementation
  • Choosing a head count for a model you are configuring
  • Someone claims raising the head count will raise accuracy

The trap

“More heads means more accuracy.” Heads add no capacity — dmodel​ is split across them, so 32 heads of 128 and 8 heads of 512 hold the same parameters and cost about the same. Raising h at fixed width makes every head thinner, and past a point each one is too thin to represent anything. The other half of the trap is calling a head a separate model. It is a slice of one projection.

The math split, attend, concat, project

headi​=Attention(XWQi​,XWKi​,XWVi​)  ·  MHA(X)=Concat(head1​…headh​)WO​  ·  dk​=dmodel​/hThe identity that answers the interview question is dk​=dmodel​/h. Llama 3 8B: 4096/32=128. Llama 3 70B: 8192/64=128. GPT-2 small: 768/12=64. The original transformer: 512/8=64. Head width sits between 64 and 128 across every one of them, and it is the head count that moves with the model width. Parameters do not depend on h at all: WQ​, WK​, WV​ and WO​ are each (dmodel​,dmodel​), so the block holds 4dmodel2​ weights whether you slice it into one head or sixty-four. That is what “roughly constant cost” means. So the answer to “why not one big head” is not a cost argument at all — it is representational. One head produces exactly one distribution over the sequence per position, and a sentence needs several relations resolved at once.

Split, attend, concat, project

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

B, n, d_model, h = 1, 6, 4096, 32          # Llama 3 8B config
d_k = d_model // h                          # 128 - the width is SPLIT
x = torch.randn(B, n, d_model)

Wq = torch.nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)    # ONE matrix, not 32
q = Wq(x).view(B, n, h, d_k).transpose(1, 2)          # (B, 32, n, 128)
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, q, q)         # per head, in parallel

merged = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, n, d_model)   # concat back to 4096
Wo = torch.nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)    # without W_O the heads
print(merged.shape, Wo(merged).shape)                 # never mix at all

Where this bites in production

Two named results make the specialisation claim concrete. Michel, Levy and Neubig (2019), “Are Sixteen Heads Really Better Than One?”, pruned heads from a trained transformer at test time and found many layers run on a single head with little loss. Voita et al. cut 48 encoder heads to 10 in a translation model for a 0.15 BLEU drop, and the survivors were the positional, syntactic and rare-word heads. A few heads are doing most of the work.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why not just use one big head?
Because one head can only place one distribution over the sequence per position. A pronoun that needs binding, a verb that needs its subject and a bracket that needs closing are three relations at one position, and a single softmax has to pick. Splitting dmodel​ into h subspaces buys several at once for the same parameters — 4dmodel2​ either way — so the cost argument runs in favour of splitting, not against it.
d_model 4096 with 32 heads. Give me the shapes end to end.
Head dimension 128, and everything is one reshape. Project to (B,n,4096), view as (B,n,32,128), transpose to (B,32,n,128) so attention runs per head; the output is (B,32,n,128), transposed and reshaped back to (B,n,4096). Then WO​, a (4096,4096) matrix, mixes the heads. Skip WO​ and you have 32 channels that never interact.
Is grouped-query attention just using fewer heads?
No — it keeps every query head and shares the keys and values. Llama 3 70B has 64 query heads but only 8 KV heads, so groups of eight queries read the same K and V. The query side of the computation is unchanged; what shrinks is the KV cache, by the ratio of query heads to KV heads, which is 8× here. It is a memory optimisation, not an architecture simplification, and answering it as “fewer heads” misses the entire reason it exists.

Say this back tomorrow

d_k = d_model / h  ·  the width is split, not copied, so extra heads are nearly free
  • Head dimension is the model width divided by the head count — 4096 over 32 is 128
  • Parameters are four times d_model squared whatever the head count, so cost is roughly flat
  • Heads specialise: previous-token, induction and syntactic heads are identifiable in trained models

  • d_model / h
  • head_dim 128
  • concat then W_O
  • induction heads
  • GQA is different

Causal Masking

Minus infinity in the upper triangle, written before the softmax runs. That one line is what makes a decoder a decoder.

A model that writes text must never see the answer while it is learning to predict it. But the whole sentence is sitting there in the tensor, so something has to stop each position reading ahead. The trick is to write a very large negative number into every score that points forwards, and to do it before the scores are turned into shares. The step that makes shares is exponential, and the exponential of a very large negative number is zero — not small, zero. So a position ends up giving no weight at all to anything that comes after it. The payoff is that you can train on the whole sentence in one pass. The fourth position learns to predict the fifth word, the ninth predicts the tenth, all at once, in the same forward pass. A model forced to walk the sentence one word at a time could never do that.

Like an exam sat with the paper face down. Every question on the page exists already, but the invigilator covers everything below the line you are working on. You answer question five knowing only questions one to four. The whole class sits every question at once, each with its own line drawn, and one sitting marks the lot.

After computing QK⊤/dk​​ you add a mask M where Mij​=0 for j≤i and −∞ for j>i, then softmax. Because e−∞=0, every future position gets exactly zero weight and each row still sums to 1 over the positions it is allowed to see. The order is the thing people get wrong. Masking after the softmax leaves a row that no longer sums to 1, so you have to renormalise — and you are renormalising a distribution that already mixed in the future. In practice implementations use a large finite negative value, −109 or the dtype minimum, because a fully masked row under true −∞ gives 0/0 and a NaN. Note also that the mask is not a compute saving: the upper-triangular scores are computed and then discarded, which is precisely why a fused causal kernel that never visits those blocks is worth roughly a factor of two.

Now the efficiency argument, because that is the real question. With the mask in place, one forward pass over a sequence of length n produces n training examples. The hidden state at position t attended only to positions up to t, so the logits there are a legitimate prediction of token t+1, and cross-entropy is taken at every position at once. An RNN cannot do this: its state at t depends on its state at t−1, so the sequence must be walked in order and the GPU sits mostly idle. That is the real reason decoder-only transformers won — not that the architecture is cleverer, but that it turns a sequential problem into one large matrix multiply. Note the asymmetry at inference: training is parallel over positions, generation is not, because token t+1 does not exist until you have sampled it. Same mask, opposite behaviour, and that split is where the KV cache and the whole prefill-versus-decode distinction come from. An encoder such as BERT drops the mask entirely and sees both directions, which is why it is strong at classification and cannot generate.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a decoder-only model cannot see ahead
  • A from-scratch training loop whose loss falls suspiciously fast
  • Being asked why decoder-only architectures won
  • Working out where prefill and decode actually differ

The trap

Two versions of the same error. The first is thinking the mask is applied to the weights after the softmax — it is added to the scores before, which is what makes the zeros exact and lets every row still sum to one. The second is claiming it saves compute. It does not: the full n by n score matrix is built and half of it thrown away. Only a fused kernel that never visits those blocks saves the work.

The math added before the softmax, never after

Mij​=0 if j≤i,−∞ otherwise  ·  A=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​+M)  ·  e−∞=0Read the three parts in order. M is an n by n matrix, zero on and below the diagonal and −∞ above it, added to the scores — addition rather than multiplication, because the softmax exponentiates, and adding −∞ before the exponential is what produces an exact zero instead of a small number. Every row of A then still sums to 1 over the allowed positions, so nothing has to be renormalised. Implementations substitute a large finite value such as −109 or torch.finfo(dtype).min: with a true −∞, a row that is entirely masked gives 0/0 and a NaN, which is a real failure when a padding mask and a causal mask are combined on a right-padded batch. The training payoff is one line of arithmetic. A batch of B sequences of length n yields B×n supervised predictions from a single forward pass, because position t only ever saw positions up to t.

Mask first, then softmax

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

n = 5
scores = torch.randn(n, n)                        # QK^T / sqrt(d_k), scaled
mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))  # BEFORE the softmax

A = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
print(A[0])          # tensor([1., 0., 0., 0., 0.])  exact zeros, sums to 1
print(A.sum(-1))     # tensor([1., 1., 1., 1., 1.])  no renormalising needed

# what you ship: the kernel skips the upper blocks instead of discarding them
# out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
# masking AFTER the softmax is the bug - the row no longer sums to 1

Where this bites in production

Two library facts worth carrying. PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention takes is_causal=True rather than a mask tensor, precisely so a fused kernel can skip the upper-triangular blocks instead of computing and discarding them. And in Hugging Face, attention_mask is the padding mask you pass in; the causal mask is built inside the model from the config. That distinction produces a steady stream of bug reports from people who assume passing an attention mask has made their model causal.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why does this make training so much cheaper than an RNN?
Because one forward pass over n tokens gives you n training examples. With the mask in place, position t has attended only to positions up to t, so its logits are a legitimate prediction of token t+1 and the loss is taken at every position simultaneously. An RNN’s state at t depends on its state at t−1, so it must be walked in order and the hardware idles. That parallelism, not the attention operation itself, is why decoder-only models won.
Your training loss falls to almost nothing in the first hundred steps. What do you check?
The mask, before anything else. A loss that good means the model is reading the answer, and the usual cause is a mask that is off by one on the diagonal, applied after the softmax, or silently dropped when a custom attention path is taken. Check that position t’s attention row is exactly zero beyond t, and check the label shift: the target at t must be the token at t+1.
Is the mask applied before or after the softmax, and does it save compute?
Before, and no it does not. The mask is added to the scores so that the exponential drives those entries to exactly zero and each row still sums to one; applying it afterwards leaves an unnormalised row built from information the model should not have had. As for cost, the full n by n matrix is still computed and half of it discarded. The saving only arrives with a fused causal kernel that never visits those blocks at all.

minus infinity above the diagonal, added before the softmax  ·  n predictions from one pass

Positional Encoding & RoPE

Attention is a set operation. With no position signal, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are the same input.

Strip out the positions and attention has no idea what order anything arrived in. It compares every token with every other token and adds up the results, and addition does not care about order. Shuffle the words and the same set of comparisons happens, so a model with no position signal reads a sentence about a dog biting a man exactly as it reads one about a man biting a dog. Something has to put the order back. The first models added a fixed wave pattern to each token, one that varies with how far along the token sits. The next generation learned a separate vector for every slot instead. The method almost everything uses now takes a different route: rather than adding anything, it rotates each token’s question and each token’s advertisement by an angle that grows with position. Rotate two of them by different amounts and the angle left between them depends only on the gap.

Think of two clock hands. Turn one to the hour a message was sent and the other to the hour the reply came back. Look only at the angle between them and neither hand tells you the absolute time — and that angle is the same whether the pair sat at two and five o’clock or at nine and midnight. What survives the rotation is the gap.

Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: permute the input rows and the output rows permute with them, values unchanged. Position has to be injected. Sinusoidal encodings (2017) add sin(pos/100002i/d) on even indices and cosine on odd ones to the input embeddings — fixed, no parameters. Learned absolute embeddings (BERT, GPT-2) are a lookup table of shape (max positions, dmodel​) added at the input; they train well and cannot produce a row that was never trained, so the window is hard-capped. RoPE, which Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma all use, does neither. It takes the query and key vectors, splits each into dk​/2 two-dimensional pairs, and rotates pair i at position m by angle mθi​ with θi​=10000−2i/dk​. Because rotations compose, the dot product of a query at m with a key at n depends only on m−n. Absolute rotation in, relative distance out, applied inside every layer rather than once at the input.

The distinction people fumble is what RoPE touches and when. A learned absolute embedding is added to the token vector once, at the input, before layer one. RoPE rotates the query and key vectors inside every attention layer, and it never touches the value vectors at all — so RoPE carries no positional information into the payload, it only shapes which positions attend to which. That is also why RoPE hands you a lever a lookup table cannot: the angle is a function with a base in it, so you can rescale it. Position interpolation squeezes the position indices so that 32k positions land inside the range the model saw at 8k. NTK-aware scaling and YaRN adjust the base per frequency band rather than uniformly, leaving the fast-rotating dimensions intact so local structure survives. Llama 3 raised the base itself from 10,000 to 500,000. All of these need a short continued-pretraining run and an evaluation at length, because advertised context is not usable context — that is the long-context card, and it is the follow-up you should expect here. ALiBi takes a third route entirely: no rotation, just a linear distance penalty added straight to the scores.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a transformer needs positions at all
  • Reading rope_theta and rope_scaling in a model config file
  • Being asked how a model trained at 8k serves 128k
  • Comparing RoPE, ALiBi and learned absolute positions

The trap

Confusing RoPE with a learned absolute embedding. A learned embedding is a lookup table added to the token vector once, at the input. RoPE rotates the query and key vectors inside every attention layer, and never touches the values. The consequence is what matters: a lookup table cannot produce a row it never trained, so the window is hard-capped, whereas RoPE’s angle is a function you can rescale — which is why every long-context extension trick is a RoPE trick.

The math absolute rotation in, relative distance out

PE(pos,2i)=sin(100002i/dpos​)  ·  RoPE: ⟨Rm​q,Rn​k⟩=⟨Rm−n​q,k⟩The second identity is the whole of RoPE. Rm​ is a block-diagonal rotation that turns the i-th two-dimensional pair of a vector by mθi​, with θi​=10000−2i/dk​ — early pairs rotate fast, late pairs rotate slowly, so one encoding covers short and long ranges at once. Rotations are orthogonal and they compose, so Rm⊤​Rn​=Rn−m​, and the score between a query at m and a key at n collapses to a function of m−n alone. Absolute positions go in, relative distance comes out, and no parameters are added anywhere. Two consequences to keep ready. The rotation is applied to Q and K only, never V, so nothing positional rides in the payload. And the base 10,000 is a config constant: raise it and every angle turns more slowly, which is the crudest form of context extension — Llama 3 ships 500,000.

RoPE in eight lines, and the relative-distance property

import torch

def rope(x, pos, base=500000.0):        # Llama 3 uses base 5e5, Llama 2 1e4
    d = x.shape[-1]
    theta = base ** (-torch.arange(0, d, 2).float() / d)   # one angle per pair
    a = pos[:, None] * theta[None, :]                      # (n, d_k/2)
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]                    # the 2-D pairs
    return torch.stack([x1 * a.cos() - x2 * a.sin(),
                        x1 * a.sin() + x2 * a.cos()], -1).flatten(-2)

q, k = torch.randn(1, 64), torch.randn(1, 64)
for m, n in [(2, 5), (200, 203)]:       # same gap of 3, very different places
    qm = rope(q, torch.tensor([m]))
    kn = rope(k, torch.tensor([n]))
    print(m, n, round(float(qm @ kn.T), 4))   # identical: only m - n matters

Where this bites in production

Open a real config file and it is all there. Llama 3 8B ships rope_theta: 500000.0 with max_position_embeddings: 8192. Llama 3.1 keeps that base and adds a rope_scaling block — rope_type: llama3, factor: 8.0, original_max_position_embeddings: 8192 — to reach 131,072 tokens from a model trained at 8k. Llama 2 used rope_theta: 10000.0, the original RoFormer value. The base is a number you can read, and raising it is what stretched the window.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why does a transformer need positional information at all?
Because attention is permutation-equivariant. Every query is dotted with every key and the results are summed, and neither operation depends on order — permute the input and you get the same outputs, permuted. Without a position signal, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are literally the same input to the layer. Position is injected either into the embeddings, into the query and key rotations, or straight into the scores.
RoPE versus a learned absolute embedding — what is actually different?
What is touched, when, and whether it can be extended. A learned absolute embedding is a lookup table added to the token vector once at the input; RoPE rotates the query and key vectors inside every attention layer and leaves the values alone. Because rotations compose, RoPE scores depend only on the distance between positions. And because the angle is a function with a base, you can rescale it — a lookup table simply has no row for position 100,000.
How do you take a model trained at 8k out to 128k?
Rescale the RoPE angles, then continue pretraining, then evaluate at length. Position interpolation compresses the indices into the trained range; NTK-aware scaling and YaRN adjust the base per frequency band so the fast dimensions keep local detail. None of them is free — you need a short continued-pretraining run on long documents, and you must test retrieval across the whole window, because advertised context is not usable context. That is a card of its own.

attention is order-blind  ·  RoPE rotates Q and K so the score depends only on the gap
  • Without positions, attention is permutation-equivariant — a sentence is just a bag of tokens
  • RoPE rotates query and key inside every layer; learned absolute adds a vector once at the input
  • Rotations compose, so the score between positions m and n depends only on m minus n

  • rope_theta 500000

Residuals, LayerNorm & RMSNorm

Every block writes an update into a running sum instead of replacing it. That is the reason a hundred layers can be trained at all.

Picture one wide lane of numbers running from the bottom of the model to the top. Each block reads the lane, works out a small correction, and adds that correction back in. Nothing overwrites the lane. That single choice is why a very deep stack trains at all: on the way back down, the correction signal has an unbroken path from the top to the bottom, so the lowest layers still get told what to change. Alongside it, each block rescales what it reads before working on it, so the numbers arriving at the next operation always sit in the same range whatever the layer below happened to produce. Older models rescaled in two steps, first shifting everything so it averaged out to nothing and then dividing by the spread. Modern ones skip the shifting and simply divide by the typical size. Fewer operations, and in practice the models train just as well.

Like a long relay of editors working on one manuscript. Nobody rewrites the book. Each editor reads it, pencils a set of changes in the margin, and hands the same manuscript on. If one editor has a bad day the book survives with a few odd notes. If each produced a fresh rewrite from scratch, the original would be unrecognisable by the tenth desk.

The residual stream is the object to describe. Each sublayer computes x←x+f(Norm(x)), so a block writes an update into a running sum rather than transforming it. Two things follow. Forward, every layer reads and writes the same dmodel​-wide space, which is what lets you stack 32 or 80 identically shaped blocks. Backward, the derivative of x+f(x) with respect to x is 1+f′(x), so a path of gradient exactly 1 runs from the loss to layer one; that identity term is what stops the product of Jacobians vanishing across depth. On normalisation: LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation across the feature axis, then applies a learned gain and bias. It is computed per token, not per batch, which is why it survives variable sequence lengths where BatchNorm does not. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the bias — divide by the root mean square, multiply by a learned gain, done.

Pre-norm versus post-norm is the follow-up. The 2017 paper is post-norm, x←Norm(x+f(x)), with the normalisation on the outside — so the residual path itself passes through a LayerNorm at every layer and the clean identity route to the input is broken. That trains at six layers with a learning-rate warmup and becomes unstable past roughly twelve to twenty without careful tuning. Pre-norm moves the normaliser inside the branch, x←x+f(Norm(x)), leaving the stream untouched all the way down; deep stacks then train without warmup and tolerate larger learning rates, which is why every modern decoder is pre-norm. The cost is a slow drift — the residual stream grows in magnitude with depth — so a final norm before the output head is mandatory, not optional. RMSNorm then trims the arithmetic: no mean, no bias, measurably faster, with no quality loss anyone has been able to demonstrate, which is why Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma all ship it. Two details that show experience: the norm gain is one of the few parameter groups people exclude from weight decay, and the norm itself is computed in fp32 even in a bf16 model, because the variance of a bf16 sum is where silent NaNs are born.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining how an eighty-layer stack is trainable at all
  • Reading a config and seeing RMSNorm where you expected LayerNorm
  • A training run diverges partway through and you are asked where to look
  • Someone describes normalisation as making training stable

The trap

Describing normalisation as “it makes training stable” with no statement of what quantity is held steady. Name it: LayerNorm fixes the mean and variance of the activations across the feature axis of every token, so the next matrix multiply gets a known scale whatever the layer below produced. RMSNorm fixes only the root mean square. And do not fold the residual into that sentence — it is an identity term in the derivative, not a normalisation trick.

The math pre-norm, and the two normalisers

x←x+f(Norm(x))  ·  LN(x)=γ⊙σ2+ϵ​x−μ​+β  ·  RMS(x)=γ⊙d1​∑i​xi2​+ϵ​x​The first line is the pre-norm block, and the plus sign is the important character in it: ∂(x+f(x))/∂x=1+f′(x), so a gradient path of exactly 1 runs from the loss to the first layer however deep the stack. Post-norm is Norm(x+f(x)) — the same components with the brackets moved — which puts a normaliser on the residual path itself, and that is why deep post-norm stacks need a warmup schedule. LayerNorm normalises over the feature axis of a single token: μ and σ2 are computed across dmodel​, never across the batch, which is what makes it independent of batch size and of sequence length. RMSNorm keeps the division and drops everything else — no μ, no β — so you save d subtractions and one parameter vector per norm. In both, ϵ is typically 10−5 or 10−6 and it lives inside the square root, not outside it.

Pre-norm, and RMSNorm by hand

import torch

class Block(torch.nn.Module):              # pre-norm: the modern arrangement
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))   # x + ..., never x = self.attn(...)
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))    # the stream is added to, not replaced
        return x

def rms_norm(x, g, eps=1e-5):              # LayerNorm minus the mean-centring
    r = x.float().pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True).add(eps).rsqrt()
    return (x.float() * r).type_as(x) * g  # fp32 inside, cast back after

x = torch.randn(4096) * 12                 # any scale going in
print(float(rms_norm(x, torch.ones(4096)).pow(2).mean().sqrt()))   # 1.0

Where this bites in production

Read a Llama config and it is all visible: RMSNorm with rms_norm_eps: 1e-5, two per block, plus a final one before the output head. The switch is dateable. The 2017 transformer was post-norm with a learning-rate warmup that was not optional; GPT-2 moved the normaliser inside the residual branch and added that final norm; Xiong et al. (2020) then showed post-norm gradients grow with depth at initialisation, which is what the warmup had quietly been compensating for.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why can a hundred-layer transformer be trained at all?
Because of the addition, not the attention. Each block computes x+f(x), so the derivative carries an identity term, 1+f′(x), and a gradient path of exactly 1 runs from the loss all the way to layer one. Without it you multiply a hundred Jacobians together and the signal reaching the bottom vanishes. The residual stream is also why every block has the same shape, which is what makes the stack repeatable.
Pre-norm versus post-norm — why did pre-norm win?
Because post-norm puts a normaliser on the residual path and breaks the clean gradient route. Post-norm is Norm(x+f(x)); pre-norm is x+f(Norm(x)), so the stream itself is never touched. Post-norm needs a learning-rate warmup and gets unstable past a dozen or so layers; pre-norm trains deep stacks without one. The price is that the stream grows in magnitude with depth, so a final norm before the output head is mandatory.
RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction. Why is that safe, and what does it buy?
Because the re-centring was doing almost nothing; the re-scaling was doing the work. RMSNorm divides by the root mean square and applies a learned gain, with no mean and no bias term, so you lose d subtractions and one parameter vector per norm — and there are two norms in every block of every layer. It measures faster with no quality loss anyone has demonstrated, which is why Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma all use it.

Say this back tomorrow

every block adds into the stream, never replaces it  ·  norm inside the branch, not on the path
  • The residual is an identity term in the derivative, giving a gradient path of 1 down to layer one
  • Pre-norm keeps the residual path clean; post-norm normalises it and needs a warmup
  • RMSNorm is LayerNorm without the mean and the bias — fewer operations, same behaviour

Unlocks

  • residual stream
  • pre-norm
  • RMSNorm
  • gradient path of 1
  • final norm

The Feed-Forward Block

Attention is where tokens talk to each other. This is where each one thinks alone — and it holds two thirds of the weights.

Attention is the only place in a transformer where tokens see each other. Everything else that happens to a token happens to it alone, and this block is that everything else. One token’s vector arrives, gets widened out to roughly four times its size, passes through a switch that lets some directions through and flattens others, and is then squeezed back down to the width it came in at. Every position gets the same treatment from the same weights, and no position learns a single thing about its neighbours here. It looks like the dull half of the block. It is also where most of the model sits: about two of every three numbers in a transformer layer live in this one step, nowhere near attention. Newer models add a second wide projection that acts as a volume control on the first, then narrow both so the count comes out the same.

Like a lone reader at a very large desk. The meeting is over and everyone has heard what everyone else had to say. Now each person goes back to their own desk, spreads the notes across a surface four times wider than they need, crosses out almost all of it, and writes one tighter paragraph. Nobody speaks. And the desk, it turns out, is where the filing cabinet lives.

The block is FFN(x)=W2​ϕ(W1​x), applied at every position independently with the same weights — a per-token MLP with no mixing across the sequence at all. Classically dff​=4dmodel​, so W1​ is (d,4d) and W2​ is (4d,d): 8d2 parameters against attention’s 4d2 for WQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​. Eight over twelve is where two thirds comes from. Modern models use a gated variant, SwiGLU: (SiLU(xWgate​)⊙xWup​)Wdown​, where one branch multiplies the other element-wise and acts as a learned gate. That is three matrices, not two — 12d2 at the same width, half as much again — so you shrink the hidden dimension by a third to get back to 8d2, giving dff​=38​dmodel​. Llama 2 7B is exactly that: dmodel​=4096 and dff​=11008, which is 38​×4096=10923 rounded up to a multiple of 256.

Two things this block is not. It is not where tokens interact — nothing in it looks sideways, which is why it parallelises perfectly and why it is the part replaced wholesale in a mixture-of-experts model, one expert per feed-forward. And it is not merely a reshaping of what attention found. Geva et al. (2021) showed the first matrix behaves like a bank of keys: each row fires on a recognisable input pattern, and the matching column of the second matrix is a value that promotes a distribution over the vocabulary. Meng et al. (2022) took that further and changed a specific fact in GPT-2 with a rank-one edit to a single down projection. So when an interviewer asks where the knowledge lives, the defensible answer is the feed-forward layers, with attention as the routing that decides which memories get queried. It also explains the shape of a LoRA config: the standard target list is q,k,v,o plus gate,up,down, and leaving the last three off means leaving two thirds of the model untouched.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining a transformer block past the attention half
  • Reading intermediate_size in a config and checking the ratio
  • Being asked where a model actually stores what it knows
  • Costing a LoRA run and choosing which modules to target

The trap

Assuming attention is where the knowledge lives. Attention moves information between positions — it is routing. The feed-forward layers are two thirds of the parameters, and the evidence says they behave like key-value memories: rows of the first matrix fire on specific input patterns, columns of the second promote specific vocabulary. Model editing changes a fact with a rank-one edit to one down projection. Nobody edits a fact by touching WQ​.

The math two matrices, or three and a gate

FFN(x)=W2​ϕ(W1​x)  ·  SwiGLU(x)=(SiLU(xWgate​)⊙xWup​)Wdown​  ·  dff​=38​dmodel​Do the accounting in units of d2 and the whole card is four numbers. Attention holds WQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​, each (d,d), so 4d2. An ungated feed-forward at dff​=4d holds W1​ at (d,4d) and W2​ at (4d,d), so 8d2. Twelve in total, eight of them here: two thirds, and it is exact rather than a rule of thumb. Gating adds a third (d,dff​) matrix, so keeping dff​=4d would cost 12d2 and change the model’s size for reasons that have nothing to do with the idea being tested. Multiply the width by 32​ instead: dff​=38​dmodel​, three matrices, 8d2 again. Llama 2 7B: 38​×4096=10923, rounded up to 11008 so the matrices tile on the hardware, giving 135.3M feed-forward weights against 67.1M of attention per layer — 66.8%. Llama 3 8B ignored the rule, took dff​=3.5d, and combined it with grouped-query attention, which shrinks the other half: the split there is 176.2M against 41.9M, or 81%.

SwiGLU, and the parameter count

from torch import nn

d_model, d_ff = 4096, 11008     # Llama 2 7B: 8/3 of 4096, rounded to 256s

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):        # three matrices where an ungated MLP has two
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.up   = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.down = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):       # x is (B, n, 4096) - every token, alone
        return self.down(nn.functional.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x))

ffn, attn = sum(p.numel() for p in SwiGLU().parameters()), 4 * d_model ** 2
print(ffn / 1e6, attn / 1e6, round(ffn / (ffn + attn), 3))  # 135.27 67.11 0.668

Where this bites in production

Open config.json for Llama 2 7B: hidden_size: 4096, intermediate_size: 11008. That 11008 is 38​×4096 rounded up to a multiple of 256, exactly the correction the SwiGLU paper (Shazeer, 2020) prescribes so a gated block matches an ungated 4d one. Llama 3 8B then broke the rule — intermediate_size: 14336, or 3.5d — and spent the extra on the feed-forward side while grouped-query attention was shrinking the other side.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is the hidden size 11008 and not 16384?
Because gating adds a third matrix, so you shrink the width by a third to keep the parameter count. An ungated block at 4d holds 8d2. SwiGLU has gate, up and down, so at 4d it would hold 12d2; scaling the hidden width by 32​ brings it back. For d=4096 that is 38​×4096=10923, rounded up to 11008 so the matrices tile cleanly. Llama 3 later chose 14336 and simply paid for it.
Where do the parameters actually sit in a transformer block?
Roughly two thirds in the feed-forward, one third in attention. With multi-head attention and dff​=4d it is exactly that: 8d2 against 4d2. Llama 2 7B per layer is 135.3M feed-forward against 67.1M attention. With grouped-query attention the split moves further — Llama 3 8B is 176.2M against 41.9M, so 81% — because GQA shrinks the attention half and nothing shrinks this one.
Does the feed-forward block do anything across tokens?
No, and that is the division of labour. The same weights are applied at each position independently, so it is a per-token MLP: shuffle the sequence and the outputs shuffle with it. Attention is the only operation in the block that moves information between positions. It is also why this half batches so cleanly, and why mixture-of-experts replaces exactly this block and never attention.

Say this back tomorrow

attention mixes tokens, the feed-forward thinks alone  ·  8 d squared here against 4 d squared there
  • Widen to about four times the model width, apply a non-linearity, project back — per token, no mixing
  • Two thirds of a block’s parameters live here, and gating makes the share larger still
  • Gating adds a third matrix, so the hidden width drops to 8/3 of the model width to match the count

Unlocks

  • 4x expansion
  • SwiGLU gate
  • 8/3 d_model
  • key-value memories
  • intermediate_size

Decoder-Only vs Encoder-Decoder vs Encoder-Only

Three families, one difference that matters: which positions each token is allowed to look at.

Three shapes, and the only real difference is who is allowed to look at whom. In the first, every token sees the whole passage in both directions. That is excellent for judging a piece of text and useless for writing one, because a model that can see ahead cannot be asked to guess what comes next. In the second, one stack reads the input with that full view while a separate stack writes the output one token at a time, glancing back at the first whenever it needs to. That suits work with a clear before and after: this language into that one, this document into a summary. The third keeps only the writing stack. Everything is one stream, each token may read what came before it and nothing after, and the input and the output are just earlier and later parts of that same stream. The third is what nearly every model you use today is.

Think of three ways to run a room. In the first, everyone reads the finished document and comments on it. In the second, one group reads the source aloud while a second group writes the translation line by line, glancing back whenever they need to. In the third there is one group and one growing page, and each person may read only what is already written above their own line.

Encoder-only, BERT and its descendants: no causal mask, so every token attends in both directions, trained by corrupting about 15% of tokens and predicting them. The output is one contextual vector per token — classification, tagging, embeddings, cross-encoder reranking — and it cannot generate left to right. Encoder-decoder, T5 and Whisper: a bidirectional encoder over the source, a causal decoder over the target, and cross-attention from decoder to encoder. It fits transduction, where the input and the output are separate objects. Decoder-only, GPT and Llama and Claude: one stack, one causal mask, next-token prediction over everything. The masking is the architecture — the three differ mainly in which entries of QK⊤ are allowed to survive. And the reason the third won is not that its block is better. It is that a causal loss is taken at every one of n positions, while masked language modelling only supervises the 15% you corrupted.

Give the three reasons in order. First, training signal density: one pass over n tokens yields n supervised predictions under a causal mask, against roughly 0.15n for BERT-style masking, so you extract several times more learning per token of data and per unit of compute. Second, one stack is simpler to scale: no cross-attention, no encoder and decoder widths to balance, no second objective, one set of shapes to shard across GPUs and one KV cache to manage at serving time. Third, in-context learning falls out of the objective for free — the pretraining corpus is full of question-and-answer pairs, translations and worked examples, so a model trained to continue documents is one you steer with a prompt rather than with a task-specific head. Two honesty points that score well in the room. Raffel et al.’s T5 study compared these families under matched conditions and found encoder-decoder ahead on their benchmarks, so this was never a pure quality argument. And encoder-only did not die — it moved into your retrieval path, where every embedding model and every cross-encoder reranker is still a BERT-family encoder.

You reach for it when

  • Being asked to compare BERT, T5 and GPT in one answer
  • Choosing a model family for a high-volume classification job
  • Explaining why the same block can be an encoder or a decoder
  • Picking the embedding and reranker models for a RAG stack

The trap

Reciting the task mapping — BERT understands, GPT generates, T5 does both — and stopping there. That is a table, not an explanation, and the follow-up is always “so why did decoder-only win?” The answer is masking and training efficiency: one causal pass supervises all n positions, masked language modelling supervises about 15% of them, and a single stack with no cross-attention is far easier to scale and to serve.

The math the mask is the architecture

causal: Mij​=−∞ for j>i  ·  bidirectional: M=0  ·  supervised positions per sequence: n against 0.15nEverything on this card is one matrix M added to the scores before the softmax. Set M=0 everywhere and you have an encoder: position i attends to all n positions, in both directions, and its output vector contains information from the future. Set Mij​=−∞ for j>i and you have a decoder: position i is a legitimate prediction of token i+1. Split the sequence into a source of length s and a target, allow every position to see the source and apply the causal rule only within the target, and you have the prefix pattern that an encoder-decoder computes across its two stacks. The efficiency argument is arithmetic on the same object. A causal pass over n tokens produces a loss term at each of the n positions. BERT-style masked language modelling corrupts about 15% of tokens and takes a loss only there, so a sequence of 512 tokens yields roughly 77 supervised predictions rather than 512 — the same forward pass, most of it unsupervised. That is why decoder-only models extract more from the same corpus and the same GPU hours.

The three masks, in three lines

import torch

n = 4
full   = torch.zeros(n, n)                                 # encoder-only: BERT
causal = torch.triu(torch.full((n, n), float("-inf")), 1)  # decoder-only: GPT
prefix = causal.clone()
prefix[:, :2] = 0                       # enc-dec: the source is always visible

for name, m in [("encoder", full), ("decoder", causal), ("prefix", prefix)]:
    print(name, int((m == 0).sum()))    # encoder 16   decoder 10   prefix 11

# the mask is only half the story. the other half is where the loss is taken:
# causal LM supervises all n positions, MLM only the ~15% it corrupted.

Where this bites in production

Look at what a production RAG service actually loads. The generator is decoder-only. The embedding model and the reranker are encoder-only — BGE, E5 and Cohere Rerank are all BERT-family encoders, and ModernBERT (December 2024) is a fresh one built for exactly that slot with an 8,192-token window. Whisper is encoder-decoder: audio frames in, text out. Three architectures, one product, and the decoder-only model is only one of them.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why did decoder-only win?
Denser training signal, one stack to scale, and in-context learning for free. Under a causal mask every one of n positions is a supervised prediction, where masked language modelling supervises about 15% of them — several times more learning from the same tokens and the same GPU hours. One stack means no cross-attention and no second objective to balance. And because pretraining is next-token prediction over documents that already contain examples, prompting works without a task-specific head.
Mechanically, why can BERT not generate text?
Because it has no causal mask, so every position’s representation already contains the future. Ask it to predict token t+1 and its vector at position t was built by attending to positions t+1 onwards, which is the answer. You can bolt on iterative mask-filling, but it is not left-to-right generation and the training objective never rewarded coherent continuation. Generation needs the triangle.
You are classifying 200-token support tickets at 5,000 requests a second. Do you use an LLM?
No — fine-tune an encoder. A BERT-sized encoder is one forward pass over 200 tokens with no decoding loop, runs on CPU or a small GPU, and on a fixed label set with a few thousand labelled examples it will usually beat a prompted LLM on both accuracy and cost by orders of magnitude. Decoder-only is the right tool when the output is open-ended text, not when it is one of eight labels.

Say this back tomorrow

the mask is the architecture  ·  causal supervises every position, MLM about fifteen percent
  • Encoder-only sees both directions, encoder-decoder splits source and target, decoder-only is one causal stack
  • Decoder-only won on training efficiency and scaling simplicity, not on architecture quality
  • Encoder-only models are still in your stack — every embedding model and reranker is one

Unlocks

  • bidirectional
  • cross-attention
  • causal LM
  • MLM 15%
  • in-context learning

The O(n squared) Problem

Every token is compared with every other token. Double the prompt and the score matrix quadruples.

Attention works by comparing every token with every other token. Ten tokens means a hundred comparisons. A thousand tokens means a million. Whatever you feed it, the number of comparisons is the length multiplied by itself, so doubling the prompt does not double the work, it quadruples it. At a hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens that table of comparisons holds about sixteen billion entries, and there is one such table for every head in every layer. This is also why a long prompt is expensive in a way that a long answer is not. Reading the prompt is one enormous pass over the whole table. Writing the reply adds a single row at a time. So the cost you actually feel is the wait before the first word appears, and it grows faster than the prompt does.

Like introducing everyone at a party. Ten guests and you make forty-five introductions. Double it to twenty guests and you do not make ninety, you make a hundred and ninety. The room did not get twice as hard to host, it got four times as hard. At ten guests nobody notices. At a thousand, the party is the introductions.

Attention is quadratic in sequence length at fixed model size — that distinction is the whole question. QK⊤ is (n,n), so compute is O(n2d) per head per layer and naive memory is O(n2). At n=128,000 the score matrix holds about 1.6×1010 entries, roughly 33 GB in BF16, for one head in one layer. Everything else in the model — the projections, the feed-forward — is O(nd2), linear in n. So attention only takes over once n is comparable to d. For Llama 3 70B with dmodel​=8192 the crossover is around 52k tokens: at an 8k prompt attention is about 13% of prefill FLOPs, at 128k it is 71%, at 1M it is 95%. And it lands on prefill, which processes the whole prompt in one pass. Decode with a KV cache attends over n keys per new token, so it is linear per token and bandwidth-bound instead.

Four escape routes, and only one of them is everywhere. Sparse attention (Longformer, BigBird) keeps a local band plus a handful of global tokens for O(n), at the cost of being an approximation with awkward kernels. Sliding-window attention caps how far back any token may look — Mistral 7B shipped a 4,096-token window, and Gemma 2 alternates local and global layers so some layers still see everything. Linear attention and state-space models (Performer, Mamba, RWKV) drop the softmax or replace attention outright for O(n) compute, and are genuinely different models rather than a drop-in swap. FlashAttention changes nothing about the maths at all: it is exact, compute stays O(n2d), and it removes only the O(n2) memory by never writing the score matrix out. That is the one that shipped, and it is two cards on. Be able to say which of these four is exact and which are approximations, because that is the discriminating half of the question. One more thing worth saying out loud: quadratic attention is not what makes a 70B cost more than an 8B. Parameters and sequence length are separate axes.

You reach for it when

  • Being asked why long context costs so much
  • Estimating time to first token for a very long prompt
  • Choosing between a longer window and a retrieval step
  • Someone says attention is quadratic and stops there

The trap

Saying attention is quadratic without saying quadratic in what. It is quadratic in sequence length at fixed model size, because the score matrix is (n,n). It is not quadratic in parameters, and it is not why a 70B costs more than an 8B. The second half of the trap is forgetting where it lands: prefill builds the whole (n,n) matrix at once, while decode over a KV cache does O(n) work per token.

The math quadratic in n, linear in everything else

QK⊤∈Rn×n  ·  compute O(n2d), naive memory O(n2)  ·  the rest of the model is O(nd2)Two terms, and the interview lives in their ratio. Attention costs O(n2d) per layer — QK⊤ and then the multiply by V, each about 2n2d FLOPs. Everything else costs O(nd2): the four attention projections and the three feed-forward matrices are all (n,d) times (d,⋅), linear in n. Divide one by the other and the sequence length only matters relative to the model width: attention takes over when n is of the order of d. Put Llama 3 70B in: dmodel​=8192, 80 layers, 68.4B parameters in the blocks. The linear term is 2×68.4B×n FLOPs; the attention term is 80×4×n2×8192. They are equal at n≈52,200. At n=8,192 prefill is 1.1 PFLOPs linear against 0.2 attention; at n=131,072 it is 17.9 against 45.0. And the raw object: 128,0002=1.6×1010 entries, 33 GB in BF16, per head, per layer — which is the number that made FlashAttention necessary rather than merely nice.

Where the crossover actually is

d_model, layers = 8192, 80                  # Llama 3 70B, 68.45B block params

def prefill_pflops(n):
    linear = 2 * 68.45e9 * n                # projections + feed-forward: O(n d^2)
    attn   = layers * 4 * n * n * d_model   # QK^T and then PV:          O(n^2 d)
    return linear / 1e15, attn / 1e15

for n in (8_192, 32_768, 131_072):
    lin, att = prefill_pflops(n)
    print(n, round(lin, 1), round(att, 1), f"{att / (lin + att):.0%}")
# 8192 1.1 0.2 14%    32768 4.5 2.8 39%    131072 17.9 45.0 72%

print(128_000 ** 2 / 1e9)          # 16.4 billion entries in the score matrix
print(128_000 ** 2 * 2 / 1e9)      # 32.8 GB in BF16, for ONE head in ONE layer

Where this bites in production

This is why serving stacks have a chunked-prefill setting. One 128k prompt is a single enormous compute-bound pass, and while it runs, every other request on that GPU stops producing tokens — one user’s long document becomes everyone else’s stutter. vLLM splits long prefills into chunks and interleaves them with decode steps (enable_chunked_prefill) for exactly that reason. It is also why prompt caching exists: a cached prefix skips the quadratic pass entirely, and providers discount those tokens by around 90%.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Quadratic in what, exactly?
In sequence length, at fixed model size. QK⊤ produces one score per ordered pair of positions, so the matrix is (n,n): compute O(n2d), naive memory O(n2). It is not quadratic in parameters, and doubling the model does not quadruple anything. The rest of the network is O(nd2), so attention only dominates once n approaches dmodel​ — about 52k tokens for a model 8192 wide.
Your prompt goes from 8k to 128k. What happens to time to first token, and to time per output token?
Time to first token grows about fifty-fold for sixteen times the tokens; time per output token barely moves. Prefill has a linear term that grows 16× and a quadratic term that grows 256×, and for Llama 3 70B the total goes from roughly 1.3 to 63 PFLOPs. Decode is different: each new token attends over a longer cache, so per-token cost grows linearly and slowly, and it is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. Long prompts hurt latency at the front, not throughout.
Of the long-context tricks, which one is exact?
FlashAttention, and only FlashAttention. Sparse attention, sliding windows and linear attention all change which pairs are compared or how they are combined, so they compute a different function and trade quality for cost. FlashAttention computes the identical softmax over the identical scores in a different order, so the output matches; what it removes is the O(n2) memory, not the O(n2) compute. Putting it in the approximation list is a common and costly slip.

Say this back tomorrow

quadratic in sequence length, not in parameters  ·  double n and the score matrix quadruples
  • The score matrix is n by n, so compute is O(n squared d) and naive memory is O(n squared)
  • The rest of the model is linear in n, so attention only dominates once n approaches d_model
  • It hits prefill, which is one parallel pass over the prompt — decode is linear per token

Unlocks

  • n by n scores
  • O(n^2 d)
  • prefill-bound
  • crossover at n = d
  • sliding window

The KV Cache: Why It Exists

Generating token 1000 would mean recomputing 999 keys and values. Keep them instead — then find room for them.

When a model writes a reply it produces one token at a time, and each new token has to look back over everything before it. That looking-back needs two things from every earlier token, and neither of them ever changes once that token exists. So recomputing them for the whole history at every single step would be pure waste. Instead you keep them. Each new token computes only its own share, appends it to the pile, and reads the whole pile. The catch is the pile. It grows by a fixed amount for every token in the conversation, and you need a separate pile for every conversation you are serving at once. The weights of the model are a fixed cost you pay once and never again. This is the part that grows, and on a busy server it is this, not the weights, that decides how many people you can serve.

Like a barrister with a running bundle of notes. Every time a new witness speaks you could re-read the whole transcript, or you could keep the one-line summary you wrote for each witness as they finished. You keep them. The trouble is the bundle: it grows with every witness, you need one per trial you are running at once, and the desk is only so big.

At generation time the keys and values of every earlier token are fixed, so you store them and compute only the new token’s query. There is no Q cache, because a query only ever belongs to the token you are producing right now. Memorise the size: 2×nlayers​×nkv​×dhead​×bytes per token, where the 2 is K and V, then multiply by sequence length and by batch size. Llama 3 70B in BF16: 2×80×8×128×2=327,680 bytes, so 320 KB per token. At 128k context that is 43 GB for one request, on top of 140 GB of weights. On an eight-GPU H100 node with 640 GB you have roughly 500 GB left after weights, which is about 1.5M tokens of cache: 186 concurrent requests at 8k each, or eleven at 128k. That is the sentence to land — it is the cache, not the weights, that caps your concurrency.

Two properties do the work in an interview. It grows linearly in sequence length and linearly in batch, so sixteen users at 8k cost exactly what one user at 128k costs — 43 GB either way — and admission control therefore has to reason in tokens, not in requests. And it is per request: two users share nothing unless their prompts share a prefix and your server does prefix caching. Three levers shrink it, in the order people reach for them. Fewer KV heads, which is grouped-query attention and the next card — without it Llama 3 70B would need 2.5 MB per token rather than 320 KB. Fewer bytes, which is FP8 or INT8 KV quantisation, halving it again. And fewer wasted blocks: naive contiguous pre-allocation to max_model_len wastes 60–80% of the cache, which is the problem PagedAttention solves. The serving arithmetic that follows from all this — paging, continuous batching, admission control, the utilisation ceiling — continues in the In Production tier.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why generation speeds up after the first token
  • Sizing GPU memory for a model you are about to serve
  • Working out the largest batch that still meets a latency target
  • A long-context request starts causing preemption on a busy server

The trap

Not knowing it grows linearly in both sequence length and batch size. People quote a per-token figure and stop, then size a server as though the cache were a fixed overhead. Sixteen users at 8k cost exactly what one user at 128k costs. The other half of the trap is believing the weights are what fill the GPU: a 70B is 140 GB of weights and can easily be carrying 300 GB of cache alongside them.

The math the one formula to memorise

bytes per token=2×nlayers​×nkv​×dhead​×bytes  ·  total=bytes per token×n×batchRead the factors left to right and none of them is mysterious. The 2 is K and V, the two tensors you keep and the one you do not — there is no Q cache. Then one entry per layer, because every layer has its own attention and its own keys. Then nkv​, the number of key-value heads, which is where grouped-query attention does its work. Then dhead​, and finally the bytes per element: 2 for BF16, 1 for FP8. Llama 3 70B is 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, BF16: 2×80×8×128×2=327,680 bytes, or 320 KB per token. Llama 3 8B is 32 layers and comes to 128 KB; Llama 3.1 405B is 126 layers and comes to 504 KB. Now multiply. 70B at 128k, batch 1: 327,680×131,072=43 GB. Batch 8: 344 GB. And invert it for the answer they actually want: 500 GB of free memory divided by 320 KB per token is 1.5M tokens of cache, which is eleven concurrent 128k requests or 186 concurrent 8k ones.

The formula, then the concurrency it implies

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes   # the 2 is K and V

llama_70b = dict(layers=80, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128)       # GQA: 64 q, 8 kv
per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(**llama_70b)
print(per_token / 1024)                    # 320.0 KB per token, per request

for ctx, batch in [(4096, 1), (131072, 1), (131072, 8)]:
    print(ctx, batch, round(per_token * ctx * batch / 1e9, 1))   # 1.3 43.0 343.6

free = 640e9 - 140e9                       # 8x H100 minus the BF16 weights
print(int(free / per_token / 131072))      # 11 concurrent requests at 128k
print(int(free / per_token / 8192))        # 186 concurrent requests at 8k

Where this bites in production

vLLM tells you this at startup. It loads the weights, measures what is left under --gpu-memory-utilization (default 0.90) and prints the KV cache size in tokens. Ask for more than fits and you get a real error: The model’s max seq len (131072) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache, followed by advice to raise the utilisation or lower max_model_len. Engineers hit that line on their first 128k deployment and it is this card, in production.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Compute the KV cache for a 70B at 128k.
About 43 GB for a single request. 2×80 layers×8 KV heads×128×2 bytes=327,680 bytes per token, so 320 KB; times 131,072 tokens is 43 GB. That sits on top of 140 GB of BF16 weights, so one long-context request needs more than half of a single H100 for its cache alone. Batch 8 at that length is 344 GB.
Why is there no query cache?
Because a query belongs only to the token being generated right now. At each decode step you compute one new query and dot it against every cached key; the previous tokens’ queries are never needed again, since their outputs were already produced and written into the stream. Keys and values are different — every future token will read them, and they never change. That asymmetry is the whole reason the cache is called KV.
Your service is stable at batch 8 with 8k prompts. A customer starts sending 100k-token documents. What breaks first?
Memory, and it shows up as preemption rather than as an error. Each 100k request holds about 33 GB of cache instead of 2.7 GB, so a batch that comfortably fit now does not; the scheduler starts evicting or recomputing sequences and throughput collapses for everyone, not just the large requests. The fixes are admission control on total tokens rather than request count, a separate queue or replica for long context, and chunked prefill so one long prompt does not stall every decode step.

Say this back tomorrow

2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes, per token  ·  times length, times batch
  • Keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so you store them; there is no query cache
  • 320 KB per token for Llama 3 70B, so 128k context is 43 GB for one single request
  • It grows linearly in both sequence length and batch — it, not the weights, caps concurrency

  • 320 KB/token
  • linear in batch
  • paged KV
