GQA, MQA & MLA

One number in the config decides the size of your KV cache. These three are three ways of making that number smaller.

Every attention head normally keeps its own pair of stored vectors for every token it has ever seen, and that store is the thing that fills the server. So the trick is to share. In the extreme version, all the heads share one single store between them: far smaller, but every head is now forced to look through the same lens and quality suffers for it. The version everyone actually ships splits the difference. Heads are put into groups, and each group shares one store. The heads still ask their own separate questions; they just read from a shared shelf. Divide the number of asking heads by the number of shelves and you have the saving, exactly. A newer approach squeezes the stored pair into one small compressed summary instead, and expands it back out when it is needed. All three exist for one reason, and it is not elegance. It is memory.

Like a newsroom with shared filing cabinets. Every reporter used to keep a private copy of the archive at their own desk, which is thorough and takes up the whole floor. Give each team of eight reporters one cabinet to share and the floor empties out. They still chase their own stories and ask their own questions. They have just stopped keeping eight identical copies of the same files.

All three shrink the same term. The KV cache is 2×nlayers​×nkv​×dhead​×bytes per token, and nkv​ is the only factor an architect controls. Multi-head attention sets nkv​=nq​, one K and V per query head. Multi-query (Shazeer, 2019) sets nkv​=1, a single K/V head broadcast to every query. Grouped-query (Ainslie et al., 2023) sets nkv​ to a group count in between. The saving is exactly nq​/nkv​. Llama 3 70B is 64 query heads over 8 KV heads, so 8×: 320 KB per token instead of 2.5 MB, and 43 GB at 128k instead of 344 GB. Llama 3.1 405B is 128 over 8, so 16×. Nothing changes on the query side — K and V are repeated back out to all 64 heads before the scores are computed — so attention FLOPs are unchanged. What shrinks is bytes stored and bytes read.

Be honest about the quality cost and precise about MLA. Sharing keys and values removes capacity: multi-query measurably loses quality and was reported unstable in training, which is why almost nobody ships nkv​=1 at scale. Grouped-query at eight groups sits within noise of full multi-head on most benchmarks, and the GQA paper reached it by uptraining an existing multi-head checkpoint with about 5% of the original pretraining compute rather than training from scratch — a cheap conversion, which is part of why it spread so fast. Multi-head latent attention, from DeepSeek-V2, takes a different route: instead of sharing heads it projects K and V down into a single low-rank latent vector per token, caches that, and expands it back up inside the attention computation, with a small separate rotated component because a RoPE’d key cannot be absorbed into the projection. DeepSeek report roughly a 93% cut against multi-head with quality at or above the baseline. And there is a speed argument people miss: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so reading 8 KV heads per step instead of 64 makes each generated token faster, not merely cheaper to store.

You reach for it when

  • Reading num_key_value_heads in a config file
  • Explaining why a 70B serves more users than its size suggests
  • Being asked to cut KV cache without quantising anything
  • Comparing the attention designs of Llama, Mistral and DeepSeek

The trap

Discussing these as architecture trivia. They are not quality improvements and were never proposed as such — every one exists to shrink the KV cache, and the answer that scores names the memory in its first sentence. Asked about GQA, lead with a ratio: 64 query heads over 8 KV heads is 8× less cache, 43 GB instead of 344 GB at 128k. Then admit the cost, which is that MQA does lose quality — precisely why grouped-query, not multi-query, is what ships.

The math one ratio, and it is the whole card

reduction=nq​/nkv​  ·  MHA nkv​=nq​, GQA 1<nkv​<nq​, MQA nkv​=1  ·  Llama 3 70B: 64/8=8The cache formula has five factors and four of them are fixed by the model you chose. 2 for K and V, nlayers​ for depth, dhead​ for width, bytes for precision. Only nkv​ is a design decision, and the reduction against full multi-head is exactly nq​/nkv​. Llama 3 70B, 80 layers, head dimension 128, BF16: at nkv​=64 it would be 2×80×64×128×2=2.5 MB per token; at nkv​=8 it is 320 KB; at nkv​=1 it would be 40 KB. Over a 128k context that is 344 GB, 43 GB and 5 GB. Note what does not change: nq​ stays 64, the score matrices stay (n,n) per query head, and the FLOPs are the same, because K and V are repeated back out to 64 heads before the scores are computed. Parameters move a little — WK​ and WV​ become (8192,1024) rather than (8192,8192), taking attention from 268M to 151M per layer — but that is a side effect, not the point. MLA replaces the sharing idea altogether: cache a c-dimensional latent per token instead of nkv​ heads of K and V.

Where the K and V heads get broadcast back

import torch

n_q, n_kv, head_dim, layers = 64, 8, 128, 80        # Llama 3 70B

k = torch.randn(1, n_kv, 16, head_dim)              # only 8 KV heads are stored
k_wide = k.repeat_interleave(n_q // n_kv, dim=1)    # broadcast to 64 to compute
print(k.shape, k_wide.shape)      # [1,8,16,128] -> [1,64,16,128], no new memory

def kv_kb_per_token(kv_heads):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * 2 / 1024

for name, h in [("MHA", 64), ("GQA", 8), ("MQA", 1)]:
    print(name, kv_kb_per_token(h))          # 2560.0    320.0    40.0  KB
print(n_q / n_kv)                 # 8.0 - the reduction factor IS the head ratio

Where this bites in production

Read the configs and the design is in two fields. Llama 3 70B: num_attention_heads: 64, num_key_value_heads: 8. Llama 3.1 405B: 128 and 8. Mistral 7B: 32 and 8. Llama 2 7B and 13B were plain multi-head, both fields 32; Llama 2 70B was the first in that family to ship GQA, and by Llama 3 every size had it. DeepSeek-V2 threw the scheme out for MLA, compressing K and V into a 512-dimensional latent plus a small rotated part. When those two fields differ, you are looking at grouped-query attention.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How much does GQA save on Llama 3 70B, in gigabytes?
Eight times, which is 43 GB at 128k instead of 344 GB. 64 query heads over 8 KV heads is a reduction of 64/8=8, so the cache is 320 KB per token rather than 2.5 MB. Without it a single 128k request would need more than twice the memory of the model’s own weights. The reduction factor is always just the head ratio — no other term in the formula moves.
Does GQA make attention faster, or only smaller?
Both, and for a reason worth naming. The FLOPs are unchanged, because K and V are repeated back out to all 64 query heads before the scores are computed. But decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: every generated token reads the whole cache for that sequence, so reading an eighth of the bytes makes each step faster as well as cheaper. That is also why FP8 KV quantisation speeds up decode rather than just saving space.
Why does almost nobody ship multi-query, if it saves the most?
Because it costs quality, and grouped-query gets most of the saving without it. Collapsing to one K/V head removes real capacity and was reported to bring training instability; the GQA paper positioned groups as the interpolation that holds on to multi-head quality at close to multi-query memory. Eight groups is the number that stuck across Llama, Mistral and Qwen. MLA is the current attempt to beat that trade rather than sit on it.

Say this back tomorrow

the saving is query heads over kv heads  ·  64 over 8 is eight times less cache
  • These exist for the KV cache, not for quality — naming the memory is the whole answer
  • Reduction equals query heads divided by KV heads: 64/8 is 8 times, 128/8 is 16 times
  • MQA at one head loses quality, GQA at eight groups does not, MLA caches a latent instead

  • 64 over 8
  • repeat_interleave
  • MLA latent

FlashAttention

It is exact. The same numbers come out — the score matrix simply never reaches the memory it would not fit in.

A graphics card has two kinds of memory. There is a large pool, tens of gigabytes of it, where everything lives and which is comparatively slow to reach. And there is a tiny scratchpad sitting right next to the arithmetic units, a few tens of megabytes at most, which is many times faster. The ordinary way of computing attention builds the enormous table of comparisons in the big slow pool, writes it out, reads it back to normalise it, reads it again to use it, and then throws it away. Almost all of the time goes on that traffic, not on the arithmetic. The fix is to never build the table at all. Work through it in small tiles that fit on the scratchpad, keep a running total as you go, and let each tile go before fetching the next. The answer that comes out is the same answer. Nothing is dropped and nothing is approximated.

Like doing the accounts on a small desk. You could print the whole ledger, spread it across the office floor, and walk over for each figure. Or you could bring one page at a time to the desk, keep a running total in your head, and send each page away when you are done. The same total at the end. Far less walking, and no floor required.

FlashAttention is exact. It computes softmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V and returns the same result as the naive implementation; the arithmetic is reassociated, so the last bits can differ the way any reordered floating-point sum differs, but nothing is dropped or approximated. Three ideas. Tiling: split Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM and loop over them. An online softmax: carry a running maximum and a running normaliser, and rescale the partial output whenever a new block raises the maximum, so you never need a whole row before you can start. Kernel fusion: score, mask, softmax and the multiply by V all happen in one kernel, so the (n,n) matrix is never written to HBM at all. Memory goes from O(n2) to O(n). Compute stays at O(n2d) — it does more FLOPs, because the backward pass recomputes scores rather than storing them. The win is IO.

Put numbers behind “the win is IO”. On an A100, HBM is 40 to 80 GB at roughly 1.5 to 2 TB/s, while on-chip SRAM is about 20 MB at roughly 19 TB/s — four orders of magnitude smaller, one order faster. Attention at these shapes is memory-bound, not compute-bound: at 8k tokens the (n,n) matrix for one head in one layer is 134 MB, and the naive version writes it, reads it back, writes the softmaxed copy and reads that again, so more than half a gigabyte crosses the bus in order to turn 6 MB of Q, K and V into 2 MB of output. Dao et al. (2022) measured about 9× fewer HBM accesses and a 7.6× faster attention kernel on GPT-2, which came out as a 3× end-to-end training speedup. FlashAttention-2 roughly doubled it again by fixing the work partitioning between warps, and FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper with asynchrony and FP8. The consequence that outlives the benchmark numbers: O(n) memory is what turned 128k context from a research problem into a configuration value.

You reach for it when

  • Being asked how long context became practical at all
  • Setting attn_implementation on a Hugging Face model
  • Explaining why attention is memory-bound rather than compute-bound
  • Someone lists FlashAttention alongside Longformer as an approximation

The trap

Calling it an approximation, or filing it next to sparse and linear attention. It is exact — the same softmax over the same scores, computed in a different order, so the output matches to floating-point reassociation and nothing else. The related error is saying it reduces FLOPs. It does not: compute stays O(n2d) and the backward pass deliberately recomputes scores rather than keeping them. What it reduces is bytes moved, and at these shapes bytes are the bottleneck.

The math the online softmax, in one line

memory O(n2)→O(n), output unchanged  ·  m′=max(m,maxj​sj​)  ·  o←oem−m′+es−m′Vblock​The middle identity is what makes tiling possible. A safe softmax needs the maximum of the whole row before it can exponentiate, and that row is exactly the thing you are trying not to materialise. So carry a running maximum m and a running normaliser ℓ. When a new block raises the maximum to m′, correct everything accumulated so far by the factor em−m′ — which is algebra, not approximation, since es−m=es−m′em′−m — then add the new block’s contribution and divide by ℓ at the very end. Only m, ℓ and the running output are kept, which is why memory falls from O(n2) to O(n). The IO complexity is O(n2d2/M) HBM accesses for SRAM of size M, against O(nd+n2) naively — the factor of roughly 9 that Dao et al. measured on GPT-2. The backward pass keeps only m and ℓ and recomputes the scores from Q and K: more arithmetic, far fewer bytes, and still faster, which is the clearest statement of what memory-bound means.

The online softmax, exactly

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

n, d, tile = 4096, 64, 512
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 1, n, d) for _ in range(3))
ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)   # the whole (n, n), one shot
s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / d ** 0.5          # a real kernel never builds s
m, out = torch.full_like(s[..., :1], -torch.inf), torch.zeros_like(ref)
l = torch.zeros_like(m)
for j in range(0, n, tile):                     # one tile of K and V
    b = s[..., j:j + tile]
    mn = torch.maximum(m, b.max(-1, keepdim=True).values)
    p, r = (b - mn).exp(), (m - mn).exp()       # r rescales the running total
    out, l, m = out * r + p @ v[..., j:j + tile, :], l * r + p.sum(-1, True), mn
print(torch.allclose(out / l, ref, atol=1e-5))  # True - exact, in O(n) memory

Where this bites in production

PyTorch dispatches scaled_dot_product_attention to one of several backends and falls back silently to the plain maths kernel when your inputs do not qualify — fp32 inputs, an unsupported head dimension, or an arbitrary additive attn_mask instead of is_causal=True. Your “flash” path can quietly not be flash, and the only symptom is memory use. Hugging Face makes it explicit with attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", which raises rather than degrading when the model or dtype is unsupported.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Does it change the maths?
No. It is exact, and that is the whole point of the question. It computes the same softmax over the same scores and returns the same output; only the order of operations changes, so results differ at most in the last bits, as any reassociated floating-point sum does. Sparse, sliding-window and linear attention all compute a different function. FlashAttention computes the same one in O(n) memory.
Why is it faster when it does more arithmetic?
Because attention at these shapes is bound by memory bandwidth, not by FLOPs. HBM runs at about 2 terabytes per second while on-chip SRAM runs at around 19, so a kernel that writes and re-reads an (n,n) matrix spends its time waiting on the bus. Fusing the whole operation and tiling through SRAM cuts HBM accesses by roughly 9×. The backward pass then recomputes scores instead of storing them: more FLOPs, fewer bytes, still a large net win.
You switched on flash_attention_2 and nothing got faster. What do you check?
Whether it is running at all, and then whether attention was ever your bottleneck. The kernel needs fp16 or bf16, a supported head dimension, and is_causal rather than a custom additive mask — miss any of those and PyTorch quietly uses the maths backend. Then check the shape of your workload: the gain grows with sequence length, so at 512-token prompts there is little to win, and single-stream decode is bound by reading weights and cache, where attention is a small slice of the step.

Say this back tomorrow

exact, not approximate  ·  the n by n matrix never reaches HBM, so memory is O(n)
  • It computes the same softmax over the same scores — the output matches, it is not an approximation
  • Tiling plus an online softmax plus one fused kernel turns O(n squared) memory into O(n)
  • The win is bytes moved, not FLOPs — it does more arithmetic and still runs several times faster

Unlocks

  • exact attention
  • tiling
  • online softmax
  • SRAM vs HBM
  • IO-aware

9. Mixture of Experts — Fewer multiplications per token, exactly the same weights in memory. It buys FLOPs, and it buys you nothing on VRAM
10. Extending Context: Interpolation & YaRN — You do not get 128k by asking for it. You rescale the rotation, train briefly on long documents, and then pay for it on every request
11. Scaling Laws & Chinchilla — Twenty tokens per parameter is the cheapest way to train a model. If you are the one paying for inference, it is the wrong objective
12. Catastrophic Forgetting — Your domain metric climbs all the way through the run. Everything you did not measure goes down quietly beside it

Pretraining, SFT & Alignment

Three stages, three different lessons. The facts arrive in the first one and never again.

A model is built in three passes, and each one teaches something different. The first reads an enormous amount of text and learns to continue it. Everything the model will ever know about the world arrives here, along with grammar, register and the shape of an argument. The second pass shows it worked examples: a request, then a good answer, written out by a person. Nothing new about the world is learned. What it learns is to answer the question rather than carry on writing more questions of its own. The third pass shows a person two acceptable answers and records which one they preferred, then nudges the model towards the sort they keep choosing. Again, no new facts. Keep the sizes in mind, because the sizes are the argument. The first pass sees trillions of words. The second sees tens of thousands of examples. The third sees a pile of comparisons. Nearly all the money is spent before the first pass ends.

Like training a solicitor. Years of reading put every statute they know into their head. A few weeks of watching a partner answer client letters teaches them to reply to the question asked instead of reciting the statute back. And a supervisor going through a stack of drafts saying “that one, not that one” teaches taste. Only the reading taught them any law.

Stage one is pretraining: next-token prediction over trillions of scraped tokens. That is where every fact and every syntactic habit comes from, and it is where essentially all the compute goes. Stage two is supervised fine-tuning — the same next-token loss, but on curated prompt-and-response demonstrations with the loss masked to the response tokens, tens of thousands of them. It teaches turn structure, a chat template and an instruction-following prior: the model answers instead of continuing. Stage three is preference alignment, RLHF or DPO, and it trains on comparisons rather than demonstrations — given two acceptable responses, which did a human prefer? Llama 2 is the documented example: 2T pretraining tokens, 27,540 SFT annotations, 1,418,091 binary comparisons. OpenAI reported InstructGPT’s 175B SFT run at 4.9 petaflop/s-days and its PPO run at 60, against 3,640 for GPT-3’s pretraining. Behaviour is cheap. Knowledge is not.

Two consequences worth saying out loud. First, no stage after pretraining installs a fact. If the model has never seen your API, SFT on a thousand demonstrations of that API teaches it the shape of a plausible answer and it will hallucinate the endpoint names more fluently than before — the fix is retrieval, three cards on. Second, the later stages can take things away. Ouyang et al. named it the alignment tax: InstructGPT regressed against GPT-3 on public NLP benchmarks, and they mixed pretraining gradients back into the PPO objective (the PPO-ptx variant) to claw it back. Anything trained after pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, which is why you keep a general-capability holdout and re-run it after every stage rather than only measuring the thing you were trying to improve. Know the vocabulary boundaries too: continued pretraining is more of stage one, not fine-tuning; instruction tuning is stage two; RLHF, DPO, KTO and constitutional AI all live in stage three; and reasoning RL against a verifiable answer is a fourth stage bolted on after it.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a fine-tune did not teach the model your facts
  • Deciding which stage a proposed change belongs in
  • Costing a post-training programme against the pretraining run
  • Reading a model card that lists SFT and DPO data separately

The trap

Blurring SFT and RLHF into one “we trained it on human data” step. SFT trains on demonstrations — a human wrote the answer and the model copies it. Alignment trains on comparisons — a human ranked two of the model’s own answers and the model learns the ranking. The other half of the trap is thinking alignment adds knowledge. It reweights behaviour the base model already had; if the fact was never in the corpus, no volume of preference data puts it there.

The math the ratio is the whole argument

pretrain ≈1013 tokens  ·  SFT ≈104 demonstrations  ·  align ≈105 comparisons  ·  post-training compute <2% of pretrainingDo not memorise a loss here — memorise the orders of magnitude, because they are what the follow-up is really about. Pretraining: Llama 2 saw 2 trillion tokens and Llama 3 about 15 trillion, at roughly 20 tokens per parameter for a compute-optimal run. Supervised fine-tuning: Meta stopped at 27,540 annotations for Llama 2 after finding that quality beat quantity, and LIMA got most of the way there on 1,000 curated examples — call it 104, nine orders of magnitude below stage one. Alignment: 1,418,091 binary comparisons for Llama 2’s reward models, 33k reward-model prompts and 31k PPO prompts for InstructGPT. Now the money. OpenAI reported 4.9 petaflop/s-days to fine-tune the 175B SFT model and 60 for the PPO model, against 3,640 petaflop/s-days to pretrain GPT-3: 4.9/3640=0.13% and 60/3640=1.6%. That asymmetry is why one pretraining run supports a dozen post-trained variants, and why “we fine-tuned it” is a far smaller claim than it sounds.

The one line that separates pretraining from SFT

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct")
msg    = [{"role": "user", "content": "Convert 20C to F."}]
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(msg, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)

ids    = tok(prompt + "68 degrees Fahrenheit.").input_ids
labels = list(ids)                    # pretraining stops here: predict them all
for i in range(len(tok(prompt).input_ids)):
    labels[i] = -100                  # SFT: no loss on the prompt, only on y
print(sum(x != -100 for x in labels), "supervised of", len(ids))

# stage three never sees this object. it sees (prompt, chosen, rejected) and the
# loss is over which of the two a human picked - not over the tokens of either.

Where this bites in production

Meta published the whole split for Llama 2, which is why it is the example to quote: 2 trillion pretraining tokens, 27,540 SFT annotations, 1,418,091 binary human comparisons. They also reported stopping the SFT annotation at that point — they had set aside millions of third-party examples as too noisy and found that a few tens of thousands of their own was enough. That is the same finding LIMA published as “less is more for alignment”, from the other direction.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What does each stage actually teach?
Knowledge, then answering, then taste. Pretraining is next-token prediction over trillions of tokens and it installs every fact and stylistic habit the model will ever have. SFT trains on written demonstrations with the loss masked to the response, and teaches turn structure — the model answers rather than continuing your text. Alignment trains on comparisons between two acceptable answers and teaches which one a human prefers. Only the first stage adds knowledge.
Your model does not know your internal product names. Which stage fixes it?
None of them — that is a retrieval problem. Weights hold statistical regularities, not records you can look up, so SFT on your documentation teaches its cadence and vocabulary and then invents the specifics with more confidence. Continued pretraining on a very large domain corpus is the only training-shaped answer, and it is stage one, not fine-tuning. For a few thousand documents that change weekly, retrieval is cheaper, current, citable and deletable.
How much of the total compute goes into the stages after pretraining?
A couple of per cent at most. OpenAI reported 4.9 petaflop/s-days for the 175B SFT model and 60 for the PPO model, against 3,640 for GPT-3’s pretraining — 0.13% and 1.6%. That is why every lab ships many post-trained variants off one base run, and why post-training is where a small team can realistically compete. Nobody is out-pretraining anybody on a startup budget.

Say this back tomorrow

knowledge comes from pretraining  ·  behaviour comes from everything after it
  • Pretraining installs the facts and the fluency, and takes over 98% of the compute
  • SFT copies demonstrations and teaches the model to answer instead of continuing
  • Alignment learns from comparisons between two valid answers — it adds no knowledge

Unlocks

  • next-token loss
  • loss masking
  • demonstrations
  • preference pairs
  • alignment tax

RLHF and the Reward Model

Humans do not write the answers here. They pick between two the model wrote, and a second model learns to imitate that judgement.

Suppose you want a model to answer the way people actually like. You cannot write down a rule for that, and you cannot have a person grade every answer during training. So it is done in three moves. First you collect judgements: show a person two answers the model wrote to the same prompt and ask which is better. Tens of thousands of those. Then you train a second, separate model whose only job is to predict that judgement, so it can grade any answer at any hour without a human present. Finally the first model practises against it: it writes an answer, the grader scores it, and the model shifts towards whatever scores well. There is a leash on that last step and there has to be, because a model told to chase a score will find ways of scoring that nobody intended, and the grader is only a model too.

Think of a chef and a food critic. You cannot afford the critic at every service, so you have them taste a few hundred pairs of dishes and say which they preferred. Then you train an apprentice to guess the critic’s verdict, and the kitchen cooks against the apprentice. It works well, until the chef notices the apprentice rewards big portions, and starts sending out nothing but big portions.

Three stages, on top of an SFT checkpoint. One: collect preferences — sample two or more completions per prompt from the SFT model and have annotators rank them. Two: train a reward model, usually the same architecture with the language head swapped for a scalar head, under the Bradley-Terry loss −logσ(r(x,yw​)−r(x,yl​)), so it learns a score whose differences reproduce human choices. Three: optimise the policy against that reward with PPO, subject to a per-token KL penalty against the frozen SFT reference: max E[r(x,y)]−βKL(πθ​∥πref​). Four models are live at that point — policy, frozen reference, reward model, value network. InstructGPT’s documented sizes: about 13k SFT prompts, 33k reward-model prompts, 31k PPO prompts, with a 6B reward model steering a 175B policy. Humans wrote none of the responses in stages two and three.

Reward hacking is what to name concretely, because “the model games the reward” is not an answer. Length bias: reward models reliably score longer responses higher, PPO discovers that padding raises the score, and Singhal et al. found response length explains much of the apparent reward gain on several datasets. Sycophancy: agreeing with a view the user has already stated scores better than correcting it, which Sharma et al. measured across five production assistants. Formatting tricks: bullet points, a restated question, a confident opening. All three are genuine preferences of the annotators, learned faithfully, then pushed far past the point where they help. The KL term is the containment. It prices every step away from the SFT reference, which limits how far the policy can walk into the region where the reward model is out of distribution and therefore confidently wrong. Set β too high and nothing moves; too low and you get fluent nonsense that scores 9 out of 10. And the reward model is a model: 65–75% accuracy on held-out comparisons is normal, so you are optimising hard against a judge that is wrong on a quarter to a third of the pairs.

You reach for it when

  • Being asked to describe RLHF end to end
  • Explaining why an aligned model got longer and more agreeable
  • Choosing between PPO and DPO for a preference run
  • Reading a model card that reports reward-model accuracy

The trap

Describing RLHF as “training on human answers”. That is SFT — a person wrote the response and the model copied it. In RLHF humans write nothing: they rank responses the model produced, a reward model learns to imitate those rankings, and the policy is optimised against the reward model rather than against people. Miss the reward model and you have described the wrong stage, and you can then explain neither reward hacking nor what the KL term is holding on to.

The math one loss to learn taste, one objective to chase it

LRM​=−logσ(r(x,yw​)−r(x,yl​))  ·  maxθ​ E[r(x,y)]−βKL(πθ​∥πref​)The first line is Bradley-Terry: the probability a human prefers yw​ to yl​ is σ(rw​−rl​), so the loss depends only on the gap between two scores and never on their absolute value. That is why a reward model’s output has no units, why you cannot compare scores across two reward models, and why people normalise the reward inside the PPO batch. It also means the scalar head can be bolted onto any base checkpoint — InstructGPT used a 6B reward model to steer a 175B policy, because the judge does not need the capacity of the thing it judges. The second line is what PPO maximises, and in practice the KL is folded into the reward per token as rt​−β(logπθ​−logπref​) rather than added as a separate term. β is the only dial that matters: TRL exposes it as init_kl_coef, typically starting around 0.2 with adaptive control that raises it when the measured KL overshoots a target. Watch the measured KL during a run, not the reward — a reward climbing while KL runs away is the signature of hacking rather than learning.

The reward loss, then the KL-penalised reward

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

# stage 2 - the reward model. only the gap between the two scores is trained.
r_chosen, r_rejected = torch.tensor([2.4]), torch.tensor([1.1])
print(float(-F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected)))       # 0.2410  Bradley-Terry

# stage 3 - what PPO actually maximises, per token, over one response
logp     = torch.randn(20)          # the policy being trained
logp_ref = torch.randn(20)          # the FROZEN sft model, never updated
beta     = 0.2                      # trl init_kl_coef; adaptive during the run

reward     = torch.zeros(20)
reward[-1] = 2.4                    # the reward model scores the WHOLE response
print(float((reward - beta * (logp - logp_ref)).sum()))  # score minus the drift

Where this bites in production

Meta trained two reward models for Llama 2, one for helpfulness and one for safety, after finding that a single model traded one off against the other. They also ran it five times — RLHF-V1 through V5 — collecting fresh preference data against the current policy at each round, because a reward model fitted on last month’s samples goes stale as the policy moves off the distribution it was trained on. That staleness is what reward hacking looks like from the operations side.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the KL penalty for?
To keep the policy close to the SFT model so it cannot exploit the reward model. The reward model is accurate near the distribution it was fitted on and unreliable outside it, so an unconstrained policy will find high-scoring text no annotator would endorse. The KL term prices each step away from the frozen reference, and it is the difference between a run that improves and a run that produces fluent nonsense scoring 9 out of 10.
Give me a concrete example of reward hacking.
Length, and it is the best-documented one. Annotators mildly prefer thorough answers, so the reward model scores longer responses higher, and PPO discovers that padding raises the score without improving anything — Singhal et al. found length explains much of the reward gain on several datasets. Sycophancy is the second: agreeing with a view the user already stated outscores correcting it. Both are real annotator preferences, learned faithfully, then over-optimised.
Your reward model scores 68% on held-out comparisons. Is that good?
Roughly normal — and the right comparison is human-human agreement, not 100%. Annotators agree with each other only about 70 to 80% of the time on open-ended preferences, so a reward model in the mid-sixties to mid-seventies is near the ceiling the data supports. What matters more is where the errors sit: check accuracy on your hardest slices, and check calibration on responses far from the SFT distribution, because that is exactly where PPO will push.

Say this back tomorrow

humans rank, a reward model scores, PPO chases the score, and the KL holds the leash
  • Preferences, then a reward model, then PPO against it — humans write none of the answers
  • The KL penalty pins the policy near the SFT reference so it cannot exploit the reward model
  • Reward hacking is concrete: length bias, sycophancy, formatting — all learned faithfully

Unlocks

  • Bradley-Terry
  • scalar head
  • KL penalty
  • reward hacking
  • length bias

DPO and Why It Won

Same preference file, no reward model. The policy is its own scorer, and the loss is a classification between two answers.

The older method needs three things: a pile of human comparisons, a second model trained to score answers, and a practice loop in which the first model writes, gets scored and is nudged. That is three moving parts, and the middle one is a model that can be wrong — which the first model will happily discover and exploit. The newer method deletes the middle. It goes straight from the comparisons to the model in a single training run that looks much like ordinary supervised training: here is a prompt, here is the answer people preferred, here is the one they did not, raise the first and lower the second, measured against where the untouched model started. One run instead of three parts, nothing to sample from, and no scorer to be gamed. The catch is that it takes the comparison file entirely at its word.

Like marking essays without writing a rubric. The old way drafts a rubric first, has every essay scored against it, and watches the students learn to write for the rubric. The new way skips it: you show the marker the pair, say this one over that one, and let them move. Faster, and cleaner. You have also lost the ability to score anything you were not shown.

DPO’s result is that the optimal policy under a KL-constrained reward objective has a closed form, and it can be inverted: the reward is recoverable from the policy itself, r(x,y)=βlogπref​(y∣x)πθ​(y∣x)​+logZ(x). Substitute that into the Bradley-Terry loss and the intractable partition function cancels between the chosen and rejected terms, leaving something you can compute with two forward passes on the policy and two on a frozen reference. So there is no reward model to train, no sampling from the policy during training, no value head, no clipping and no rollout schedule — two models in memory instead of four, one hyperparameter that matters (β, usually 0.1), and a training loop that looks exactly like supervised fine-tuning. That is why it displaced PPO for most teams: not that it is better, but that it is one thing to get right instead of three, and it runs on the hardware and the skills a team already has.

Now the honest counterpoint, which is the half that scores. PPO can still win at the frontier, because with a good reward model you sample fresh on-policy responses and score anything the policy currently produces — the model learns from its own present mistakes. DPO only ever learns from the pairs in the file, so it is far more sensitive to preference-data quality and to going off-distribution: if the chosen responses came from a much stronger model than yours, you are dragging your policy towards text it would never have generated. The well-known symptom is that the log-probability of the chosen response falls during training alongside the rejected one, with the gap widening while both sink. The variants are patches on exactly this. KTO drops pairs and trains on single responses labelled good or bad, which is the shape of the feedback you actually collect in production. IPO adds a regulariser so the loss cannot saturate and overfit deterministic labels. GRPO keeps the RL loop but deletes the value network, sampling a group of responses per prompt and using the group mean as the baseline — the method behind DeepSeek-R1’s reasoning training.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing an alignment method for a team with no RL specialist
  • Being handed a file of chosen and rejected pairs
  • Explaining why a DPO run made the model worse
  • Someone claims DPO is strictly better than PPO

The trap

Saying DPO is simply better. It is simpler, which is a different claim, and the follow-up tests whether you know what it costs. DPO never samples from the policy during training, so it can only correct mistakes that appear in the file, and it degrades when the chosen responses come from a much stronger model than the one you are training. PPO with a good reward model still wins at the frontier, which is precisely why the frontier labs kept the RL loop.

The math the reward was hiding inside the policy

r(x,y)=βlogπref​(y∣x)πθ​(y∣x)​+logZ(x)  ·  LDPO​=−logσ(βlogπref​(yw​∣x)πθ​(yw​∣x)​−βlogπref​(yl​∣x)πθ​(yl​∣x)​)Read the two lines as one move. The first says that under a KL-constrained objective the optimal policy and the reward are two views of the same thing, so any policy already implies a reward: the log-ratio against the reference, scaled by β. The second substitutes that into Bradley-Terry, where only the difference of two rewards appears — and logZ(x), the one intractable term, is the same for both responses to a shared prompt, so it cancels exactly. What is left needs four log-probabilities per training example: chosen and rejected under the policy, chosen and rejected under the frozen reference. No sampling, no reward model, no value function. β plays the same role it played in PPO, pricing drift from the reference: TRL defaults to 0.1, and higher values pin the policy harder to the SFT model. Two things to watch during a run, both printed by TRL: the implicit reward margin, which should rise, and the accuracy of that implicit reward on a held-out preference split, which should sit somewhere in the sixties or seventies rather than at 99% — a margin that explodes while quality falls is the DPO shape of over-optimisation.

The whole run, in three arguments

from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer
from datasets import Dataset

pairs = Dataset.from_dict({          # the entire dataset format: three columns
    "prompt":   ["Summarise the refund policy."],
    "chosen":   ["Refunds are issued within 14 days of delivery."],
    "rejected": ["Great question! I'd be happy to help you with refunds..."]})

cfg = DPOConfig(beta=0.1, learning_rate=5e-6, num_train_epochs=1)

# no reward model is passed, because there is not one. ref_model=None tells TRL
# to use the base weights with the adapter disabled as the frozen reference.
DPOTrainer(model, ref_model=None, args=cfg, train_dataset=pairs).train()
# logs rewards/chosen, rewards/rejected, rewards/margins, rewards/accuracies

Where this bites in production

Zephyr-7B-beta was the run that made the public case: Mistral-7B, a distilled SFT stage on UltraChat, then DPO on the UltraFeedback preferences — no reward model anywhere in it — and it beat Llama-2-70B-chat on MT-Bench with a tenth of the parameters, on a budget a small team could repeat. Compare what the two trainers ask for in TRL: PPO wants a reward model, a value head, generation settings and a rollout schedule; DPO wants three columns and beta=0.1.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why did DPO displace PPO for most teams?
It deletes the reward model and the sampling loop, so three moving parts become one training run. The optimal policy under a KL-constrained reward has a closed form you can invert, so the reward is expressible as a log-ratio between the policy and a frozen reference; substituting that into Bradley-Terry cancels the partition function and leaves a classification-style loss on chosen and rejected pairs. Two models in memory instead of four, and a loop that looks like ordinary supervised fine-tuning.
What is beta doing in the DPO loss?
Exactly what it did in PPO — pricing drift away from the reference model. It scales the log-ratio between policy and frozen reference, so a large beta keeps the policy pinned near the SFT checkpoint and a small one lets it move far to satisfy the preference labels. TRL defaults to 0.1. It is the first thing to raise when a run produces a model that satisfies the pairs and has lost general capability.
Your DPO run finished and the model is worse. Where do you look first?
At the pairs, then at how far off-distribution they sit. DPO trusts the file absolutely: noisy or inconsistent labels are learned as taste, and chosen responses generated by a much stronger model pull your policy towards text it would never produce. Check the logged chosen reward — if the log-probability of the chosen response is falling too, both are being pushed down and only the gap is growing. Then raise beta, or move to KTO if your real signal is unpaired thumbs.

  • DPO rewrites preference learning as a classification loss on chosen and rejected pairs
  • No reward model, no sampling, no value head — two models resident instead of four
  • The cost is that it learns only from the file: data quality and off-distribution pairs bite

Fine-Tune vs RAG vs Prompt

Fine-tuning teaches form and behaviour. Retrieval supplies facts. Almost every complaint you will be handed is a facts complaint.

There are three ways to change what a model does for you, and they are not interchangeable. Prompting means writing better instructions and putting examples in the request itself. Retrieval means going and finding the relevant documents at the moment of the question and placing them in front of the model. Fine-tuning means changing the weights with more training. One rule decides between them. Fine-tuning teaches the model how to behave: the shape of an answer, a house style, a narrow output format, a professional register. Retrieval supplies what it needs to know: your prices, your policies, yesterday’s ticket, the clause on page forty. So when the complaint is that the model does not know something, that is a retrieval job, and training on documents to make it remember them is the mistake almost everybody reaches for first. Start with the prompt anyway, because it is free and you can undo it.

Think of a new colleague. If they keep writing to clients in the wrong tone, you coach them, and that is fine-tuning. If they do not know this quarter’s pricing, coaching will not help and will produce a confident wrong number. You hand them the price list, and that is retrieval. Nobody sends a colleague on a course to memorise a spreadsheet that changes every week.

Take them in cost order. Prompting and few-shot examples cost one deployment and are reversible in a text editor. Retrieval costs an index and adds latency — roughly 200 to 500ms for embed, search and rerank — but the facts are current, attributable and deletable, and you change an answer by editing a document. Fine-tuning costs a labelled dataset, a training run, an eval suite and a model version you now own forever, and it changes behaviour without adding reliable facts: train on documents and the model absorbs their style and surface statistics, then invents the specifics more fluently than before. The sentence that settles it is that a knowledge problem is a retrieval problem. What justifies fine-tuning is a format or style you cannot prompt into it reliably, a domain register, a latency or cost target you hit by shrinking the model, or a narrow task with a lot of examples and a small output space. The data floor is roughly 1,000 high-quality examples; below that, prompt.

They compose, and the strong answer says so. Production usually ends up as a small fine-tuned model behind a retrieval pipeline: the fine-tune fixes the shape and register of the output, retrieval fixes the facts, and the prompt remains the cheap steering layer above both. Then give the order of operations, because that is what is really being scored. Build the eval set first. Get a prompted baseline. Add retrieval and measure whether your failures are retrieval failures or generation failures. Only then reach for weights. Two liabilities to name. A fine-tune is an eval liability forever — every base-model upgrade means retraining and re-evaluating, and last year’s fine-tuned 7B routinely loses to this year’s prompted model. And LoRA has made fine-tuning cheap enough that people now do it before they should; cheap to run is not the same as cheap to own. The exception worth volunteering is distillation: when a large model already does the task well, generating traces and fine-tuning a small one on them is a legitimate and very common way to buy back latency and cost.

You reach for it when

  • The first architecture question in an AI engineer screen
  • A stakeholder asks you to train the model on the company wiki
  • Answers are correct but the tone or the format is consistently wrong
  • You need the same quality at a third of the cost per call

The trap

Fine-tuning to fix a knowledge problem. “Train it on our documentation” is the most common wrong answer in the loop. Weights store statistical regularities, not retrievable records, so the model learns your documentation’s vocabulary and cadence and then invents the specifics fluently. It is stale the day the run finishes, it cannot cite a source, and you cannot delete one fact from it. Retrieval is current, attributable, permissioned and edited by changing a document.

The math when a fine-tune pays for itself

nbreakeven​=few-shot tokens×price per tokencost of the training run​  ·  data floor ≈1,000 good examplesFine-tuning has exactly one clean cost argument, and it is worth being able to do out loud. If a fine-tune lets you delete a 2,000-token few-shot block from every call, and input tokens cost roughly three units per million, you save about 0.006 units per call; a 100-unit training run therefore pays for itself somewhere around 17,000 calls, and everything after that is profit — plus the latency you get back from a shorter prompt. That arithmetic is why fine-tuning wins on high-volume, narrow, stable tasks and loses on low-volume, broad, changing ones. Set against it the costs that do not appear in the sum: a dataset somebody has to build and clean, an eval suite you now need before and after, a model version pinned to a base checkpoint that will be superseded within the year, and a retraining bill every time you move. On the floor: the commonly quoted figure is about 1,000 high-quality examples, LIMA got strong instruction-following from exactly 1,000 curated ones, and OpenAI’s own guidance is that 50 to 100 can move a narrow formatting task. Below that you are prompting whether you meant to or not.

Three levers, in the order you pull them

# 1. prompt - free, reversible, and where you always start
prompted = f"Answer in the house format.\n{FORMAT_SPEC}\n\nQ: {q}"

# 2. retrieval - the FACTS, fetched at question time. current and citable.
docs      = rerank(q, index.search(q, k=50))[:5]
retrieved = f"Use only these sources.\n{docs}\n\nQ: {q}"

# 3. fine-tune - changes none of the above. it changes the SHAPE of the
# answer, and it is worth the run when this file is long and stable:
jsonl = [{"messages": [{"role": "user",      "content": q},
                       {"role": "assistant", "content": house_style_answer}]}
         for q, house_style_answer in examples]     # aim for 1,000+, not 50
# a doc dump here teaches cadence, not facts. that is the whole card.

Where this bites in production

OpenAI’s own accuracy guide draws this as two axes rather than a ladder: context optimisation for what the model needs to know, model optimisation for how it needs to act. Retrieval moves you along one, fine-tuning up the other, and most real systems need some of both. Their fine-tuning documentation says the same thing in plainer words — start at 50 to 100 examples for a narrow format task, and do not use fine-tuning to add knowledge to the model.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What would actually make you fine-tune?
A behaviour you cannot prompt reliably, or a cost target you cannot otherwise hit. Four honest cases: a strict output format or house style that prompting gets right most of the time but not consistently; a domain register the base model does not have; latency and cost, where a fine-tuned small model matches a prompted large one at a fraction of the price; and a narrow task with thousands of examples and a small output space. In all four the model already knows enough — it just behaves wrongly.
A stakeholder wants to fine-tune on 4,000 support tickets so the bot knows the answers. What do you say?
That it will change how the bot sounds and not what it knows. Four thousand tickets is a fine style corpus and a poor knowledge store: the model will learn the phrasing and then invent order numbers and policy details more convincingly than before. Index the tickets and retrieve instead, which is also current and lets you cite. If the tone still misses after that, fine-tune on the same corpus for form — the two compose.
Your fine-tune is better at the task and worse at everything else. How should you have caught that?
With a general-capability holdout you ran before and after — catastrophic forgetting is only visible if you kept one. Narrow fine-tuning shifts the whole distribution, so instruction-following, refusals and formatting outside your task can all degrade while your task metric climbs. Keep a fixed general eval alongside the task eval, run both every checkpoint, and lower the learning rate or the epoch count when the general one moves.

fine-tuning teaches form and behaviour  ·  retrieval supplies facts  ·  prompt first
  • A knowledge problem is a retrieval problem — training on documents teaches cadence, not facts
  • Fine-tune for format, style, register, or to shrink a model for latency and cost
  • The floor is around 1,000 good examples, and the three levers compose rather than compete

LoRA & QLoRA

Freeze the weights, learn a thin correction beside them, add it in at the end. One per cent trained, and nothing extra runs at inference.

Full fine-tuning means every number in the model is a number you are training, and each one needs a gradient and two optimiser statistics stored alongside it. For a large model that is more memory than most people have. The trick is to leave every original number exactly as it is, and learn a small correction beside it instead. The correction is kept as two thin slabs that multiply together to give something the same shape as the original weight, but with far less detail in it. Only those slabs are trained, and they come to about one per cent of the model. When training ends you multiply the slabs out and add the result into the original weights, so what you serve is an ordinary model of exactly the original size. Nothing extra runs when a request arrives. Keep them separate instead and you can slide a different correction on for each customer.

Like tracing paper over a drawing. The original stays untouched underneath, you draw the changes on a thin sheet on top, and the sheet is cheap to keep, cheap to post and easy to throw away. When you are happy, you photocopy the two together and what comes out is one drawing, no thicker than the first. Keep the sheets separate and you can lay a different one down per client.

LoRA freezes W0​ and learns ΔW=BA, with A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r for r≪d, so the forward pass is h=W0​x+rα​BAx. A is initialised random and B at zero, so the adapter is an exact no-op at step 0 and training starts from the base model’s behaviour rather than from noise. For a 4096×4096 projection at r=16 that is 131k trainable parameters against 16.8M — 0.78% — and the memory saving is larger than the parameter count suggests, because Adam keeps two states per trainable parameter and you have just dropped them for the frozen 99%. Defaults to quote, marked task-dependent: r between 8 and 64, starting at 16 or 32; α at r or 2r; targets q,k,v,o plus gate,up,down; learning rate 2e-4, roughly ten times a full fine-tune’s; one to three epochs. QLoRA freezes a 4-bit base underneath, which puts a 70B fine-tune under 48 GB.

The merge is the fact they probe. W=W0​+rα​BA is one addition of two matrices of the same shape, done once at load time, and afterwards there is no adapter, no second matmul and no added latency — a merged LoRA is an ordinary checkpoint and nothing downstream can tell. Decline to merge and you buy the other property: one base model resident, the adapter selected per request, which is how vLLM’s --enable-lora and S-LoRA serve many tenants’ fine-tunes off one set of weights for a small per-token cost. Choosing r: it is capacity, not quality. Style, tone and output format transfer at 8; a genuinely new domain or task wants 32 to 64; past that you are usually short of data rather than short of rank, and the first thing to fix is almost always the target list, not the number — the original paper adapted only Wq​ and Wv​, and adding the feed-forward modules matters because two thirds of the parameters live there. α is a scale and not a second rank: the update is multiplied by α/r, so holding α=2r keeps the effective scale fixed while you sweep r. The honest limits: LoRA trails full fine-tuning when you are teaching genuinely new capability at scale, and QLoRA trades a little quality and some speed for the memory.

You reach for it when

  • Being asked why LoRA is preferred over full fine-tuning
  • Sizing a fine-tune against the GPU you actually have
  • Serving one base model for many customers or many tasks
  • Someone worries that an adapter will slow down inference

The trap

Explaining LoRA as “freezing most of the layers and training the last few”. That is a different and older technique. In LoRA every targeted layer is adapted and none of the original weights move at all — the update is factorised, not localised. The second half is claiming an inference cost. Merged, the adapter is gone: one addition at load time and the served model is exactly the original shape. The cost exists only if you deliberately keep adapters separate in order to hot-swap them.

The math two thin matrices, then one addition

h=W0​x+rα​BAx, W0​ frozen  ·  B∈Rd×r, A∈Rr×k, B=0 at init  ·  merge: W=W0​+rα​BACount it once on a real model and the claim stops being a slogan. Llama 3 8B: dmodel​=4096, 32 layers, 8 KV heads so the k and v projections are (4096,1024), and dff​=14336. At r=16 across the standard seven targets that is 131,072 parameters for each of q and o, 81,920 for each of k and v, and 294,912 for each of gate, up and down — 1,310,720 per layer, 41,943,040 in total, which is 0.52% of 8.03B. Halve r and it halves; the parameter count is exactly linear in the rank. Memory is the real prize: mixed-precision full fine-tuning costs roughly 16 bytes per parameter once you count fp32 master weights, gradients and the two Adam moments, so an 8B needs about 128 GB before activations, while LoRA holds 16 GB of frozen bf16 weights plus optimiser state for 42M parameters and fits on one 24 GB card. QLoRA drops the base to 4-bit NormalFloat with double quantisation and paged optimisers — the paper’s headline was fine-tuning a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU while matching 16-bit performance. The scale factor α/r is the reason α=2r is a convention rather than a discovery: it keeps that multiplier at 2 while you sweep the rank.

The config, and the merge

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

cfg = LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32,           # the update is scaled by alpha/r = 2.0
    lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",     # attention
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"])       # and the FFN

model = get_peft_model(base, cfg)          # base is Llama 3 8B, bf16 or 4-bit
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# trainable params: 41,943,040 || all params: 8,072,204,288 || trainable%: 0.5196

merged = model.merge_and_unload()          # W += (alpha/r) B A, adapter discarded
merged.save_pretrained("out/")            # an ordinary checkpoint. no overhead.

Where this bites in production

Run print_trainable_parameters() on Llama 3 8B with the standard config — r=16, lora_alpha=32, the seven target modules — and you get 41,943,040 trainable against 8,072,204,288, or 0.5196%. Those are the defaults Unsloth and the Hugging Face examples ship, with lr=2e-4. vLLM serves the unmerged mode: --enable-lora --max-loras 4 keeps the base resident and applies a different adapter per request, which is how one GPU serves several tenants’ fine-tunes at once.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How do you pick the rank, and what does alpha do?
Rank is capacity; alpha is a volume knob, not a second rank. Start at 16 or 32, use 8 for style and format transfer, and 32 to 64 when the task is genuinely new to the model — and treat all of it as task-dependent. The update is scaled by alpha over r, so setting alpha to twice the rank holds that multiplier at 2 while you sweep. If a run plateaus, widen the target modules before you raise the rank: leaving the feed-forward projections out leaves two thirds of the model untouched.
Does an adapter add latency at inference?
Not if you merge it, and merging is a single addition. The update has the same shape as the frozen weight, so you fold it in once at load time and what you serve is an ordinary checkpoint with no extra matmul in the path. You only pay when you deliberately keep adapters separate to swap them per request — that costs a small amount per token and buys you many fine-tunes on one resident base model.
You have one 24 GB card and want to fine-tune a 70B. What do you do?
QLoRA, and you still will not fit 70B on 24 GB. A 4-bit 70B is roughly 35 to 40 GB of base weights before any activations, so the honest answer is a 48 GB card — the QLoRA paper’s headline was a 65B on exactly one of those. On 24 GB you comfortably do a 4-bit 13B, or an 8B with room for longer sequences. Say the number rather than agreeing that it fits.

Say this back tomorrow

the base is frozen, the update is two thin matrices, and it merges away to nothing
  • Freeze the weights and learn a rank-r factorised update — about 1% of the parameters
  • Adapters merge into the base at inference, so a merged LoRA adds exactly zero latency
  • Rank is capacity and alpha over r is the scale; QLoRA quantises the frozen base to 4-bit

Quantization: What Actually Gets Quantized

Weights, activations and the KV cache are three separate decisions. Four-bit is a memory saving first, and a speed-up only where memory was the bottleneck.

Every number in a model is stored with a certain amount of detail, and you choose how much. The usual choice is two bytes per number. You can halve that to one byte, and halve it again to half a byte, and the model shrinks to match: a seven billion parameter model goes from twenty-eight gigabytes at the most detailed setting, to fourteen, to seven, to three and a half. The rounding costs some accuracy, and how much depends on the method. The part people get wrong is what they have bought. Squeezing the numbers into fewer bytes does not make the arithmetic four times faster. It makes the model four times smaller, so it fits on a cheaper card, and it means far less has to be hauled out of memory for every word the model writes. Writing is limited by that hauling, so writing speeds up. Reading your prompt is limited by arithmetic instead, and barely moves.

Think of shipping a library on paper. Printing at half the size halves the shelf space and halves what the courier has to carry, and the carrying was most of the delay. It does not make anybody read faster. So the fetching gets quicker, the reading does not, and if you shrink the type far enough the words stop being legible at all.

Three separate decisions, and the question is checking that you know they are separate. Weight-only quantisation is the common one: bytes per parameter is 4 for fp32, 2 for fp16 or bf16, 1 for int8 and 0.5 for int4, so a 7B is 28, 14, 7 or 3.5 GB of weights and a 70B is 140 or 35. Activation quantisation is harder, because activations carry outlier channels that only appear at run time — that is what W8A8 schemes such as SmoothQuant exist to handle, and it is what you need before int8 tensor cores actually do anything for you. KV cache quantisation is separate again, usually fp8, and it is the one that buys concurrency at long context. Then the speed claim: 4-bit is not 4× faster. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so moving a quarter of the bytes per token makes decode meaningfully quicker; prefill is compute-bound and the weights are usually dequantised back to 16-bit for the matmul anyway, so it barely helps. Name the phase or do not quote the number.

Post-training quantisation is the default: take a trained model, push a few hundred calibration samples through it, fit per-channel or per-group scales, and you are done in minutes to hours with no gradients and no training set. Quantisation-aware training simulates the rounding during training so the weights land somewhere robust to it — clearly better at very low bit widths, and it costs a training run plus the original data, which is why nobody outside a model provider does it. Two details separate users from engineers. Granularity: per-tensor scales are fastest and worst, per-channel is standard, and per-group — one scale for every 64 or 128 weights — is what the 4-bit methods use, which is why “4-bit” is nearer 4.5 bits once you count the scales and zero points. And outliers: a handful of activation channels carry values orders of magnitude larger than the rest, they get worse with scale, and every serious method has an answer for them — LLM.int8() keeps them in 16-bit, SmoothQuant migrates the difficulty into the weights, AWQ protects the salient one per cent of weight channels using a calibration pass. Approximate quality, model- and task-dependent: int8 is essentially lossless, good int4 lands around 97–98%, and naive round-to-nearest int4 is where it falls over.

You reach for it when

  • Fitting a model onto the GPU you actually have
  • Being asked what you trade away for 4-bit
  • A quantised model is smaller but no faster on your benchmark
  • Sizing a long-context service where the KV cache dominates

The trap

Quoting a speed-up without naming the phase. “We went to 4-bit and got 4× faster” is wrong twice over: 4× is the byte count, and the gain lands almost entirely on decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound, and hardly at all on prefill, which is compute-bound and usually dequantises back to 16-bit for the matmul. The second trap is treating one knob as three. Weights, activations and the KV cache are quantised separately, by different methods, for different reasons.

The math one multiplication, then the phase question

bytes=P×b, with b = 4, 2, 1, 0.5  ·  7B: 28 / 14 / 7 / 3.5 GB  ·  decode time ∝ bytes moved, prefill time ∝ FLOPsThe first expression is the whole memory story: parameters times bytes per parameter, plus about 20% for activations, workspace and fragmentation. 7B at bf16 is 14 GB, at int4 3.5 GB; 70B is 140 GB and 35 GB, which is the difference between a multi-GPU node and one 48 GB card. The second is the part that answers the speed question, and it is a roofline argument. Generating one token at batch 1 reads every weight in the model exactly once, so the floor on time per token is bytes divided by memory bandwidth: 14 GB over an A100’s roughly 2 TB/s is 7 ms, a ceiling of about 143 tokens per second no matter how fast the arithmetic is. At int4 that becomes 3.5 GB, 1.75 ms, about 571 tokens per second. In practice you see 2 to 3× rather than 4, because dequantisation is not free. Prefill is the other regime: it processes the whole prompt in parallel, arithmetic intensity is high, it is compute-bound, and shrinking the weights does close to nothing for it. Same model, same change, two different answers — which is exactly why the interviewer asks which phase you mean.

The ladder, then the decode roofline

def weights_gb(params_b, bits):
    return params_b * 1e9 * (bits / 8) / 1e9        # bytes per param = bits / 8

for bits in (32, 16, 8, 4):
    print(bits, weights_gb(7, bits), weights_gb(70, bits))
# 32 28.0 280.0   16 14.0 140.0   8 7.0 70.0   4 3.5 35.0

bw = 2.0e12                          # A100 HBM bandwidth, bytes per second
for bits in (16, 4):                 # decode at batch 1 reads EVERY weight
    secs = weights_gb(7, bits) * 1e9 / bw
    print(bits, round(secs * 1e3, 2), round(1 / secs))   # 7.0ms 143 | 1.75ms 571

# prefill does not move like this: it is compute-bound and often dequantises
# back to 16-bit for the matmul. and the KV cache is a third, separate decision.

Where this bites in production

vLLM prints this arithmetic at startup: it loads the weights, subtracts them from --gpu-memory-utilization of the card, and whatever is left becomes your KV cache. Take a 7B from bf16 to int4 on a 24 GB A10G and the weights go from about 14 GB to 3.5, which turns roughly 7 GB of usable cache into roughly 18 — from about 53,000 cached tokens to about 137,000, at 128 KB per token. The user-visible win was never the model getting smaller. It was the concurrency.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Weights, activations, or the KV cache?
Three separate decisions, and weight-only is the one people usually mean. Weight-only is easy, needs at most a small calibration set, and buys you the memory footprint. Activation quantisation is harder because of run-time outlier channels, and it is what W8A8 schemes like SmoothQuant exist for — you need it before int8 tensor cores do anything. KV cache quantisation, usually fp8, is separate again and is what buys concurrency at long context. Say which one you changed.
Does 4-bit make it four times faster?
No. It makes it four times smaller, and that speeds up decode only. Decode at small batch is memory-bandwidth-bound — every token reads the whole model — so a quarter of the bytes lifts the ceiling from about 143 tokens per second to about 571 on an A100, and dequantisation overhead means you typically see 2 to 3×. Prefill is compute-bound and barely moves, and at large batch you become compute-bound again and the gap narrows.
When is quantisation-aware training worth it?
Almost never for you, routinely for whoever trained the model. QAT simulates the rounding during training so the weights land somewhere robust to it, which matters at very low bit widths — but it needs the original training data and a training run, and you have neither. Post-training quantisation with a good calibration set gets you essentially lossless int8 and around 97 to 98% at int4, in minutes. Reach for QAT only when you own the training pipeline and int4 post-training has measurably failed your evals.

bytes per parameter: 4, 2, 1, 0.5  ·  memory first, decode second, prefill hardly at all
  • Weights, activations and the KV cache are three separate decisions with different methods
  • A 7B is 28 / 14 / 7 / 3.5 GB at fp32 / fp16 / int8 / int4 — a 70B is 140 or 35
  • 4-bit is a memory saving that speeds up bandwidth-bound decode, not compute-bound prefill

  • PTQ vs QAT

GGUF vs AWQ vs GPTQ

Three formats for three different machines. Getting it wrong is not a quality mistake, it is a deployment mistake.

A quantised model is shipped as a file, and there are three families of file. The first is built for a laptop: it runs on an ordinary processor, it uses the graphics chip in an Apple machine well, and it arrives as one self-contained download you can run in a minute. The second is built for a server with an NVIDIA card, and it is what a real serving stack loads. The third is the older version of the second, still common, usually a little worse at the same size. The interesting one is the second. Instead of rounding every number the same way, it first pushes a sample of ordinary text through the model to see which channels carry the very large values, and protects those. A small handful of channels do most of the damage when you round them carelessly, so guarding that handful is most of the win.

Think of abridging a legal contract. Most of it can be tightened and nobody notices. A handful of clauses cannot — change a word there and the meaning goes with it. A careless abridgement treats every sentence alike. A careful one reads a stack of real contracts first, works out which clauses carry the weight, and spends its space on those.

Three artefacts, three targets. GGUF is llama.cpp’s format: one self-contained file with the quant type in the name, built for CPU inference and Apple Silicon Metal, with optional GPU offload by layer. It is what Ollama and LM Studio run underneath. AWQ is activation-aware weight quantisation — int4 at a group size of 128 — and it is the production answer for NVIDIA serving under vLLM, TensorRT-LLM or SGLang. Its idea is that weights are not equally important: push a few hundred calibration samples through the model, find the salient channels by activation magnitude rather than weight magnitude, and scale those up before rounding so the error lands where nobody notices. GPTQ is the older GPU format, a one-shot layer-wise method that uses second-order information to compensate rounding error column by column. Same hardware as AWQ, usually a point or two behind it at int4.

Then the ladder, and say out loud that it is approximate and model- and task-dependent, because it is: Q8_0 keeps about 99.9% of the original quality, Q6_K about 99.6%, Q5_K_M about 98.6%, AWQ int4 about 97 to 98%, GPTQ int4 about 95 to 97%, and Q4_K_M about 94 to 95%. Measure it on your own eval before you quote any of it. Two details that separate a user from an engineer. Group size: int4 is never four bits once you count the scale and the zero point — at group 128 it is nearer 4.16 bits per weight, and GGUF’s k-quants are mixtures, which is why Q4_K_M (Q6_K for half the value and down projections, Q4_K elsewhere) beats a flat Q4_0 at almost the same size. And calibration: AWQ needs a few hundred general samples, not your domain corpus — the paper’s point is that it does not backpropagate or reconstruct against the calibration set, so it does not overfit to it. The last practical fact is the one people miss. A GGUF served on a GPU is slower than the same model as AWQ under vLLM, because you have left behind paged attention, continuous batching and tensor parallelism. The format decides which serving stack you get, and the serving stack decides your throughput.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing which quantised checkpoint to actually deploy
  • Someone hands you a GGUF and asks you to put it behind an API
  • Explaining what AWQ does that round-to-nearest does not
  • Sizing the same model for a laptop demo and a production endpoint

The trap

Naming Ollama when you are asked how you would serve it. Ollama is llama.cpp with a friendly wrapper: exactly right for a laptop, a demo or local development, and a mild negative in a serving question, because you have given up paged attention, continuous batching and tensor parallelism. The production answers are vLLM, TensorRT-LLM or SGLang loading an AWQ or FP8 checkpoint. The other half of the trap is ranking the three by quality when the real axis is hardware.

The math nothing called four-bit is four bits

AWQ int4 at group 128: 4+12816+4​≈4.16 bits per weight  ·  GGUF Q4_K_M ≈4.85  ·  Q5_K_M ≈5.7  ·  Q8_0 ≈8.5Group-wise quantisation stores the weights at 4 bits and then one scale and one zero point for every group of 128, so the real cost is 4+(16+4)/128≈4.16 bits per weight — a 7B lands near 3.9 GB rather than 3.5. Drop to group 32 and the numbers get more accurate and the file gets bigger: 4+20/32=4.63. GGUF’s k-quants are mixtures rather than one width, which is where the letters come from: the M in Q4_K_M means medium, keeping Q6_K for half of the attention value and feed-forward down projections and Q4_K for the rest, about 4.85 bits per weight overall, and that mixture is why it beats a flat 4-bit scheme of the same size. Q5_K_M is about 5.7 bits, Q6_K about 6.6, Q8_0 about 8.5. Now the quality ladder, and mark it as approximate every time you say it: Q8_0 ~99.9%, Q6_K ~99.6%, Q5_K_M ~98.6%, AWQ int4 ~97–98%, GPTQ int4 ~95–97%, Q4_K_M ~94–95%. The spread within a rung across models is wider than the gap between two neighbouring rungs, which is the real reason to run your own eval rather than to argue about the table.

The same model, two deployment targets

from vllm import LLM

# production, NVIDIA: an AWQ int4 checkpoint under vLLM's Marlin kernels.
llm = LLM("TheBloke/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2-AWQ",
          max_model_len=8192, gpu_memory_utilization=0.90)
# vLLM reads quantization out of config.json and picks the kernel itself;
# passing quantization="awq_marlin" is an override, not a requirement.

# local, laptop or Apple Silicon: the SAME model, a different artefact.
#   llama-cli -m mistral-7b-instruct-v0.2.Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 33
#   ollama run mistral:7b-instruct-q4_K_M
# one file, the quant type in the name, -ngl offloads layers to the GPU.
# do not put this path in front of production traffic: no paged attention,
# no continuous batching, and one process per model.

Where this bites in production

The AWQ paper (Lin et al., MLSys 2024) is worth quoting precisely: roughly 1% of weight channels, chosen by activation magnitude rather than weight magnitude, carry most of the int4 loss — and because mixed precision is awkward for real kernels, they get the same protection by scaling those channels up before rounding instead. vLLM reads the quantization field out of config.json and selects the Marlin kernel itself on Ampere and newer.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You are serving a 7B on an A100 with vLLM. Which format, and why not the other two?
AWQ int4, or FP8 if the card supports it. AWQ is built for NVIDIA GPU serving, vLLM has fast Marlin kernels for it, and it keeps roughly 97 to 98% of quality at about 4.16 bits per weight. GPTQ runs on the same hardware and is usually a point or two behind at int4, so pick it only when that is the checkpoint that exists. GGUF is the wrong family entirely — it is llama.cpp’s format, built for CPU and Apple Silicon, and serving it on a GPU throws away paged attention and continuous batching.
What is AWQ actually doing that round-to-nearest is not?
Protecting the salient channels, and using calibration data to find them. Weights are not equally important: a small fraction of channels carry outsized activations, and rounding those is where most of the int4 damage comes from. AWQ pushes a few hundred general calibration samples through the model, ranks channels by activation magnitude rather than weight magnitude, and scales the salient ones up before quantising so the rounding error lands on channels that do not matter. No backpropagation, no reconstruction against the calibration set, so it does not overfit to it.
Someone proposes running your production API on Ollama. What do you say?
That it is llama.cpp underneath, and it is a local-development tool. It is the right answer for a laptop, a demo or an air-gapped box, and naming it as a serving answer is a mild negative in an interview. You lose paged attention, continuous batching and tensor parallelism, which is most of your throughput at any real concurrency. Say vLLM, TensorRT-LLM or SGLang with an AWQ or FP8 checkpoint, and keep Ollama for the machine under your desk.

Say this back tomorrow

GGUF for the laptop  ·  AWQ for the NVIDIA GPU  ·  GPTQ is the older GPU answer
  • The format picks your serving stack, and the serving stack picks your throughput
  • AWQ protects the salient channels found by activation magnitude on a calibration set
  • The quality ladder runs Q8_0 to Q4_K_M and every rung is model- and task-dependent

  • GGUF
  • AWQ
  • GPTQ
  • salient channels
  • group size 128
