Distillation

Train a small model to imitate a large one. The interview is not about the loss — it is about what signal you feed the student.

You have a large model that does the job and costs too much to run. So you train a new, smaller model to imitate it. The plain version collects a pile of questions, records the big model’s final answers, and trains the small one on those. The better version records more than the answer. When the big model chose a word, it also had opinions about all the words it did not choose: this one was nearly right, that one was possible, this other one was never in the running. That ranking over the wrong answers is where most of the teaching is, because it shows the student what the teacher thinks is similar to what. The modern version of the same idea is to make the teacher write out its full working, then train the student on the working rather than on the conclusion.

Like learning from a marked exam paper. A tick tells you the answer was right and nothing else. A marker who writes “this one was nearly right, that one was never plausible, and here is the working” teaches you to reason rather than to recall. Distillation is the difference between collecting ticks and collecting the working.

Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, 2015: train the student to match the teacher’s output distribution, not its argmax. Both sets of logits are softened by a temperature T, the student minimises the KL to the teacher’s softened distribution, and because gradients through a softmax at temperature T scale as 1/T2 you multiply that term by T2 to keep it comparable with the ordinary cross-entropy on the hard label. The soft targets are the point: the relative probabilities the teacher assigns to the wrong tokens encode the similarity structure it learned, which a one-hot label throws away. For language models it splits into two regimes. Logit distillation needs the teacher’s full distribution over a 128k vocabulary at every position, so it needs open weights and a lot of bandwidth. Sequence-level distillation samples completions from the teacher and fine-tunes the student on the text, which is what “distilled” means on almost every model card you will read.

Signal design is the actual follow-up, so have an ordered answer. Draw the prompts from your own traffic, not from a benchmark — the student only has to cover your input distribution, and that is the entire reason a 3B can replace a frontier model on one task. Ask the teacher for the reasoning trace and the answer, not the answer alone. Then filter: keep only the traces whose final answer verifies against a checker, a unit test, a database or a second model, which is rejection sampling and is usually worth more than any change to the loss. Dedupe, stratify by slice so your rare cases survive, and hold out a set the teacher never saw. Three honest limits. The student inherits the teacher’s mistakes, including confidently wrong traces whose final answer happens to be right. Closed APIs give you top-k logprobs at best and their terms of service often forbid training a competing model on the outputs, so with a hosted teacher you are doing sequence-level distillation whether you wanted to or not. And a student trained only on teacher text never sees its own mistakes; the on-policy variants — sampling from the student and having the teacher score or correct it — exist to close exactly that gap.

You reach for it when

  • Asked how you would shrink a model that already works
  • Building a training set out of a bigger model’s outputs
  • Explaining why a small open model is unexpectedly strong
  • Choosing between distilling and quantising to hit a latency target

The trap

Filing distillation next to quantisation and pruning. Those two shrink the model you already have — the same weights at fewer bits, or the same architecture with parts cut out. Distillation trains a different model, which can have its own depth, width, tokeniser and architecture, and the teacher is only a source of labels. The corollary is that the three compose: distil to a small model, then quantise that, and you have taken two independent bites at the cost.

The math soft targets, scaled back up

L=αT2KL(σ(zt​/T)∥σ(zs​/T))+(1−α)CE(y,σ(zs​))Read it left to right. zt​ and zs​ are the teacher’s and the student’s logits; dividing both by T>1 before the softmax flattens them, which lifts the small probabilities on the wrong answers into a range where they contribute a usable gradient. T between 2 and 5 is the usual range, task-dependent, and T=1 collapses the whole thing back to matching the teacher’s ordinary output. The T2 is not decoration: gradients through a softened softmax scale as 1/T2, so without it the soft term shrinks as you raise T and the hard term quietly takes over. α weights the two, and for a strong teacher people run it high — 0.9 upwards, sometimes 1.0 with no hard-label term at all. Then the practical arithmetic that decides the regime. A full teacher distribution is vocabulary-sized: 128,256 entries for Llama 3, at 2 bytes, at every position, which is about 256 KB per token and hundreds of gigabytes for a modest corpus. That is why logit distillation happens inside labs with both models in the same cluster, and why everyone else samples text from the teacher and fine-tunes on it. DeepSeek-R1’s distilled models are the reference point for the second regime: about 800k curated samples generated by R1, supervised fine-tuning only, no reinforcement stage.

The loss, and the part that actually matters

import torch.nn.functional as F

T, alpha = 2.0, 0.9                     # T > 1 softens BOTH distributions
soft = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1),
                F.log_softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1),
                reduction="batchmean", log_target=True) * (T * T)   # T^2 restores
hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)      # the one token that was right
loss = alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

# with a hosted teacher you never see teacher_logits, so you distil sequences:
#   1. draw prompts from YOUR traffic, not from a benchmark
#   2. ask for the reasoning trace, not just the answer
#   3. keep only traces whose final answer verifies. that filter is the quality.
#   4. dedupe, stratify by slice, hold out a set the teacher never saw

Where this bites in production

Meta says it plainly for Llama 3.2: the 1B and 3B were pruned from the larger models and then recovered using logits from Llama 3.1 8B and 70B as token-level targets. DeepSeek published the other regime — about 800k samples generated by R1, supervised fine-tuning only, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B beat much larger open models on reasoning benchmarks. Gemma 2’s 9B and 2B were trained the same way, from a larger teacher’s distributions.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How would you build the student’s training set?
From your own traffic, with the teacher’s working, filtered by verification. Sample prompts from production logs so the student covers the distribution it will actually serve, ask the teacher for the full reasoning trace and not just the answer, then keep only the traces whose final answer verifies against a checker, a test or a second model. Dedupe, stratify so rare slices survive, and hold out a set the teacher never saw. The rejection-sampling filter usually buys more than any change to the loss.
Why do soft targets beat hard labels?
Because the teacher’s uncertainty over the wrong answers is itself training signal. A one-hot label says every wrong token is equally wrong. The teacher says a plausible alternative scores a hundred times higher than an absurd one, and that ratio encodes the similarity structure it learned over the whole vocabulary. Raising the temperature lifts those small probabilities into a range where the gradient can use them, and the loss is multiplied by the temperature squared to keep its scale comparable with the hard-label term.
Is distillation just another word for compression?
No — quantisation and pruning modify the model you have, distillation trains a new one. The student can have a different depth, width, tokeniser and architecture; the teacher is only a source of labels, and once training is finished it is not needed at all. That also means they compose rather than compete: distil to a small model first, quantise that model second, and the two savings multiply. Most of the small strong models you can download today are distilled from a bigger sibling.

Say this back tomorrow

quantising shrinks the model you have  ·  distillation trains a new one to imitate it
  • The student is a new model; the teacher only supplies labels and can be discarded
  • Soft targets and logits carry the teacher’s ranking over the wrong answers — hard labels do not
  • With a hosted teacher you distil sequences: traces from your own traffic, filtered by verification

Unlocks

  • soft targets
  • temperature
  • dark knowledge
  • reasoning traces
  • rejection sampling

Mixture of Experts

Fewer multiplications per token, exactly the same weights in memory. It buys FLOPs, and it buys you nothing on VRAM.

Inside every block of a transformer sits one wide feed-forward layer that every token passes through. A mixture of experts replaces it with several copies, say eight, and adds a small router in front. The router looks at each token and picks two of the eight. Only those two do any arithmetic. So the work per word is roughly a quarter of what the model’s size suggests, and it answers faster and cheaper for the same quality. Here is the part people get wrong. All eight have to be sitting in memory, because the very next word might be sent to any of them, and there is no time to fetch one. So the card you need is sized by the total, and the speed you get is set by the two. There is a training failure too: if the router settles on a couple of favourites, the rest never learn.

Think of a clinic with eight specialists. Every patient sees the receptionist first, who sends them on to two of the eight. Only those two spend any time, so each consultation is quick. But all eight are on the payroll and all eight need a room, because tomorrow’s patient could need any of them. And if the receptionist keeps favouring the same two, the other six never get any better.

The dense feed-forward block in each layer is replaced by N expert feed-forward blocks plus a router: a single linear layer to N logits, take the top k, softmax over just those k, and sum the chosen experts’ outputs weighted by those gates. Attention is shared and untouched, and routing happens per token per layer, so two consecutive tokens usually take different paths. The config to quote is Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing, 46.7B parameters in total, 12.9B active per token. The name is a misnomer — 8 times 7 is not 46.7 — because attention and embeddings are shared rather than replicated. Now the answer they are waiting for. VRAM is set by the total: 46.7B at bf16 is about 93 GB, so it does not fit on one 80 GB card, while a dense model with the same 12.9B of compute per token would need 26 GB. Compute per token is set by the active count. They are two different numbers and they answer two different questions.

Load balancing is what makes it train at all. Left alone, the router finds a few experts that are slightly better early on, sends more tokens their way, trains those harder, and the rest starve — expert collapse, and you have paid for parameters that do nothing. The standard fix is the Switch Transformer auxiliary loss: penalise the product of the fraction of tokens routed to each expert and the router’s mean probability for it, summed over experts and scaled by α=0.01, which is minimised when traffic is uniform. Add a router z-loss to keep the logits from drifting large, and note the modern alternative — DeepSeek-V3 drops the auxiliary loss entirely and instead nudges a per-expert bias up or down during training to even the load, on the grounds that an auxiliary loss fights the task loss. Two serving facts worth volunteering. At batch 1 you read only the active experts’ weights per token, so decode really is faster; at large batch every expert gets hit by somebody, the whole model is read anyway, and that advantage narrows. And once the model spans GPUs, expert parallelism turns routing into an all-to-all exchange every layer, which is why MoE serving is unusually sensitive to interconnect. Expert specialisation is the last myth to drop: the Mixtral authors looked and found no clear topical split, only some positional structure.

You reach for it when

  • Reading a model card that lists total and active parameters separately
  • Sizing the GPU for an MoE checkpoint
  • Explaining why an MoE is fast and still will not fit
  • A training run where a handful of experts take all the traffic

The trap

Calling MoE a memory saving. It is a compute saving: the router sends each token to two experts of eight, so FLOPs per token fall, and every one of the eight stays resident in VRAM because the next token may need any of them. Mixtral 8x7B activates 12.9B parameters and occupies 46.7B worth of weights, about 93 GB at bf16. Quote the active count for latency and the total for the shopping list, and never the wrong one.

The math two numbers, two different questions

Pactive​=Pshared​+Nk​Pexperts​  ·  Mixtral: N=8, k=2, 46.7B total, 12.9B active  ·  VRAM ∝ total, FLOPs ∝ activeCount Mixtral 8x7B out once and both published figures fall out. dmodel​=4096, dff​=14336, 32 layers, 8 experts, top-2, GQA with 32 query and 8 key-value heads, vocabulary 32,000. One expert is a SwiGLU feed-forward block, so three matrices of 4096×14336: 3×58.7M=176.2M parameters. Eight of those per layer is 1.409B, and across 32 layers that is 45.1B sitting in experts alone. Attention adds 16.8+4.2+4.2+16.8=41.9M per layer, so 1.34B, and the two embedding matrices add 0.26B. Total 45.1+1.34+0.26=46.7B, which is the number on the model card. Now the active count: two experts of eight, so 2×176.2M×32=11.3B, plus the same shared 1.6B, giving 12.9B — also exactly the published number. At bf16 that is 93.4 GB to hold and 25.8 GB worth of arithmetic to do, which is the whole card in one line. DeepSeek-V3 is the same trick at another scale: 671B total, 37B active, 256 routed experts plus one shared expert, top-8.

The router, and the loss that stops it playing favourites

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

N, K = 8, 2                          # Mixtral: 8 experts per layer, top-2
logits = router(x)                   # (tokens, 8) - one linear layer, that is all
w, idx = torch.topk(logits, K, dim=-1)
w = F.softmax(w, dim=-1)             # renormalise over the CHOSEN two only
y = sum(w[:, j:j+1] * experts[idx[:, j]](x) for j in range(K))   # maths, not kernel

# load balancing, Switch Transformer: penalise the router for favouritism
f = torch.bincount(idx[:, 0], minlength=N).float() / len(x)   # tokens per expert
P = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1).mean(0)                         # mean gate per expert
loss = task_loss + 0.01 * N * (f * P).sum()      # alpha = 0.01 is the usual default

# every one of the 8 expert modules is on the GPU for every token. two of
# them do work. that sentence is the whole VRAM answer.

Where this bites in production

Mixtral 8x7B is the config to have memorised: 46.7B total, 12.9B active, matching or beating Llama 2 70B on most benchmarks at roughly a sixth of the compute per token — and needing about 93 GB of bf16 weights, so two 80 GB cards or a 4-bit quantisation. Mistral also looked for topical specialisation in the routing and reported finding none, only a tendency for consecutive tokens to reuse an expert.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Total versus active parameters — which one determines your VRAM?
The total, every time. All experts stay resident because routing is decided per token per layer and the next token could need any of them; there is no time to page one in mid-decode. Mixtral 8x7B is 46.7B of weights, about 93 GB at bf16, and no 80 GB card holds it. The active count — 12.9B — sets FLOPs per token and therefore latency and cost per token. Two numbers, two questions: total for the shopping list, active for the speed.
What is the auxiliary loss for?
To stop the router collapsing onto a few favourite experts. Routing is a positive feedback loop: an expert that gets slightly more traffic trains faster, gets better, and attracts more, while the rest starve and become dead weight you are still paying VRAM for. The Switch Transformer loss penalises the product of the token fraction and the mean gate per expert, scaled by 0.01, and is minimised when the load is uniform. DeepSeek-V3 does it without an auxiliary term, adjusting a per-expert bias during training instead.
You have one 80 GB H100. Can you serve Mixtral 8x7B?
Not at bf16 — 46.7B of weights is about 93 GB before you allocate a single KV block. Your options are two cards with tensor parallelism, an 8-bit build at roughly 47 GB, or a 4-bit build at roughly 23 GB, which leaves real room for the cache. Notice what quoting the 12.9B active figure would have done here: it suggests 26 GB and a comfortable fit, and you would have ordered the wrong hardware.

Say this back tomorrow

MoE cuts FLOPs per token, not VRAM  ·  every expert stays resident
  • A router picks the top two of eight experts per token per layer; attention is shared
  • VRAM follows the total parameter count, latency and cost follow the active count
  • Without a load-balancing loss the router collapses onto a few experts and the rest starve

  • router
  • top-2 routing
  • auxiliary loss
  • expert collapse
  • total vs active

Extending Context: Interpolation & YaRN

You do not get 128k by asking for it. You rescale the rotation, train briefly on long documents, and then pay for it on every request.

Position is carried into the model as an angle that turns a little further for every step along the text. A model trained on shorter documents has only ever seen angles up to a certain point, so if you hand it something much longer the angles run off into territory it has never seen and the output falls apart. There are two repairs. The first squeezes the position numbers so a long document lands back inside the range it knows. That works, but it blurs the fine detail, because the fastest-turning parts get squeezed hardest and those are the parts that carry which word sits next to which. The second is cleverer: leave the fast parts alone and squeeze only the slow ones, which carry roughly where you are in the document. Then train briefly on genuinely long documents to let it settle.

Like re-tuning a clock. The seconds hand tells you where you are in the minute, the hour hand where you are in the day. Stretch the day into a week by slowing every hand equally and you can no longer read seconds at all. Slow only the hour hand and the fine reading survives, which is exactly the trick.

RoPE rotates the query and key pair i at position m by mθi​, with θi​=b−2i/d and base b=10,000. Every extension method is a change to that one angle. Position interpolation divides the position index by the scale factor s, so 128k positions land inside the 8k the model trained on — uniform, easy, and it compresses the high-frequency dimensions that encode local order, so it needs a fine-tuning run to recover, about 1,000 steps in the original paper. NTK-aware scaling changes the base instead, b→bsd/(d−2), which barely moves the fastest dimensions and stretches the slowest ones. YaRN generalises that per frequency band: a dimension whose wavelength is shorter than the trained context is left alone, one whose wavelength exceeds it is interpolated fully, a ramp handles the band in between, and the attention logits get a small temperature correction. YaRN reached 128k with about 400 steps on roughly 0.1% of the original pretraining tokens. Then you continue pretraining on long documents and evaluate by length.

Say what you pay, unprompted, because that is where the card earns its place. Prefill is quadratic in prompt length, so time to first token grows faster than the prompt does. The KV cache is linear in sequence length and in batch: Llama-3-70B is about 320 KB per token, so one 128k conversation is roughly 43 GB of cache, half an H100 before you serve a second user. And recall in the middle of a long window degrades well before the advertised limit, so a model that scores well at 8k can be materially worse at 100k. Then the run-time half, which is a different question wearing the same hat: what do you do when an agent fills the window on turn 30? The trap answer is to drop the oldest messages, which is precisely the system prompt and the early tool results — you have deleted the contract and the evidence and kept the small talk. What you actually do is pin and compact: keep the system prompt and the last few turns verbatim, summarise the middle into a running brief, push large tool outputs to a file or a scratchpad and re-read them on demand, and evict by relevance rather than by age. Watch the prompt cache while you do it: compaction rewrites the prefix, so every cached token after that point is invalidated. Compact rarely, at a stable boundary, and always reserve room for the completion.

You reach for it when

  • Asked how a model got from 8k to 128k
  • Setting rope_scaling on a checkpoint you did not train
  • An agent that fills its window halfway through a long session
  • Deciding what to drop first when the prompt will not fit

The trap

Answering “truncate the oldest messages” when the window fills. The oldest messages are the system prompt and the first tool results — the contract the agent is working under and the evidence it gathered — so you have deleted the two things it cannot rebuild and kept the pleasantries. Pin the system prompt and the recent turns, compact the middle into a summary, and evict by relevance. The related mistake is quoting a context length you have never evaluated at.

The math three ways to change one angle

θi​=b−2i/d, rotate by mθi​  ·  PI: m→m/s  ·  NTK: b→bsd/(d−2)  ·  YaRN: per band, and 1/t​=0.1lns+1Going from 8,192 to 131,072 is a scale factor s=16, and the three methods spend it differently. Position interpolation applies m→m/16 everywhere, so the fastest dimension — wavelength about 2π tokens, the one that distinguishes adjacent words — is compressed sixteen-fold along with everything else. NTK-aware scaling instead raises the base by sd/(d−2), which leaves θ0​ almost unchanged and stretches the slowest dimensions the most; Llama 3 did a blunt version of the same thing by shipping a base of 500,000 rather than 10,000. YaRN makes the split explicit using the wavelength λi​=2π/θi​: if λi​ is shorter than the trained context, that dimension saw whole cycles during training and is left alone; if it is longer, the model only ever saw part of one cycle and it is interpolated; a ramp covers the band between, tuned with α=1 and β=32 for Llama models. The attention temperature is the last piece: longer sequences spread attention thinner, so YaRN scales the logits by a factor fitted as 1/t​=0.1lns+1, which costs nothing because it folds into the existing 1/dk​​. Then the bill, which no rescaling can avoid: prefill is O(n2), and at 320 KB per token a 70B holding 128k tokens is about 43 GB of KV cache for a single sequence.

Extension in a config, compaction in a line

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",
    rope_scaling={"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0,        # 32k -> 131k
                  "original_max_position_embeddings": 32768})
# vLLM takes the same dict: --rope-scaling '{"rope_type":"yarn","factor":4.0}'
# static YaRN scales EVERY prompt, so a 2k request pays for it too. enable it
# for the long-context deployment, not for the general one.

# the run-time half. never this:
#   history = history[-10:]        # drops the system prompt AND the tool results
kept = [system, summarise(history[:-6])] + history[-6:]   # pin, compact, pin
# and note the compaction rewrote the prefix: your prompt cache is cold from here.

Where this bites in production

Qwen2.5 ships the whole argument in its model card: add a rope_scaling block with "factor": 4.0 and original_max_position_embeddings of 32,768 to reach 131,072 — and their own guidance is to add it only when you are actually processing long inputs, because static YaRN rescales every position regardless of the input length and measurably degrades short prompts. Llama 3.1 went from 8k to 128k the expensive way, in six stages of continued pretraining.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How do you take a model trained at 8k out to 128k?
Rescale the RoPE angle, then train briefly on long documents, then evaluate by length. Position interpolation squeezes the position indices into the trained range and is simple but blurs local detail; NTK-aware scaling and YaRN change the frequency bands unevenly, leaving the fast dimensions intact so adjacent-word structure survives. YaRN reached 128k with roughly 400 steps on about 0.1% of the original pretraining tokens. None of it is free at run time, and none of it is finished until you have a length-stratified eval.
Your agent hits the context limit on turn 30. What now?
Pin and compact — never evict by age. Dropping the oldest messages throws away the system prompt and the early tool results, which is the contract and the evidence. Keep the system prompt and the last few turns verbatim, summarise the middle into a running brief, spill big tool outputs to a file the agent can re-read, and reserve headroom for the completion. Do it at a stable boundary, because rewriting the prefix invalidates every cached token after it.
What does running at 128k actually cost you?
Quadratic prefill, a linear KV cache, and worse recall in the middle. Time to first token grows faster than the prompt, because attention is quadratic in length. The cache grows linearly in both sequence length and batch size — about 320 KB per token on Llama-3-70B, so roughly 43 GB for one 128k conversation, which is what caps your concurrency. And accuracy on material buried mid-prompt degrades before you reach the advertised limit, so advertised length is a capacity and not a promise.

Say this back tomorrow

interpolation squeezes every band  ·  YaRN squeezes only the slow ones  ·  then you fine-tune
  • Every extension trick is a rescaling of the RoPE angle, then a short continued-pretraining run
  • YaRN leaves the high-frequency bands alone, which is why it needs far less training than interpolation
  • At run time you pin the system prompt and recent turns and compact the middle — never truncate by age

Scaling Laws & Chinchilla

Twenty tokens per parameter is the cheapest way to train a model. If you are the one paying for inference, it is the wrong objective.

Suppose you have a fixed budget of computing time for training. You can spend it on a bigger model or on more text, and for years almost everyone spent it on size. A result from 2022 showed the balance was wrong: for a given budget the two should grow together, at roughly twenty words of text for every number in the model, and a model four times smaller trained that way beat the giant it was compared against. Now the part that matters to you. That rule answers one question only, which is the cheapest way to reach a given quality during training. If you are going to serve the model, the training bill is paid once and the serving bill never stops. So you deliberately break the rule: choose a smaller model, train it on far more text than the rule allows, and make every future request cheaper for ever.

Think of buying a delivery van. The cheapest way to get one van on the road is one calculation. The cheapest way to run a fleet for five years is a different calculation, and it buys a smaller van with a better engine. Chinchilla answers the first question very well. You are almost always asking the second one.

Kaplan et al., 2020: loss falls as a smooth power law in compute, parameters and data, with no wall in sight. Hoffmann et al., 2022 — Chinchilla — re-fit it with the learning-rate schedule handled properly and found the earlier work had systematically undertrained. For a compute-optimal run, parameters and tokens should scale in roughly equal proportion, which lands at about 20 tokens per parameter. The demonstration was Chinchilla at 70B on 1.4T tokens against Gopher at 280B on 300B tokens, same compute, and the smaller model won broadly and was four times cheaper to serve afterwards. Then the turn that gets you the offer: compute-optimal is a training objective. It minimises training FLOPs for a target loss and is silent on the cost of running the thing. If you serve it, you push data far past 20 to 1 and take a smaller model at a slightly worse loss. Llama 3 8B was trained on about 15T tokens — roughly 1,875 per parameter, some 94 times Chinchilla — with Meta reporting performance still improving log-linearly.

Four caveats, and each of them is a follow-up in its own right. First, the law predicts loss, not capability. Cross-entropy comes down smoothly and tells you nothing about when a particular ability appears; much of the apparent discontinuity in emergence plots is an artefact of scoring with a discontinuous metric like exact match, and the same runs look smooth under a graded one. Second, it assumes an endless supply of fresh tokens. Repeating data is not free: up to about four epochs it behaves close to new data, and after that returns fall away fast, which is the data wall behind synthetic data and aggressive filtering. Third, 20 to 1 is a fitted constant, not a law of nature — it moves with architecture, tokeniser and data quality, so quote it as a ratio worth knowing rather than a number to obey. Fourth, there is now a third axis: spending compute at inference time on longer reasoning traces buys accuracy on some tasks without touching the weights at all, and that trades against everything above. The practitioner’s summary is short. Over-train a small model, then distil, then quantise. All three make the number you pay per request smaller, and only the first has anything to do with Chinchilla.

You reach for it when

  • Asked why small models are trained far past compute-optimal
  • Choosing a model size for something you will serve at volume
  • Someone quotes 20 to 1 as though it settles the question
  • Justifying a pretraining budget to someone who signs for it

The trap

Quoting 20 to 1 with no idea what it implies. It is the ratio that minimises training compute for a target loss, fitted on one model family in 2022, and it is silent on inference. Recite it as a rule and the follow-up — so how should that change the model you pick? — has no answer. The answer is that anyone paying per request deliberately over-trains a smaller model, which is why an 8B trained on 15T tokens exists at all.

The math one budget, split two ways

C≈6ND  ·  compute-optimal: D≈20N  ·  L(N,D)=E+NαA​+DβB​The first expression is the one to be able to write down: training compute is about six FLOPs per parameter per token, two for the forward pass and four for the backward. It is what makes the trade-off concrete — at a fixed C, halving N doubles D. The third is Chinchilla’s fitted form, and their constants were E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7, α=0.34, β=0.28: the two exponents are close, which is the entire finding, because it means parameters and tokens deserve roughly equal shares of any new budget. Put numbers on it. A 70B at 20 to 1 wants 1.4T tokens and costs 6×7×1010×1.4×1012≈5.9×1023 FLOPs, which is Chinchilla. Llama 3 8B on 15T tokens costs 6×8×109×1.5×1013≈7.2×1023 — more training compute than Chinchilla, for a model an eighth the size. Now the argument that justifies it, and it is one line. Inference costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so the training bill is repaid once you have served 6ND/2N=3D tokens. The model size cancels. For Llama 3 8B that is 45 trillion served tokens, and any product with real traffic gets there — which is why every serving team over-trains and no one who trains a model to publish a benchmark does.

The budget, and when inference overtakes it

def train_flops(N, D):               # the standard approximation
    return 6 * N * D                 # forward + backward, per parameter, per token

chinchilla = 70e9, 1.4e12            # 20 tokens per parameter - compute-optimal
llama3_8b  = 8e9,  15e12             # 1,875 per parameter - about 94x Chinchilla

for name, (N, D) in [("chinchilla-70B", chinchilla), ("llama-3-8B", llama3_8b)]:
    print(f"{name:>15} {D/N:>7.0f} tok/param  {train_flops(N, D):.1e} FLOPs")
# chinchilla-70B      20 tok/param  5.9e+23 FLOPs
#     llama-3-8B    1875 tok/param  7.2e+23 FLOPs   <- MORE compute, smaller model

# inference is about 2N FLOPs per token, so training is repaid after
# 6ND / 2N = 3D served tokens. N cancels. for llama-3-8B that is 45e12 tokens.

Where this bites in production

Chinchilla is the experiment worth quoting: 70B on 1.4T tokens against Gopher’s 280B on 300B tokens at the same compute, and the four-times-smaller model won broadly — 67.5% against 60% on MMLU — while being far cheaper to run afterwards. Llama 3 is the counter-move: an 8B trained on over 15T tokens when Chinchilla would have said roughly 200B, with Meta reporting that performance kept improving log-linearly the whole way.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

20 to 1 — why does that matter to you?
Because it is a training objective and you are paying for inference. Chinchilla minimises the compute needed to reach a target loss, and it is silent on the bill that starts the day you deploy. If you serve the model, you want a smaller one trained on far more tokens than 20 to 1 allows: slightly worse loss, dramatically lower cost and latency on every request. That is exactly why an 8B trained on 15T tokens exists, at about 94 times the Chinchilla ratio.
What does the scaling law not tell you?
When a capability shows up. The power law predicts cross-entropy loss, which falls smoothly and predictably; it does not predict that a model will suddenly do arithmetic or follow a schema. Much of the apparent jumpiness in emergence plots is a scoring artefact — exact-match metrics turn a smooth improvement into a step — and the same runs look continuous under a graded metric. So it is a good planning tool for loss and a bad forecasting tool for capability.
You are given a fixed budget and a product that will serve heavy traffic. How do you spend it?
Take a smaller model and push it far past 20 to 1. Compute is roughly six times parameters times tokens, so at a fixed budget every halving of the model buys a doubling of the tokens, and the bottom of the IsoFLOP curve is broad enough that you give up very little loss. Watch two limits: unique data runs out, and repeated data is close to free for about four epochs and poor after that. Then distil and quantise, which are the other two levers on the same bill.

Say this back tomorrow

compute-optimal is a training rule  ·  if you serve it, over-train something smaller
  • Chinchilla: parameters and tokens scale together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter
  • Compute-optimal minimises training cost; serving cost points the other way, to smaller and over-trained
  • The law predicts loss, not capability, and it assumes tokens you have not run out of yet

  • Chinchilla
  • 20 tokens per param
  • C = 6ND
  • over-training
  • IsoFLOP

Catastrophic Forgetting

Your domain metric climbs all the way through the run. Everything you did not measure goes down quietly beside it.

Train a model further on a narrow pile of your own data and it gets better at that. It also gets worse at things it used to do well: following an instruction, refusing what it should refuse, answering in another language, holding a format. Nothing warns you, because the only number anyone is watching is the one you set out to improve, and that one is going up the whole time. The way you find out is dull and it has to be decided before you start. You keep a second, fixed set of ordinary questions, you score it before the run so you have a baseline, and then you score it again at every checkpoint next to your own. The two lines part company well before the training loss stops falling, and the point where they part is the checkpoint you should have kept.

Think of a doctor who spends a year on nothing but dermatology. Their rash diagnoses get sharper every week, and their cardiology quietly rots, and nobody notices, because the only exam anyone has been setting is about rashes. You find out when a patient with chest pain walks in.

Fine-tuning shifts the whole weight distribution, not the small part your task happens to use, so capability outside the training distribution degrades: instruction following, refusal behaviour, other languages, output format, sometimes adherence to the chat template itself. The aligned-model version of this has a name — Ouyang et al. called it the alignment tax when InstructGPT regressed against GPT-3 on public NLP benchmarks, and they mixed pretraining gradients back into the PPO objective to claw it back. Detection is the whole question, and the answer is structural rather than clever: freeze a general-capability holdout before the run, score it to get a baseline, and then run it beside the domain eval at every checkpoint rather than once at the end. A hundred to five hundred prompts is enough, covering instruction following, format adherence, refusals, any language you serve, and some general knowledge. Then early-stop on the general curve, not on the domain one, and gate the release on the general delta.

Mitigations, in the order you should reach for them. Lower the learning rate — 2e-4 is a normal LoRA rate and roughly ten times a full fine-tune’s, and a great deal of reported forgetting is nothing more than a run that was too hot. Fewer epochs: one to three is the usual range and the damage compounds with each pass over a narrow set. Prefer LoRA to full fine-tuning, because a rank-16 update perturbs a 16-dimensional subspace of a 4096-wide projection rather than every weight in it, and because you can unload an adapter, which is the cheapest possible undo. Replay: mix general instruction data back into the training mixture, commonly 5 to 30%, task-dependent, which is the same idea as InstructGPT’s pretraining-gradient mixing at a smaller scale. Early stopping on the general eval sits over all of it. The literature has heavier machinery — elastic weight consolidation, which penalises movement in parameters with high Fisher information, and L2-SP, which penalises distance from the starting weights — and almost nobody uses either on language models, because estimating the Fisher needs the original pretraining data you do not have, while replay and a lower learning rate are cheap and work. One judgement to state plainly: a model eight points better on your domain and six points worse at instruction following is usually a worse product, because your users do not send you only the domain query.

You reach for it when

  • Planning a fine-tune, before a single step has run
  • The domain metric is up and users say the model got worse
  • Deciding what goes into an eval suite and what gates a release
  • Choosing between LoRA and a full fine-tune on a narrow corpus

The trap

Reporting only the domain metric. It rises monotonically through the run, so it can never tell you to stop, and early stopping configured on it will never fire. The general capability that pays for the rest of your product — instructions followed, refusals held, formats respected, other languages — degrades silently in the same run. Without a general holdout scored against a recorded pre-run baseline, you have no way to see it and no checkpoint to fall back to.

The math two ways to hold on to the old behaviour

EWC: L=Ldomain​+λ∑i​Fi​(θi​−θi∗​)2  ·  replay: L=Ldomain​+γLgeneral​, γ≈0.05 to 0.3The first line is elastic weight consolidation and it is worth understanding even though you will probably never run it. θ∗ is the weight vector before your fine-tune, and Fi​ is the Fisher information for parameter i — a per-parameter estimate of how much the old task cared about it — so the penalty is an anisotropic spring: parameters the old behaviour depended on are held tightly, the rest are free. The reason nobody uses it on a language model is in that definition: estimating F needs the original pretraining data, and you do not have it. The second line is what teams actually do, and it is the same idea by brute force — keep some general instruction data in the mixture so the old behaviour keeps generating gradient. Common mixes run 5 to 30% general, and it is genuinely task-dependent, so treat those as a starting sweep and not a recommendation. LoRA earns its place here for a structural reason: the update is ΔW=BA with rank r, so at r=16 on a 4096×4096 projection the perturbation is confined to a 16-dimensional subspace out of 4096 — a smaller change to make and a change you can remove entirely by unloading the adapter. And size the holdout honestly: 100 to 500 prompts, stratified across instruction following, format, refusals and any language you serve, scored before the run so that what you report is a delta rather than a number.

The callback that catches it

# the whole card is this: TWO eval sets, scored at EVERY checkpoint.
general = load("holdout/general.jsonl")   # frozen BEFORE the run. 200 prompts.
domain  = load("holdout/domain.jsonl")    # the thing you are trying to improve
base    = score(model, general)           # record it, or you have no delta later

class WatchGeneral(TrainerCallback):
    def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, model=None, **kw):
        g, d = score(model, general), score(model, domain)
        print(state.global_step, f"domain {d:.3f}  general {g:.3f} ({g - base:+.3f})")
        control.should_training_stop = g < base - 0.02   # stop on the GENERAL curve

# early stopping on the domain metric is the mistake: it rises all run and
# never fires. and save every checkpoint - the one you want is not the last.

Where this bites in production

Qi et al. (2023) is the documented case worth citing: fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo through the public API on ten adversarially chosen examples, for well under a dollar, stripped most of its safety behaviour — and fine-tuning on entirely benign, widely used instruction sets such as Alpaca and Dolly degraded it measurably too. Nobody in either case was running a safety eval after the run, which is exactly the hole this card is about.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How would you detect it?
With a general-capability holdout scored beside the domain eval at every checkpoint. You cannot detect it after the fact, because the only artefact left is a model and a rising domain curve. Freeze 100 to 500 prompts before the run — instruction following, format adherence, refusals, any language you serve, some general knowledge — record the pre-run baseline so you are reporting a delta, and run both evals on every checkpoint. Then early-stop and gate the release on the general curve, not the domain one.
Your domain score went from 0.71 to 0.86 and users say the model got worse. What happened?
You moved the whole distribution, and only measured one slice of it. A narrow fine-tune degrades instruction following, refusals, formatting and other languages along with everything else outside your training data, and none of that appears in a domain metric. Score a general holdout on the old model and on each checkpoint of the new one, find where the two curves part, and roll back to that checkpoint. Then rerun with a lower learning rate, fewer epochs, or general data mixed back in.
How do you reduce it without giving up the gain?
Lower the learning rate first, then shorten the run, then use LoRA, then replay. Most reported forgetting is a run that was too hot or went too many epochs, so start there: one to three epochs, and a rate at the low end of your sweep. LoRA confines the update to a rank-16 subspace and can simply be unloaded. Mixing 5 to 30% general instruction data back into the training set keeps the old behaviour generating gradient. Early stopping on the general eval sits over all four.

the domain metric only ever goes up  ·  the general holdout is the one that tells you
  • A narrow fine-tune shifts the whole distribution — instructions, refusals, formats and languages all move
  • You can only detect it with a general holdout, baselined before the run and scored every checkpoint
  • Lower the learning rate, run fewer epochs, prefer LoRA, replay general data, early-stop on the general curve

  • alignment tax
  • replay mixing
  • early stopping
  • LoRA perturbs less

The AI engineer stack

The biggest block, on purpose — this is where the 2026 loop actually lives. Retrieval that finds the right thing, tools the model can call, agents that stop, evaluation that is not vibes, and a serving stack whose bill you can predict. If you only have one evening, spend it here.

You are my AI/ML interview tutor. This session covers ONE block of large language models and the AI engineer stack: In Production — The AI engineer stack

The topics in this block are:
1. The RAG Pipeline, Stage by Stage — Ten stages, and four of them run before anyone asks a question. The interview is about which one broke
2. Chunking — The chunk is the unit of retrieval, so it is also the unit of missing context
3. Vector Databases, HNSW & ANN Recall — Approximate nearest neighbour search is approximate. Recall below one is a dial you set, not a bug you fix
4. Hybrid Search & Reciprocal Rank Fusion — Dense retrieval knows what your question was about. BM25 knows what it literally said
5. Reranking: Bi-Encoder vs Cross-Encoder — Two stages exist because one model can be cheap and one can be accurate, and no model is both
6. Query Transformation: HyDE, Multi-Query & Decomposition — The user typed a question. The thing you are searching is an answer. That gap is a retrieval bug you can fix before you search
7. Embedding Migration & Reindexing — Two embedding models build two coordinate systems, and there is no exchange rate between them. So the upgrade is not an edit. It is a rebuild
8. Function Calling & Structured Outputs — The model never runs anything. It writes down what it would like you to run, and everything after that is your code
9. Agents & the Agent Loop — A chain is a path you drew. An agent draws its own, one step at a time, and the interview is about how it stops
10. Agent Memory — Chat history is one of four kinds, and it is the one that runs out first
11. Multi-Agent Systems & MCP — The right number of agents is usually one. And MCP is not an API standard — it is a statement about who is allowed to decide
12. Evaluation: Golden Sets & LLM-as-Judge — Asked verbatim in OpenAI loops: is there an actual eval framework here, or is it vibes-based? Everything else on this page is downstream of the answer
13. Observability, Tracing & Cost — A trace is one user request. A span is one stage inside it. If the answer is “we log prompts and responses”, you have neither, and you cannot say what changed
14. Guardrails & Prompt Injection — A classifier filters text. The layer that stops harm is the one that decides whether an action is allowed to run at all, and it lives in your code
15. Hallucination in Production — Three different failures wear the same word, and they have three different repairs. In a retrieval system the answer is usually that nothing useful was retrieved
16. Caching: Prompt, Exact & Semantic — Three mechanisms, three keys, three failure modes. Two of them save money quietly. The third can serve a wrong answer with a completely straight face
17. Serving: vLLM, Continuous Batching & PagedAttention — Two separate fixes that candidates merge into one: paging solves wasted memory, continuous batching solves the queue. And neither lets you run the GPU flat out
18. Prefill vs Decode, TTFT vs TPOT — One half is parallel and compute-bound, the other is sequential and memory-bandwidth-bound. Every serving argument in this module is downstream of that one sentence

The RAG Pipeline, Stage by Stage

Ten stages, and four of them run before anyone asks a question. The interview is about which one broke.

Retrieval-augmented generation is two pipelines that meet at a prompt. The first runs before anyone asks anything: you take the documents, pull the text out of whatever format they arrived in, cut them into pieces, turn each piece into a vector, and store those vectors in an index. That work happens on a schedule, in bulk, and it is the half people forget to describe. The second runs while a user waits: turn their question into a vector, fetch the nearest pieces, reorder them with a slower and more careful model, paste the survivors into a prompt with an instruction to answer only from them, generate, and attach citations. When the answer is wrong, the useful question is which of those ten steps failed, because they fail differently and they are fixed differently.

Think of a library with a research assistant. Long before you arrive, someone catalogued every book, cut it into passages and filed the cards. When you ask, the assistant pulls a stack, throws out the ones that only looked relevant, and hands over the shortlist. If the answer is wrong it was the filing or the reading, and those are two different people to talk to.

Ten stages. Offline: parse (PDF, HTML, tables, OCR, and keep the structure), chunk, embed, index — batched, on a schedule, with a re-indexing path for changed and deleted documents. Online: embed the query, retrieve the top 50 to 100 by vector or hybrid search, rerank with a cross-encoder down to 5 to 10, assemble the prompt, generate, cite. Name freshness explicitly — incremental upsert on change, tombstones on delete, a periodic full rebuild — because “search plus an LLM” with no ingestion story is the classic failed answer. Then separate the metrics. Retrieval is scored with recall@k, MRR and nDCG@k against a golden set that records the ideal chunk IDs. Generation is scored with faithfulness, answer relevance and citation accuracy, conditioned on what retrieval actually returned. Different failures, different fixes, and one number over the whole pipeline hides both.

The follow-up is a debugging ladder and you walk it in order. First, did the chunk actually contain the answer? Retrieving the right document is not the same as retrieving the span that answers the question, and a page-level chunk can rank first while the sentence you need sits in the next chunk. Second, did it survive assembly? Read the prompt that was actually sent, after truncation, deduplication and ordering — a top-5 quietly cut to 3 by a token budget is a silent failure, and material in the middle of a long context is read less reliably than material at either end. Third, did the prompt tell the model to ground itself? An instruction to answer only from the provided context, to cite the chunk ID for every claim, and to say it does not know is doing real work; without it the model answers from its weights and nothing in your logs objects. Fourth, did generation ignore the context anyway? Score faithfulness against the retrieved text with a judge or an NLI model, and keep the failing case. Underneath all four sits the golden set, which is what makes any of this measurable: sample real production queries, dedupe, stratify by slice, have a subject expert write the ideal answer and record the ideal chunk IDs, version it in the repository next to the code, and feed every incident back into it. 100 to 500 queries to start and 50 to 100 per slice. When they ask how many queries are in your smallest slice, you should know the number.

You reach for it when

  • The opening technical question of an AI engineer loop
  • Debugging an answer that is wrong even though retrieval looks fine
  • Designing ingestion for a corpus that changes every day
  • Deciding what to measure before you have any metrics at all

The trap

Describing RAG as “search plus an LLM” and stopping. That answer has no ingestion story, so the interviewer asks who parses the PDFs, what happens when a document changes, and how a deleted document leaves the index — and there is nothing there. The second half of the same trap is quoting one accuracy number for the whole pipeline. Retrieval failures and generation failures need different metrics and different fixes, and a single score hides which one you have.

The math two metric families, and the ceiling one puts on the other

recall@k=∣R∣∣R∩Dk​∣​  ·  MRR=N1​∑i​ranki​1​  ·  faithfulness=claims madeclaims supported by context​Read the first two as the retrieval half and the third as the generation half, then notice the relationship between them. recall@k is the fraction of the chunks that should have been found which appear anywhere in the top k, and it is a ceiling: if the answer is not in the candidate set, no reranker, no prompt and no larger model recovers it. So measure recall@100 on the retriever and precision@5 after the reranker, because those are two different stages answering two different questions. MRR rewards putting the first relevant result high, which is what matters when only five chunks reach the prompt. nDCG@k is the one to reach for when relevance is graded rather than binary. Faithfulness is the generation-side number — split the answer into claims and ask what fraction is supported by the retrieved text — and it is deliberately blind to whether the answer is correct, because an answer can be perfectly faithful to a chunk that was the wrong chunk. That is exactly why you report both. Then the budget, illustrative rather than universal: query embedding 50 to 100 ms, vector retrieval 50 to 150 ms, rerank 100 to 300 ms, prompt assembly around 50 ms, first token 300 to 800 ms, streamed completion 500 to 1,000 ms. Everything before the first token is dead air the user is staring at, which is why reranking is the stage people cut first and the stage they miss most.

Both halves, and the two places you measure

# OFFLINE - runs on a schedule, never on the request path.
for doc in changed_since(last_run):                  # freshness IS a stage
    for ch in chunk(parse(doc)):                     # parse keeps tables + headings
        index.upsert(id=ch.id, vector=embed(ch.text), payload=ch.meta)
index.delete(ids=deleted_doc_chunk_ids)              # tombstones, or you serve ghosts

# ONLINE - every millisecond here is a user watching a spinner.
def answer(q, session):
    cands  = index.search(embed(q), limit=100, tenant=session.tenant)
    top    = rerank(q, cands)[:8]                    # cross-encoder, 100 -> 8
    prompt = build(SYSTEM, top)                      # log THIS, not the template
    return generate(prompt)                          # cite chunk ids or refuse

# two evals, not one: recall@100 on `cands`, faithfulness on the output given `top`.

Where this bites in production

The name comes from Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020: a DPR retriever over a Wikipedia index feeding a BART generator, trained end to end, marginalising the output over the retrieved passages. Almost none of that architecture survives in what teams build now — retriever and generator are separate frozen services and the “training” is prompt assembly. What survived is the shape, and the finding that grounding a generator in retrieved passages beat a much larger closed-book model on open-domain question answering.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Retrieval returns the right documents but the answer is still wrong. Where do you look?
Four places, in this order: the chunk, the assembly, the prompt, the generation. Did the retrieved chunk actually contain the answering span, or just the right document? Did it survive assembly — check the prompt that was really sent, after truncation, dedup and ordering. Did the prompt instruct the model to answer only from context and cite chunk IDs? Only then ask whether generation ignored grounded context, which you catch by scoring faithfulness against the retrieved text. Three of those four are pipeline bugs, not model bugs.
How do you evaluate a RAG system?
Two metric families against one golden set, never one number. Retrieval gets recall@k, MRR and nDCG@k, scored against the ideal chunk IDs recorded in the set; generation gets faithfulness, answer relevance and citation accuracy, conditioned on what retrieval actually returned. They fail separately and are fixed separately — recall is fixed by chunking, hybrid search and the reranker, faithfulness by the prompt and the model. A single end-to-end score tells you something is wrong and nothing about where.
Your golden set has 500 queries. How many are in your smallest slice?
If you cannot answer, the set is not stratified and the number is probably two. Build it from sampled production logs, deduped, then stratified deliberately by slice — document type, language, query intent, tenant — with 50 to 100 examples per slice, an SME-written ideal answer and the ideal chunk IDs recorded alongside. Version it in the repository and add every production incident back into it. A 500-query average can move by a point while a slice you never counted collapses.

  • Score retrieval with recall@k and nDCG@k and generation with faithfulness and citation accuracy, separately
  • Recall@k is a ceiling: what the retriever missed, no reranker, prompt or bigger model recovers

Chunking

The chunk is the unit of retrieval, so it is also the unit of missing context.

A chunk is the smallest thing your system can retrieve, so whatever a chunk leaves out is invisible at answer time. That is the whole difficulty. A financial report states on its first page that every figure in it is quoted in thousands, then prints tables for another ninety pages. Cut it page by page and the page holding the table is a perfectly good chunk that has quietly lost the sentence telling you what its numbers mean. Retrieval works, the answer is confidently out by a factor of a thousand, and nothing in the logs looks broken. The repair is to stop treating a chunk as a free-standing lump of text: write a line of context into every chunk before you embed it, carry the document title and section heading down with it, and keep a way to reach the parent when the piece alone is not enough.

Like a photocopied page from a manual. The page in your hand says tighten to 90. Ninety what? The units were printed on the cover, and the cover is in a different pile. Every number on the page is correct and every one of them is unusable, and nothing about the page itself warns you.

Chunk size is a retrieval decision, not a formatting one: too small and a chunk carries no context, too large and the embedding averages several topics into one vector and precision falls. Starting points, and say out loud that they are starting points rather than a law — 512 tokens with about 10% overlap as a general default, 128 to 256 for FAQ and support snippets, 512 to 768 for technical and code documents, 768 to 1,024 for legal and long-form, with quality degrading noticeably past about 1,000 tokens. Overlap above 25 to 30% is waste: you are paying to store, embed and search the same sentences repeatedly. The hard constraint people forget is not in that list. The embedding model’s maximum input length caps your chunk size, full stop — many BERT-family encoders take 512 tokens and truncate in silence, OpenAI’s v3 models take 8,191. Split on structure first, on headings, sections, list items and table rows, and fall back to a fixed window only where there is no structure to split on.

Four repairs for document-wide context, in the order you should reach for them. Metadata propagation is free: carry the document title, the heading path, the effective date, the version and the source URL as fields on every chunk, prepend the heading path to the text you embed, and a surprising share of the problem goes away. Contextual retrieval is the strong one — before embedding, ask a cheap model for one or two sentences situating the chunk inside the whole document, something like “from the FY24 annual report, where all amounts in this section are stated in thousands of pounds”, and prepend that to the chunk text. It is one small call per chunk, at ingestion, once, and prompt caching over the source document is what makes it affordable. Late chunking inverts the order: run the whole document through a long-context embedding model, then pool the token vectors into chunk vectors, so every chunk vector has already seen the document; it needs a model that supports it and an input window long enough to hold the document. Parent-child, sometimes called small-to-big, indexes a small precise chunk for matching and hands the generator its larger parent, which separates what makes retrieval accurate from what makes an answer complete. Then stop arguing and measure: fix the retriever and the eval set, sweep three or four chunk configurations, and read recall@20 and answer faithfulness off the golden set. The right size is an empirical result on your corpus, and it is cheap to obtain.

You reach for it when

  • Ingesting reports, contracts or manuals where the meaning sits in a header
  • Retrieval scores look fine and the answers are still wrong
  • Picking a chunk size for a corpus you have never indexed
  • Choosing an embedding model, where the input limit decides the size

The trap

Quoting “512 tokens with 50 overlap” as though it were a rule. It is a default from a tutorial, and the follow-up is simply “why?” — at which point you need the reasoning: what the retrieval unit should be for this corpus, what the embedding model’s input limit allows, and what the document’s own structure gives you for free. The related mistake is splitting on character count straight through a table or a code block, destroying the one thing that made it retrievable.

The math the size you choose, and the size you are allowed

nchunks​≈c−oL​  ·  o≈0.1c  ·  hard cap: c≤cmax​ of the embedding modelPut numbers through it. A 40,000-token document at c=512 and o=51 gives about 40,000/461≈87 chunks. Take the overlap to 30% and the same document becomes 112 chunks, so you store, embed and search 29% more vectors for exactly the same text — that is what “overlap above 25 to 30% is waste” means in practice. Scale it up: ten million documents of that size is roughly 870 million chunks, which is an index-sizing problem before it is a quality problem, and at 1,024 dimensions in float32 that is about 3.6 TB of raw vectors before any compression or quantisation. The cap is the constraint to state first, though, because it is not negotiable. If the encoder accepts 512 input tokens then c cannot exceed 512 whatever your evaluation prefers, and passing more does not raise an error — most encoders truncate silently, so the tail of every long chunk is simply absent from the vector while everything continues to look healthy. Read the maximum input length off the model card before you tune anything, and read it again the day you change models.

Structure, then context, then metadata

# 1. split on STRUCTURE first (headings, sections, table rows), then on size.
MAX_IN = 512                                   # the encoder's cap. not a preference.
chunks = split_by_heading(doc.markdown, max_tokens=480, overlap=48)   # 480 < MAX_IN

# 2. contextual retrieval: one cheap LLM call per chunk, at INGESTION, once.
def contextualise(doc_text, chunk_text):
    ctx = llm(CONTEXT_PROMPT.format(doc=doc_text, chunk=chunk_text))  # ~1 sentence
    return ctx + "  " + chunk_text             # embed THIS, store the original

# 3. metadata travels with the chunk, or the units stay on page 1 forever.
for ch in chunks:
    index.upsert(vector=embed(contextualise(doc.markdown, ch.text)),
                 payload={"text": ch.text, "doc_id": doc.id, "title": doc.title,
                          "heading": ch.heading, "effective": doc.effective_date,
                          "parent_id": ch.parent_id})   # parent-child, for later
# prompt-cache the document prefix across step 2 or the ingestion bill triples.

Where this bites in production

Anthropic’s contextual retrieval write-up is the number to quote and it is specific: prepending a short LLM-generated context line to each chunk before embedding cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 35%, adding a contextual BM25 index took it to 49%, and putting a reranker on top reached 67%. The other half of that post is the cost argument — the per-chunk context call happens once at ingestion, and prompt caching over the source document is what makes running it across a whole corpus affordable.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Page 1 says all amounts are in thousands. You chunk page by page. Now what?
The chunk is right and the answer is out by a factor of a thousand, and no retrieval metric catches it. The fix is contextual retrieval: before embedding, have a cheap model write a sentence situating the chunk in its document — the report, the period, the units — and prepend it to the chunk text. Carry the units as a metadata field too, propagate the heading path, and index a small chunk while returning its parent section. Anthropic measured 35% fewer top-20 retrieval failures from the context line alone.
How do you choose a chunk size?
Start from the retrieval unit, respect the encoder’s cap, then sweep it on your own eval set. Ask what a self-contained answer looks like in this corpus — an FAQ answer is 128 to 256 tokens, a clause of a contract is 768 to 1,024 — and start at 512 with roughly 10% overlap when you have nothing better. Then hold the retriever and the golden set fixed, sweep three or four configurations, and read recall@20 and faithfulness. Overlap past 25 to 30% is pure storage and search cost.
What actually caps your chunk size?
The embedding model’s maximum input length, and it is a hard ceiling, not a guideline. Many BERT-family encoders take 512 tokens; OpenAI’s v3 models take 8,191. Exceeding it does not error — the encoder truncates in silence, so the end of every long chunk is missing from the vector while the pipeline reports success. Check the model card first, size chunks under the limit with headroom for a prepended context line, and re-check the day you swap embedding models.

a chunk is the unit of retrieval  ·  whatever it leaves out is invisible at answer time
  • 512 tokens with 10% overlap is a starting point; the corpus and the eval set decide the real number
  • The embedding model’s max input tokens is a hard cap on chunk size, and it truncates silently
  • Contextual retrieval, late chunking, parent-child and metadata propagation all restore what the split removed

Vector Databases, HNSW & ANN Recall

Approximate nearest neighbour search is approximate. Recall below one is a dial you set, not a bug you fix.

An index that compares your question against every stored vector gives exact answers and gets slower as the collection grows. So production systems use an approximate method instead. It walks a graph of vectors, hopping to whichever neighbour sits closer to the target and stopping when nothing nearby is any better. It is fast because it never looks at most of the collection, and for exactly that reason it sometimes misses a true nearest neighbour. That miss rate is a setting, not a defect: tell it to explore harder and it finds more and takes longer. Now add a filter, such as only this customer’s documents. If you let the walk range over everything and then discard whatever does not match, you can ask for ten results and receive two, and nothing warns you. The filter has to apply during the walk, not after it.

Think of asking a stranger for the nearest chemist. You walk to whoever they point at, ask again, and keep going until nobody knows anywhere closer. You arrive somewhere good, quickly, without a map of the whole city — and occasionally you stop two streets from a closer one that nobody happened to mention.

HNSW is a navigable small-world graph in layers. The top layer holds a sparse sample of the vectors joined by long-range links, and each layer down is denser; you enter at the top, greedily hop to whichever neighbour is closest to the query, drop a layer when you can no longer improve, and repeat, which makes search roughly logarithmic in the number of vectors. Two knobs matter at query time and one at build time. efsearch​ is the size of the candidate list the walk maintains — raise it and recall rises and so does latency, and it must be at least k. M is the number of links per node: more links means better recall and more memory, with 16 to 64 the usual range. efconstruction​ buys build-time quality. The framing that scores is that recall is not 1 and is not meant to be. You choose a target, 0.95 or 0.99, and tune efsearch​ until you hit it inside your latency budget, measured against an exact brute-force scan on a sample of real queries.

Filtering is the senior question. Post-filtering runs the walk over everything and discards non-matching results afterwards, so a selective filter can leave you with two documents when you asked for ten, and recall craters silently as the filter narrows. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set before the search, which is exact but degenerates into a scan once the subset is large. What production engines actually do is filtered search: the filter is consulted during traversal so the walk only ever expands nodes that match. Qdrant builds extra graph links per payload category to keep the filtered subgraph connected, and falls back to a plain scan when the matching set is small enough that walking a graph is not worth it. Multi-tenancy sits directly on top of this. A namespace or collection per tenant gives hard isolation, trivially correct deletion and clean per-tenant cost attribution, at the price of many small indexes and a cold start for each new tenant. A shared index with a tenant-ID filter scales to far more tenants but turns isolation into a property of how you construct the query — which means the tenant filter is injected by the server from the authenticated session and is never accepted from the client, ever. Either way the invariant is the same: no retrieval crosses a tenant boundary, and every retrieval is logged with the tenant, the filter and the returned chunk IDs so you can prove it afterwards. The last thing to have ready is migration. Vectors from two different embedding models are not comparable, so upgrading means a full re-index: build a shadow index, dual-write new documents into both, compare recall on the golden set offline, then cut over. There is no gradual mixing and no partial rollout at the vector level.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing between a namespace per tenant and a shared filtered index
  • A permissioned or per-user RAG system where every query carries a filter
  • Latency is fine and users report that results are missing
  • Upgrading an embedding model on an index already in production

The trap

Assuming the index returns the true nearest neighbours, then post-filtering on top of it. ANN recall is below 1 by construction — that is what buys the speed — so an evaluation that never compares against an exact scan cannot tell you what you are losing. Post-filtering compounds it: the walk is blind to your filter, so a selective tenant filter turns a request for ten results into two, and the metric that catches it is the one you are not collecting.

The math recall is a setting, and it has a price in milliseconds

recall@k=k∣ANNk​∩exactk​∣​  ·  search ≈O(logN)  ·  efsearch​≥k  ·  graph ≈2M⋅4 bytes per vectorRecall here is measured against the exact answer, not against relevance: take a sample of real queries, run a brute-force scan for the true top k, and count the overlap with what the index returned. That is the only honest way to know your operating point and it is cheap on a thousand queries. The dial is efsearch​, the length of the candidate list the greedy walk keeps. It must be at least k, and as a rough shape recall climbs steeply from efsearch​=k up to a few hundred and then flattens while latency keeps rising roughly linearly — so there is a knee, and your job is to find it on your own data rather than quote somebody else’s. M costs memory whether you use it or not, since every node stores up to M links per layer and roughly 2M at the base layer: at M=16 and 4 bytes per link that is about 128 bytes of graph per vector on top of the vector itself. A million 1,024-dimensional float32 vectors is 4.1 GB of raw data plus about 0.13 GB of graph, and that graph is why HNSW is a memory-resident structure and why IVF-PQ starts to look attractive in the billions. Now the filter, in one line of arithmetic. If a tenant owns 0.5% of the corpus and you post-filter a top-100 result set, the expected number of surviving matches is about 0.5 — which is why post-filtering does not degrade gracefully. It returns nothing at all.

Filter inside the search, then measure what it costs

from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

hits = client.query_points(
    collection_name="docs", query=embed(q), limit=10,
    search_params=models.SearchParams(hnsw_ef=128),      # the recall/latency dial
    query_filter=models.Filter(must=[                    # applied DURING traversal
        models.FieldCondition(key="tenant_id",
            match=models.MatchValue(value=session.tenant))]),
).points
# the tenant comes from the SESSION. never from the request body, ever.

# know your operating point: compare against an exact scan on sampled queries.
exact  = brute_force_topk(embed(q), k=10)
recall = len({h.id for h in hits} & {e.id for e in exact}) / 10   # 0.90-0.99, tuned
# if you have never computed this line, you do not know what your index is losing.

Where this bites in production

Malkov and Yashunin’s HNSW paper (2016, TPAMI 2020) is the source of both the layered graph and the defaults everyone ships: pgvector defaults to an M of 16 with ef_construction 64, Qdrant to an M of 16 with ef_construct 100. Qdrant also documents the filtering problem in the open — it builds additional graph links for payload categories so a filtered subgraph stays connected, and switches to a plain scan when the matching set is small enough that walking the graph is not worth the trouble.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How does metadata filtering interact with the graph?
Post-filtering is applied after traversal and silently craters recall; you want the filter inside the walk. HNSW hops through neighbours by distance alone, so it has no idea your filter exists — ask for ten, filter to one tenant holding 0.5% of the corpus, and you can be left with nothing. Pre-filtering restricts candidates first and is exact but becomes a scan on large subsets. Filtered search, where the engine consults the filter during traversal and adds links to keep the subgraph connected, is the production answer.
Your ANN recall is 0.92. Is that a bug?
No — it is the setting you chose, whether or not you chose it deliberately. Approximate search buys its speed by never visiting most of the collection, so recall below 1 is the mechanism working. Raise ef_search and recall climbs and latency climbs with it; raise M and you pay memory at build time. Pick a target from the product, usually 0.95 to 0.99, measure it against a brute-force scan on sampled queries, and tune to the knee. The real bug is not knowing the number.
You want to upgrade your embedding model. Walk me through the migration.
Full re-index and a cutover — old and new vectors live in different spaces and cannot be mixed or compared. Stand up a shadow index with the new model, re-embed the whole corpus into it, dual-write every new or changed document to both, then compare recall and nDCG on the same golden set offline before anything moves. Cut traffic over behind a flag with the old index still warm for rollback, and only then delete it. There is no gradual migration at the vector level and no meaningful partial rollout.

Say this back tomorrow

ANN recall is below 1 on purpose  ·  post-filtering is what turns that into a silent outage
  • HNSW is a layered small-world graph; ef_search and M trade recall against latency and memory
  • Measure recall against an exact brute-force scan on sampled queries, or you do not know your operating point
  • Filter during traversal, inject the tenant from the session, and audit every retrieval that crosses the index

Unlocks

  • HNSW
  • ef_search
  • pre vs post filter
  • multi-tenancy
  • re-index and cutover
