Hybrid Search & Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Dense retrieval knows what your question was about. BM25 knows what it literally said.

Two retrievers with opposite blind spots. The vector retriever compares meanings, so it finds a document about refund policy when you asked how to get your money back, and it is hopeless with a part number or an acronym it has never seen, because there is no meaning in those to average. Keyword search is the mirror image: it counts the actual words, rewards rare ones, finds the part number instantly, and misses every document that says the same thing in other words. Running both and merging is the standard answer. The merging is where people go wrong. One retriever hands you similarity values crowded near the top of its range, the other unbounded relevance scores, and the two scales have nothing to do with each other. So you throw the numbers away and keep the ordering: a document is scored by where it placed in each list, and whatever placed well in both rises to the top.

Like two judges scoring a competition. One marks out of ten, the other awards points in the hundreds, and nobody ever wrote down how the two scales relate. You cannot add the marks together. What you can do is take each judge’s ordering and reward the competitor that both of them placed near the top.

Dense retrieval fails on precisely the queries where the literal string is the query: SKUs, error codes, version numbers, legal citations, rare proper nouns, acronyms and negation. BM25 is built for those — term frequency with saturation, an inverse document frequency weight that lets a rare token dominate, and a length normalisation, with Lucene’s defaults of k1​=1.2 and b=0.75. So you run both and fuse. The mechanics question is how, and the answer is that you do not normalise the scores. A cosine similarity of 0.83 and a BM25 score of 14.7 are not comparable, their distributions shift per query and per corpus, and min-max normalising within a result set forces the top hit of a useless list to 1.0. Reciprocal rank fusion discards the scores entirely and sums 1/(k+rank) over every list a document appears in, conventionally with k=60. Hybrid typically lifts recall@10 by 10 to 30% over dense alone, and that range is dataset-dependent.

Work the example by hand, out loud, because that is what they want to see. With k=60: rank 1 contributes 1/61=0.01639, rank 2 1/62=0.01613, rank 3 1/63=0.01587, rank 4 1/64=0.01563. A document ranked first by BM25 and fourth by the dense retriever scores 0.01639+0.01563=0.03202. A document ranked second and first scores 0.01613+0.01639=0.03252 and wins. A document that only one retriever found at all scores about 0.016 and lands below everything the two agreed on — which is the property you want, because agreement across two different retrieval mechanisms is evidence and it costs nothing to compute. The constant flattens the curve: at 60 the gap between rank 1 and rank 2 is under 2%, so a document has to be badly placed before its contribution collapses, and lowering the constant makes the top ranks dominate. Two things to add if they push. You weight a retriever by multiplying its term, not by tampering with the constant, and a mild dense weight is common on prose corpora. And RRF is deliberately lossy — it cannot express that one retriever was confident and the other was guessing — so where you genuinely have calibrated comparable scores from one model, a learned combination can beat it. For two incomparable scales it is the right default, and it is what every engine ships.

You reach for it when

  • A corpus full of part numbers, error codes, versions or citations
  • Dense retrieval works on prose queries and fails on exact identifiers
  • Asked to merge results from two retrievers with different scoring
  • Recall@10 is the number you have been asked to move

The trap

Min-max normalising the two score lists and adding them. It looks principled and it is not: BM25 scores are unbounded and their range moves with query length and corpus statistics, while cosine sits in a narrow band near the top. Normalising within a result set forces the best hit of a useless list to 1.0, so a query where lexical search found nothing still contributes a confident-looking maximum. Fuse the ranks. The other half is not knowing that BM25 alone wins outright on exact identifiers.

The math fuse the ranks, never the scores

RRF(d)=∑r∈R​k+rankr​(d)1​,k=60  ·  BM25(q,d)=∑t​IDF(t)ft,d​+k1​(1−b+b∣d∣/avgdl)ft,d​(k1​+1)​The first expression is the whole technique and it has no free parameters worth arguing about. R is the set of ranked lists, rankr​(d) is the one-based position of document d in list r, and a document missing from a list simply contributes nothing from it — there is no imputation and no penalty term. The constant k controls how quickly a document’s contribution decays with position: at k=60, rank 1 gives 1/61=0.01639 and rank 10 gives 1/70=0.01429, a spread of only 13% across the whole top ten, which is why appearing in two lists dominates appearing high in one. Drop k to 10 and rank 1 gives 0.0909 against rank 10’s 0.05, a 45% spread, and the top of each list starts to win on its own. Weighting is multiplicative and lives outside the sum, ∑r​wr​/(k+rankr​), so a 0.7 dense and 0.3 lexical split is expressible without touching k. The second expression is BM25, and the two pieces to be able to point at are the saturation — ft,d​ appears in both numerator and denominator, so the tenth occurrence of a term adds far less than the second — and the length normalisation through ∣d∣/avgdl, which stops long documents winning by sheer surface area. Lucene ships k1​=1.2 and b=0.75 and almost nobody changes them.

Twelve lines, and it beats score normalisation

from collections import defaultdict

def rrf(*ranked_lists, k=60, top=10):
    """Fuse ranked ID lists. The scores are never touched - only the positions."""
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for lst in ranked_lists:                       # each list is best-first
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(lst, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] += 1.0 / (k + rank)     # missing = contributes nothing
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)[:top]

bm25  = ["SKU-4471", "spec-sheet", "install-pdf", "faq"]        # exact match wins
dense = ["spec-sheet", "install-pdf", "overview", "SKU-4471"]   # topic match wins
rrf(bm25, dense)   # -> spec-sheet, SKU-4471, install-pdf, overview, faq

# rank 1 in ONE list  = 1/61          = 0.01639
# rank 2 in BOTH      = 1/62 + 1/62   = 0.03226   <- agreement is the signal
# weighting is w / (k + rank), a multiplier. do NOT tune k to weight a retriever.

Where this bites in production

Reciprocal rank fusion is Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher, SIGIR 2009, and the constant is a piece of history: they set it to 60 on TREC data, said plainly that they had not tuned it, and it has been the default ever since. It is what you get from Elasticsearch’s rrf retriever, whose rank_constant defaults to 60, and from the hybrid ranking in Azure AI Search, Weaviate and Qdrant. Lucene’s BM25 defaults, k1 of 1.2 and b of 0.75, are the other pair worth knowing by heart.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How do you combine two incomparable score scales?
You do not combine the scores at all — you fuse the ranks. BM25 scores are unbounded and shift with query length and corpus statistics, cosine similarities sit in a narrow band, and normalising either one within a result set invents comparability that does not exist. Reciprocal rank fusion sums one over sixty plus the position, over each list the document appears in, and orders by that sum. It needs no calibration, no training and no shared scale, and it rewards documents that both retrievers found.
Work RRF for a document ranked first by BM25 and absent from the dense list.
It scores 1/61, which is 0.0164, and loses to anything ranked second by both. A missing document contributes nothing from that list — no penalty, no imputed rank, just no term. Two mid-table appearances sum to about 0.0323, roughly double, so agreement beats a single strong opinion. That is the intended behaviour and it is also the thing to watch: if one retriever is genuinely authoritative for a query type, fusion will dilute it, which is what the per-list weight is for.
When does BM25 alone beat hybrid?
When the query is an exact string the corpus contains verbatim. Part numbers, error codes, version strings, legal citations and rare proper nouns are where the dense retriever has nothing useful to encode — it fragments the identifier into subword pieces that carry no identity, so CVE-2024-3094 and CVE-2024-3095 are neighbours. Adding a dense list there can pull genuinely irrelevant topical matches into the fused top ten. Route on the query when you can, and weight the lexical list up for identifier-shaped queries.

Say this back tomorrow

never normalise two score distributions  ·  sum one over sixty plus rank, and let agreement win
  • Dense fails on exact identifiers, acronyms, rare terms and negation; BM25 is built for exactly those
  • RRF ignores the scores entirely and sums one over sixty plus rank across every list a document appears in
  • Hybrid lifts recall@10 by roughly 10 to 30% over dense alone, and that figure is dataset-dependent

Unlocks

  • BM25
  • RRF
  • rank_constant 60
  • score normalisation trap

Reranking: Bi-Encoder vs Cross-Encoder

Two stages exist because one model can be cheap and one can be accurate, and no model is both.

There are two ways to decide whether a document answers a question. The cheap way turns the question into a vector and the document into a vector, separately, and measures how close the two are. Because the document never sees the question, you can do the document half in advance, for the whole collection, and store the results; at query time one small piece of work is left. The accurate way feeds the question and the document into a model together, in a single pass, and lets every word of one attend to every word of the other. That is far better at telling a near miss from a real answer, and none of it can be done in advance, because the result depends on the pair. Which is why you cannot run it over a million documents. You run the cheap one to get a hundred candidates, the accurate one on those hundred, and keep the best handful.

Like sorting job applications. Skim-reading every CV against a checklist is quick, and you can do it before any particular vacancy exists. Interviewing tells you far more, and there is no way to interview somebody in advance for a job you have not posted yet. So you skim a thousand, interview ten, and hire one.

A bi-encoder embeds the query and the document independently, so sim(q,d)=cos(E(q),E(d)) factorises: every E(d) is computed once at ingestion and stored, and query time is one forward pass over the query plus an ANN lookup. A cross-encoder takes the pair as a single input, [CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP], runs full self-attention across both halves, and emits one relevance score. There is no E(d) to cache, because the document’s representation depends on the query — which is exactly what makes it accurate and exactly why it cannot be precomputed. Cost is therefore one forward pass per candidate, linear in the number of candidates, so cross-encoding a ten-million-document corpus per query is not a tuning problem, it is an impossible one. The funnel that follows is retrieve 50 to 100, rerank, keep 5 to 10. Budget roughly 100 to 300 ms for the rerank stage inside a 2-second end-to-end RAG budget, and measure it on your own model, batch size and hardware.

Three things to volunteer before they ask. First, what reranking can and cannot fix. It raises precision in the top 5 and it is the cheapest way to stop a nearly-relevant chunk crowding out the right one — but it is strictly a reordering of the candidate set, so if the answer is not in the top 100 the retriever returned, no reranker recovers it. Measure recall@100 on the retriever and precision@5 or nDCG@5 after the reranker, and when recall is the problem go and fix chunking or add a lexical list instead. Second, where the latency goes. Cross-encoder cost is per pair and roughly linear in the number of candidates and in the truncated pair length, so reranking 100 candidates costs about twice reranking 50. The levers, in order: fewer candidates, a smaller reranker, a shorter maximum pair length, batching every pair into one call rather than looping, and skipping the stage entirely for queries a cheap classifier says are easy. All of it lands before the first token, which is dead air the user is watching. Third, the middle ground, because naming it separates you from someone who has read one blog post. Late-interaction models such as ColBERT store one vector per token and compute a cheap MaxSim between query tokens and document tokens, recovering much of the cross-encoder’s accuracy at index time rather than query time — and multiplying your storage, because you are now keeping a vector per token instead of per chunk. Say the technique and say what it costs.

You reach for it when

  • Retrieval finds the answer somewhere in the top 50 but never in the top 5
  • Asked why a RAG system needs two retrieval stages at all
  • Cutting latency and deciding which stage to sacrifice
  • Choosing between a bigger embedding model and adding a reranker

The trap

Describing a cross-encoder as “a better embedding model”. It produces no embedding at all — there is nothing to store, because it scores a query-document pair jointly and the document’s representation only exists relative to that query. If you cannot say that sentence, the follow-up — so why not cross-encode the whole corpus? — has no answer and the two-stage funnel stops making sense. The other trap is adding a reranker when your problem is recall, where by construction it changes nothing.

The math why one of them can be precomputed and the other cannot

bi-encoder: score=cos(E(q),E(d)), E(d) precomputed  ·  cross-encoder: score=f([q;d]), nothing factorises  ·  trerank​≈N⋅tpair​The difference is algebraic, not a matter of degree. The bi-encoder score factorises into a function of the query and a function of the document, so the document half moves offline and query time is one model call plus a graph walk regardless of corpus size. The cross-encoder score does not factorise: f([q;d]) has no separable parts, so it costs one full forward pass for every pair you want scored, and N is whatever you feed it. Put a number on that. Suppose a small reranker scores one query-document pair in about 2 ms once batched on a GPU — model- and hardware-dependent, so measure yours rather than quoting mine. Reranking 100 candidates is then about 200 ms, which fits inside a 2-second budget alongside 50 to 100 ms of query embedding, 50 to 150 ms of vector retrieval and 300 to 800 ms to first token. Reranking a ten-million-chunk corpus for one query is 107×2ms≈5.6 hours. That gap is the entire justification for a first stage. The funnel also tells you what to measure and in which order: recall@100 is a ceiling set by the bi-encoder, precision@5 or nDCG@5 is what the cross-encoder buys on top of it, and improving the second while the first is the bottleneck moves nothing at all.

The funnel, and the line that cannot exist

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2", max_length=512)

cands  = index.search(embed(q), limit=100)      # bi-encoder: doc vectors PRECOMPUTED
pairs  = [(q, c.text) for c in cands]           # 100 pairs, one query
scores = reranker.predict(pairs, batch_size=32) # 100 JOINT forward passes, ~200ms
top    = [c for _, c in sorted(zip(scores, cands), key=lambda t: -t[0])][:8]

# there is no reranker.encode(doc), and there cannot be: the score is a function
# of the PAIR, so nothing about a document can be computed before the query lands.
# 100 pairs ~ 200ms batched on a GPU. 10M pairs ~ 5.6 hours. hence the funnel.
# levers when it does not fit: fewer candidates, smaller model, shorter max_length.

Where this bites in production

The reference implementation is sentence-transformers, and its documentation states the point flatly: a cross-encoder does not produce embeddings for individual sentences, so it cannot be used to build an index. cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 is the small model people actually deploy, with BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 and Cohere Rerank as the stronger open and hosted options. The two-stage funnel comes from the same tradition — BM25 or a dense retriever produces the MS MARCO candidate set and the cross-encoder reorders it.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why can you not cross-encode the whole corpus?
Because a cross-encoder has nothing to precompute — the score is a joint function of the pair. A bi-encoder’s score factorises into a query function and a document function, so every document vector is built once at ingestion and query time is one forward pass plus an index lookup. A cross-encoder concatenates query and document and runs attention across both, so the document’s representation only exists relative to that query. Cost is one forward pass per candidate: 100 pairs is around 200 ms, ten million is hours.
What does reranking cost, and where does it sit in your budget?
Roughly 100 to 300 ms for 50 to 100 candidates, and all of it before the first token. In a 2-second RAG budget that sits after query embedding at 50 to 100 ms and vector retrieval at 50 to 150 ms, and ahead of 300 to 800 ms to first token — so it is pure silence from the user’s point of view, which is why it is the first stage people cut. Cost is roughly linear in candidates and pair length, so the levers are fewer candidates, a smaller model, a shorter max length, and one batched call.
You added a reranker and end-to-end accuracy did not move. What now?
Your problem is recall, not ordering, and a reranker cannot fix recall. It only reorders the candidate set it was handed, so if the answering chunk is not in the retriever’s top 100 it is already lost. Measure recall@100 on the retriever against the golden set’s ideal chunk IDs before you touch the second stage. If that number is low, the fixes are upstream: chunking and contextual retrieval, a lexical list fused in with RRF, or a better embedding model — then rerank.

Say this back tomorrow

a bi-encoder precomputes documents  ·  a cross-encoder cannot, so it only ever sees the shortlist
  • The bi-encoder score factorises so document vectors move offline; the cross-encoder score does not factorise at all
  • Cost is one joint forward pass per candidate, which is why the funnel is retrieve 50-100 then keep 5-10
  • Reranking buys precision@5, never recall@100 — whatever the first stage missed is already gone

Query Transformation: HyDE, Multi-Query & Decomposition

The user typed a question. The thing you are searching is an answer. That gap is a retrieval bug you can fix before you search.

A user types something short, vague and full of pronouns, and you embed it and go looking for a document that resembles it. But documents do not look like questions. They look like answers. That mismatch is fixable before you search. One trick is to ask a model to write the answer it imagines, with no retrieval at all, and search using that invented answer instead, because a made-up answer sits nearer the real one in the space you are searching even where its details are wrong. Another is to rewrite the question three ways and merge whatever each finds. A third is to notice the question has two parts, split it, and retrieve for each part separately. All of these help, and every one is a model call that happens before any searching starts, so the user waits longer for the first word.

Think of hunting for a book you half remember. Typing your vague question into the catalogue finds nothing. Writing out the sentence you believe appears in the book — even getting it slightly wrong — finds the shelf. You are searching with a guess at the answer rather than with the question, and the guess does not have to be right to point the right way.

Four transformations, each buying something different. HyDE asks the model to write a hypothetical answer to the query with no retrieval at all, embeds that document and searches with its vector — the point being that an answer sits closer in embedding space to the passage you want than a question does, and factual errors in the hypothesis matter less than you would expect because only the vector is used. Multi-query generates three or four paraphrases, retrieves for each and fuses the results, which covers vocabulary you did not think of. Decomposition splits a multi-part question — “how did our margin and our headcount change after the acquisition?” — into sub-questions retrieved separately, because no single chunk holds both halves. Expansion and acronym resolution are the cheap ones: expand the domain acronym from a glossary, resolve pronouns against the previous turn, add the obvious synonyms, none of which needs a model at all. The first three each cost at least one extra LLM call before you have retrieved anything, so 200 to 500 ms lands directly on time to first token.

Say what you would actually ship, because the trap is stacking all of them. Order by cost. Rule-based rewriting — acronym expansion from a glossary, pronoun resolution against the last turn, stripping conversational filler — costs nothing and fixes a large share of conversational RAG failures on its own, so do it always and first. Then route the rest by query type using a small classifier or one cheap call: decomposition only when the query is genuinely multi-part, HyDE only on short underspecified queries where the vocabulary gap is the problem, and nothing at all on queries containing an exact identifier, where BM25 was going to win anyway. Run the resulting retrievals in parallel rather than in sequence, and cache transformations, because the same query text recurs far more than you expect. Then measure honestly on a fixed golden set: recall@k with the transformation and without it, next to the added latency and the added tokens per query. A three-point recall gain for 400 ms of extra silence is a bad trade in an interactive product and a fine one in a batch pipeline, and the answer that scores in an interview is the one that names the trade rather than the technique. Two failure modes worth knowing. HyDE can hallucinate a confident hypothesis into an entirely wrong neighbourhood on niche or very recent topics, where the plain query would have been safer — it is strongest exactly where the model has broad background knowledge and weakest where your corpus is the only source. And multi-query returns heavily overlapping sets, so fuse the union with RRF or dedupe it, or you will simply hand the reranker four copies of the same chunk and pay to score them.

You reach for it when

  • Conversational RAG where questions are short and full of pronouns
  • A corpus whose vocabulary does not match how users phrase things
  • Questions that need two facts from two different documents
  • Weighing a recall improvement against time to first token

The trap

Stacking HyDE, four rewrites and decomposition in front of every request. That is three sequential LLM calls before a single vector has been looked up, several hundred milliseconds of added silence on time to first token, and often a couple of points of recall that a reranker would have given you for less. Route instead: cheap rule-based rewriting always, the expensive transformations only where the query type needs them, measured against latency first.

The math what you search with, and what it adds to the wait

HyDE: q→LLM→d~, search with E(d~)  ·  ΔTTFT=ttransform​≈200 to 500ms  ·  multi-query: n retrievals, one fused listThe HyDE line is the whole idea in three symbols. You never retrieve on E(q); you generate a hypothetical document d~ and retrieve on E(d~), because the distance from a question to its answering passage is larger than the distance from a plausible answer to that same passage. The hypothesis is thrown away after embedding, which is why its factual errors cost less than they look like they should — you are borrowing its shape and its vocabulary, not its claims. The second expression is the bill and it is the half candidates forget. A transformation call is a full round trip — typically 200 to 500 ms for a small model generating a short passage, provider- and length-dependent — and it is strictly sequential with everything after it, so it adds to time to first token one for one. Set it against a 2-second budget where query embedding is 50 to 100 ms, retrieval 50 to 150 ms, reranking 100 to 300 ms and the first token 300 to 800 ms, and you have just added between a tenth and a quarter of the whole budget before any work started. Multi-query costs a second way: n paraphrases means n index queries, so vector database load scales with n while the returned sets overlap heavily, and the union has to be fused with RRF or deduped before it reaches the reranker. Run the n retrievals concurrently, cache the transformation keyed on the normalised query text, and report the gain as recall@k per added millisecond rather than as recall@k alone.

Cheap rewriting always, expensive rewriting by route

import asyncio

async def transform_and_retrieve(q, history):
    q = expand_acronyms(resolve_pronouns(q, history))    # free. always do this.
    if looks_like_identifier(q):                         # a SKU? BM25 already wins.
        return await retrieve(q)

    hyde, rewrites = await asyncio.gather(               # ONE round trip, not two
        llm(f"Write a short passage that answers: {q}"), # embed the ANSWER, not q
        llm(f"Rewrite this query 3 ways, one per line: {q}"))

    queries = [hyde] + rewrites.splitlines()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(retrieve(x) for x in queries))
    return rrf(*results)                                 # union, then fuse the ranks

# every llm() above runs BEFORE any retrieval: 200-500ms straight onto TTFT.
# gate it on query type, cache on the normalised text, and report recall per ms.

Where this bites in production

HyDE is Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan, 2022 — “Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels”. They have InstructGPT write a hypothetical document, embed it with an unsupervised Contriever encoder, and beat that same encoder used the ordinary way across TREC DL and BEIR with no labelled training data at all. LangChain’s MultiQueryRetriever is the other one you will meet in a codebase: its default prompt asks for three alternative phrasings of the question and unions the results, which is the entire technique in one class.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A user’s question is short and vague and retrieval returns nothing useful. What do you try?
Fix the query before you touch the index, cheapest thing first. Resolve pronouns against the previous turn and expand domain acronyms from a glossary — no model call, and it clears a surprising share of conversational failures. If the vocabulary gap remains, HyDE: have the model write a hypothetical answer and retrieve on that vector, since an answer resembles the target passage more than a question does. If the question has two distinct parts, decompose it and retrieve for each. Route between these, do not run all of them.
What does HyDE actually embed, and why does a wrong hypothesis still help?
It embeds the generated answer, not the question, and the vector is all you keep. You ask the model to write the passage it thinks would answer the query, with no retrieval, then embed that text and search with it — the hypothesis is discarded immediately afterwards. It works because it borrows the shape and vocabulary of an answer, which is what your corpus is made of, so the errors in its claims mostly do not survive into the vector. It fails where the model has no background at all: niche, very recent or proprietary topics.
You added HyDE and multi-query and recall went up three points. Do you ship it?
Not until you have priced it against time to first token. Two transformations are two LLM calls before any retrieval, 200 to 500 ms each and strictly sequential with everything after, plus four index queries instead of one. Three points of recall for 400 ms of added silence is a poor trade in an interactive chat and a good one in a batch pipeline. Check first whether a reranker buys the same three points for less, then route the transformation to the query types that actually need it.

Say this back tomorrow

search with a guess at the answer, not with the question  ·  and pay for it in time to first token
  • HyDE embeds a generated answer because answers resemble your passages and questions do not
  • Multi-query unions several rewrites and decomposition splits multi-part questions into separate retrievals
  • Every transformation is an LLM call before retrieval, so it lands whole on TTFT — route it, do not stack it

Embedding Migration & Reindexing

Two embedding models build two coordinate systems, and there is no exchange rate between them. So the upgrade is not an edit. It is a rebuild.

An embedding model does not read the meaning off a page and write it down somewhere universal. It invents its own coordinate system during training, and the numbers it produces only mean anything inside that system. Train a different model and you get different axes, usually a different count of them, and no way to translate between the two. So the vectors you stored last year and the vectors a new model produces have nothing to say to each other. Measuring the distance between one of each is not slightly wrong, it is meaningless, and nothing in your system will complain about it. That is why upgrading is never an edit to a live index. You build a second index beside the first, put every document through the new model again, keep both fed while you check whether the new one is genuinely better on your own questions, and then switch everything over at once.

Think of two people giving directions. One measures everything in blocks from the cathedral, the other in minutes from the station. Both are precise, both are useful, and averaging one with the other puts you in the sea. There is no conversion factor to look up, because the two of them never agreed where anything starts.

Embedding spaces are not aligned across models. The axes are arbitrary artefacts of one training run, so a cosine similarity computed between an old vector and a new one is a number with no meaning, and no general rotation repairs it. If the dimensions differ — 1,536 down to 1,024, say — the index refuses the write, and that is the lucky failure, because it is loud. If they happen to match, the write succeeds and you serve nonsense in silence. So the migration is a full re-embed and reindex, and it has a fixed shape. Stand up a shadow index on the new model, backfill the whole corpus into it, dual-write every new and changed document to both while the backfill runs, compare recall@k and nDCG@k on the same golden set offline and per slice, then cut over behind a flag, atomically, with the old index still warm. Only after that do you delete anything.

Three things to volunteer before they ask. The bill first, out loud, because a senior answer prices its own plan: ten million documents at, say, twenty chunks each is two hundred million embedding calls, and at around 250 tokens a chunk that is 50 billion tokens — a four-figure API bill at two cents per million, or several days of GPU time if you host the encoder yourself, plus about 0.8 TB of new vectors at 1,024 dimensions in float32 sitting alongside the 1.2 TB of 1,536-dimensional vectors you already had, because for the duration both indexes are live. The backfill runs for days, and that is the actual reason for dual-writing rather than a nicety: the corpus keeps changing underneath it, so anything edited mid-backfill has to be embedded again. Second, rollback, which people answer badly. You can roll back the read path — a flag flips traffic to an old index that is whole and still being written — and you cannot roll back a half-migrated single index, because once vectors from two models are mixed there is no way to tell which came from which unless you wrote the model version onto every record. So write it, on every record, from day one. Third, everything downstream that was calibrated on the old score distribution moves. A similarity cutoff of 0.75, a confidence threshold on a routing classifier, a semantic cache keyed on a rounded vector, a reranker’s candidate count — all of it was tuned against a distribution that no longer exists, and all of it is re-tuned on the new index before cutover, not after the first incident. And do not migrate on a leaderboard. A model three points higher on MTEB can be worse on your corpus, because your corpus is not the benchmark; the only number that decides is recall on your golden set, read per slice.

You reach for it when

  • Asked to upgrade an embedding model on an index already serving traffic
  • Choosing an embedding dimension when index storage is the constraint
  • Pricing a reindex of a corpus in the millions of documents
  • A retrieval quality drop that started the day someone changed a model string

The trap

Saying you would migrate incrementally — re-embed as documents are touched, query across both, backfill the rest later. Old and new vectors are not comparable, so there is nothing to query across; if the dimensions match, the index accepts the mixed writes and the top-k quietly collapses to whichever space the query is in. The related mistake is planning a partial rollback. Once one index holds two spaces, there is no un-mixing it.

The math two spaces, and the bill for crossing between them

Eold​(d)∈R1536, Enew​(d)∈R1024  ·  cos(Eold​(d),Enew​(q)) is undefined  ·  cost =Nchunks​⋅tˉ⋅priceThe first line is the whole objection and it is worth saying in exactly this form. The two encoders map into different vector spaces, and when the dimensions differ the expression is not merely wrong, it does not typecheck — there is no dot product between a 1,536-vector and a 1,024-vector. That is the version that fails loudly. The dangerous version is two models that share a dimension, where every operation is well-formed and every result is meaningless, because the axes of one run have no relationship to the axes of another. There is no learned rotation you can rely on either: alignment between independently trained spaces is a research problem, not a migration plan. Now the cost, which is the half candidates skip. Ten million documents at twenty chunks each is 2×108 embedding calls; at 250 tokens a chunk that is 5×1010 tokens, so at $0.02 per million you are looking at roughly $1,000 of API spend and several days of wall-clock throughput, and storage of 2×108×1024×4≈0.8 TB for the new vectors while the old 1.2 TB is still serving. Double your index footprint for the duration and plan the capacity before you start, because running out of disk halfway through a backfill is the one failure mode that has no graceful recovery. Then the smaller, sharper number: a similarity threshold of 0.75 tuned on the old model is a different percentile on the new one, so re-derive every threshold from the new score distribution before the flag flips.

Shadow, dual-write, compare, flip

# 1. every record carries the model that produced it. from day one.
SHADOW = "docs_v3"   # new model      LIVE = "docs_v2"   # old model, serving

def upsert(chunk):                       # DUAL-WRITE while the backfill runs
    live.upsert(id=chunk.id, vector=embed_v2(chunk.text), payload={"emb": "v2"})
    shadow.upsert(id=chunk.id, vector=embed_v3(chunk.text), payload={"emb": "v3"})

# 2. compare OFFLINE on the same golden set, per slice. never on live traffic.
for slice_name, queries in golden.by_slice():        # 50-100 queries per slice
    old = recall_at_k(live,   queries, k=20)         # ideal chunk ids from the set
    new = recall_at_k(shadow, queries, k=20)
    print(slice_name, old, new)                      # one row worse = one blocker

# 3. cutover is a flag, not a merge. old index stays warm and still written to.
INDEX = SHADOW if flags.on("emb_v3") else LIVE
# there is no line here that reads from both. there cannot be one.

Where this bites in production

OpenAI replaced text-embedding-ada-002 with the v3 models in January 2024, and the guidance was explicit: the new models are not interchangeable with the old, so an ada-002 index has to be rebuilt rather than topped up. The v3 models also expose a dimensions parameter built on Matryoshka representation learning, so text-embedding-3-large can be shortened from 3,072 to 1,024 and still beat ada-002 on MTEB — a real lever when index storage, not quality, is what is binding.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You want to upgrade your embedding model. Walk me through the migration.
Full re-embed into a shadow index, dual-write, compare offline, then one atomic cutover. Old and new vectors live in different spaces, so nothing is mixable and nothing is comparable. Build the new index beside the live one, backfill the whole corpus, write every new and changed document to both while it runs, then read recall@k and nDCG@k off the same golden set per slice. Flip a flag with the old index still warm, re-tune every threshold that was calibrated on the old score distribution, and only then delete.
Can you migrate incrementally and query across both?
Not at the vector level — there is no distance between the two spaces. If the dimensions differ the index rejects the write; if they match it accepts it and the top-k silently collapses to whichever space the query came from. The only honest version of “query both” is two separate searches fused by rank, since reciprocal rank fusion never compares scores — and that costs two indexes and two searches, so it is a bridge for a cutover weekend, not a destination.
The backfill is 60% done and quality has dropped. Do you roll back?
You roll back the read path, and there is nothing else to roll back. Reads flip to the old index, which is untouched, complete and still receiving every write because you dual-wrote — that is what dual-writing bought you. The shadow index you simply keep building or throw away. What has no recovery is a single index you migrated in place: once two spaces are mixed you cannot separate them again unless every record carries the model version, which is why that field goes on from the first write.

Say this back tomorrow

different model, different space  ·  shadow index, dual-write, offline compare, one flag
  • Vectors from two embedding models cannot be compared or mixed; a matching dimension makes it silent, not safe
  • Dual-write exists because the backfill takes days and the corpus changes underneath it
  • Every threshold calibrated on the old score distribution has to be re-derived before the cutover, not after

Unlocks

  • shadow index
  • dual-write
  • atomic cutover
  • dimension mismatch
  • re-embedding cost

Function Calling & Structured Outputs

The model never runs anything. It writes down what it would like you to run, and everything after that is your code.

A model with tools cannot open a database, charge a card or send an email. It has no hands. What it produces is still only text: a small block of structured text naming a tool and the arguments it would like passed to that tool. Your code receives that block, checks it against the description you published, decides whether this user is even allowed to do it, runs the thing, and hands the result back as another message in the conversation. Then the model reads the result and carries on. Every dangerous verb in that sequence belongs to you. This matters in the interview because it decides where the fix goes when something breaks. If the model asks for the right tool with the wrong arguments, the description you published is unclear, and you repair the description rather than adding another line of pleading to the prompt.

Like a surgeon calling for an instrument. They name it and hold out a hand; the scrub nurse checks the tray, decides whether that is the right thing for this patient, and places it. The surgeon never rummages in the drawer. If the wrong instrument keeps arriving, the tray was labelled badly — you relabel the tray, you do not ask the surgeon to be more careful.

The model emits a request, your runtime executes. Concretely: you pass a list of tool schemas in the request; the model returns an assistant message containing one or more tool calls, each a name plus an arguments string; your code parses it, validates it against the schema, authorises it against the current user, executes, and appends a tool-role message carrying the result and the matching call id; then you call the model again with the extended history. The model has no execution path and no network, and that is a security property as much as a mechanical one, because every capability it has is a capability you handed it. When the tool choice is right and the arguments are wrong, the fault is nearly always the schema. Vague field descriptions, free-text where an enum belongs, ambiguous units, no required list, no examples, or one overloaded tool doing three jobs. You fix the schema, not the prompt.

Then constrained decoding, which is the follow-up that separates people who have shipped this. It compiles your schema into a grammar or finite-state machine, and at every decoding step it computes which tokens could legally continue the partial output, sets the logits of all the others to negative infinity, and samples from what remains. So malformed JSON is not unlikely, it is unreachable. Say the next sentence unprompted, because it is the point of the question: this guarantees schema validity and never semantic correctness. A perfectly valid object naming the wrong city, the wrong order or an amount in the wrong currency passes every check you have. Two things people miss. Forcing structure token by token degrades reasoning, because the model spends its generation inside a grammar rather than thinking in prose — the mitigation is to put a free-text scratchpad or reasoning field first in the schema, since generation is left to right and property order decides what gets thought about before the constrained fields are committed. And schema compilation is not free: a schema generated fresh per request can take seconds to compile into a grammar, which lands entirely on p99 while your median looks fine. Cache compiled grammars keyed on a hash of the schema, keep schemas static so they cache, and check whether your provider does this for you. Two more for the same breath: streaming defeats output validation, because you cannot validate or content-filter an object you have not finished receiving, so either buffer structured outputs or validate on completion and be prepared to retract. And on a validation failure, feed the validator’s error back as a tool message and let the model repair its own call, capped at two or three attempts before you fall back to a human.

You reach for it when

  • Any feature where the model has to touch a real system
  • The model calls the right tool with wrong or unit-ambiguous arguments
  • You need JSON that always parses, from a model that sometimes does not
  • p99 latency is bad on structured endpoints and p50 looks fine

The trap

Saying the model calls the function. It does not — it emits a structured request and your runtime executes it, which is why authorisation, rate limits and idempotency all live in your code and not in the prompt. The second half is fixing wrong arguments by adding instructions to the system prompt. Wrong arguments are a schema defect: no enum, no unit in the field name, no required list, no example. Repair the schema.

The math what constrained decoding does, at the logit level

logits[i]←−∞∀i∈/A(s)  ·  p=softmax(logits)  ·  validity =1, correctness =1This is the answer to “walk me through constrained decoding at the logit level”, and it is two lines. The grammar compiled from your schema is a state machine; s is the state after the tokens generated so far, and A(s) is the set of tokens that could legally continue from there. Every token outside that set has its logit driven to −∞ before the softmax, so its probability is exactly zero and the sampler cannot reach it whatever the temperature is. Nothing is retried and nothing is repaired after the fact; the illegal continuation was never available. Three consequences to have ready. First, the softmax renormalises over A(s) only, so the distribution you sample from is not the model’s — if the model’s preferred continuation is a sentence of reasoning and the grammar demands a closing brace, you get the brace, and that is precisely the mechanism by which forced structure degrades answer quality. Put a free-text field first and it gets to think before the grammar closes in. Second, the mask is recomputed at every step, which costs a little per token but is bounded and predictable. Third, building the machine is not: compiling a novel schema into a grammar can take seconds, and if you generate schemas per request that cost lands on every call and wrecks p99 while the median hides it. Cache compiled grammars on a hash of the schema. And read the third expression as the standing warning — the guarantee is on the shape of the output, never on whether it is true.

The schema is the fix, and the handoff is explicit

tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
  "name": "refund_order",
  "description": "Refund an order. Use ONLY after checking eligibility.",
  "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {
     "reasoning":      {"type": "string"},                 # FREE TEXT, FIRST
     "order_id":       {"type": "string", "pattern": "^ORD-[0-9]{6}$"},
     "amount_minor":   {"type": "integer", "description": "pence, NOT pounds"},
     "reason":         {"type": "string", "enum": ["damaged", "late", "duplicate"]}},
   "required": ["reasoning", "order_id", "amount_minor", "reason"],
   "additionalProperties": False}}}]

msg = client.chat.completions.create(model=M, messages=h, tools=tools).choices[0].message
for call in msg.tool_calls or []:                  # the model EMITTED. nothing ran.
    args = Args.model_validate_json(call.function.arguments)   # schema
    authorise(session.user, call.function.name, args)          # then permissions
    h.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": run(args)})
# enum, regex, units in the NAME, scratchpad first. that is where accuracy comes from.

Where this bites in production

OpenAI shipped Structured Outputs in August 2024 with strict: true over a JSON Schema subset, and published both halves of this card. On their own schema-following eval, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 scored 100% while gpt-4-0613 scored under 40% — and the docs state that the first request with a new schema pays extra latency while it is processed into a constrained grammar, with subsequent requests free because the artefact is cached. That caching note is the p99 answer.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Who executes the tool?
Your code does. The model only emits a request. It returns an assistant message containing a tool name and an arguments string — text, and inert until something on your side acts on it. Your runtime parses it, validates against the schema, authorises it for the current user, executes it, and appends a tool-role message with the result and the matching call id, which the model reads on the next turn. Authorisation, rate limits, idempotency and audit all live on your side, because that is the only side with hands.
The model picks the right tool but the wrong arguments. Why, and what do you fix?
The schema is underspecified, and the schema is what you change. Wrong arguments come from vague field descriptions, free-text where an enum belongs, units that are not stated, missing required fields, no example, or one overloaded tool doing three jobs. Fix it in the contract: an enum for reason codes, the unit inside the field name like amount_minor, a regex on identifiers, and one tool per job. Adding another instruction to the system prompt treats a specification defect as a persuasion problem.
Walk me through what constrained decoding does, and what it guarantees.
It masks logits so illegal tokens cannot be sampled — guaranteeing schema validity, never semantic correctness. The schema compiles into a grammar; at each step the decoder computes the legal continuations, drives every other logit to negative infinity, and samples from what is left, so malformed output is unreachable rather than unlikely. A valid object naming the wrong order still passes. Two costs: forcing structure token by token degrades reasoning, so put a free-text field first, and compiling a fresh schema per request can take seconds, so cache the grammar.

  • Constrained decoding masks logits to guarantee valid shape, and says nothing about whether the content is true
  • Put a free-text scratchpad field first, and cache compiled grammars or per-request schemas eat your p99

Agents & the Agent Loop

A chain is a path you drew. An agent draws its own, one step at a time, and the interview is about how it stops.

In a chain, you decided the order. Retrieve, then summarise, then format, then send — every request takes the same route because you wrote the route down. In an agent, you hand the model a set of tools and a goal and it chooses what to do next, looks at what came back, and chooses again, until it decides it has finished. That is the whole difference, and everything difficult about agents follows from it. Nobody wrote down how many steps a request takes, so it can take forty. Nobody wrote down when it is finished, so it can circle the same two tools until you stop paying. And a tool that charges a card can be called twice if the run is retried after a crash, which is not a strange edge case, it is a Tuesday. So the parts you build are the limits: a hard cap on steps, a check for repeated actions, an explicit way to declare it is done, and a way to resume in the middle without repeating what already happened.

Like the difference between a recipe and a shopping trip. The recipe is fixed: five steps, same order, every time, and you can test it. The trip is not — you go in for dinner, find the fish counter closed, change plan in the aisle, and come back when the bag is full. You cannot write the trip down in advance, and you can definitely wander for two hours if nobody sets a time.

A chain has a fixed control flow that you authored; an agent puts the model in the control flow, so the model chooses the next tool, reads the observation, and repeats. Observe, think, act, observe. Two shapes are worth naming. ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting one step at a time, so it adapts after every observation and is the right default when the environment is uncertain. Plan-and-execute produces the whole plan up front and then runs it, replanning only on failure, which is cheaper in model calls and easier to inspect, and it is better when the task decomposes cleanly. What you build in either case is the stopping machinery: a hard step budget of five to ten, two or three retries per tool call, loop detection on a hash of tool name plus arguments so a repeated no-progress action terminates the run, and an explicit termination condition — usually a final_answer tool the model must call, checked by your code, not a phrase you hope appears in the text.

The senior half is side effects. A retry must not double-charge a card, so every tool with consequences takes a caller-generated idempotency key derived from the run id and the step index, and the provider deduplicates on it — that is one line of design that turns a scary failure into a no-op. Separate read tools, which you may retry freely, from write tools, which need a key, an audit record and often a human approval gate on anything irreversible. Then checkpoint: after every step, persist the message list, the step counter, the tool results and the run id, so a crashed or timed-out run resumes at the last completed step rather than replaying from the beginning, because replaying from the beginning is exactly what charges the card twice. Two more numbers to have ready. Cost is not linear in steps: the whole history is resent on every call, so if each step adds a thousand tokens then ten steps is around fifty-five thousand input tokens, not ten thousand, and a runaway agent’s bill grows with the square of its step count. Reliability compounds the other way — a step that succeeds 95% of the time succeeds ten times in a row about 60% of the time — which is the real argument for fewer steps and for making the tools more capable rather than the loop longer. And then the question that actually gets asked: when is an agent wrong? When the workflow is fixed and known. If you can draw the flowchart, write the flowchart: it is cheaper, faster, deterministic, unit-testable, and it fails the same way twice so you can fix it. Reach for an agent when the path genuinely depends on what you find, and not before.

You reach for it when

  • Deciding between a scripted chain and a model-driven loop
  • An agent that never terminates, or terminates on the wrong signal
  • A tool with side effects that could be retried after a crash
  • Pricing a feature whose number of model calls is not fixed

The trap

Calling a fixed prompt chain an agent. If you wrote the order of the steps, the model is not deciding anything and the word is doing no work — interviewers ask specifically to catch this. The other half is an agent with no termination condition: no step budget, no loop detection, and “done” inferred from the wording of the model’s reply rather than from an explicit final-answer tool your code checks. That is an unbounded bill with a user attached.

The math why the budget is small, in two lines of arithmetic

prun​=pstepN​: 0.9510≈0.60  ·  tokens ≈21​TN2  ·  hard cap N≤10Both expressions argue for fewer steps, from opposite directions. The first is reliability under composition: if a single step — one tool call plus the decision that follows it — is right 95% of the time and the steps are roughly independent, then a ten-step run is right about 60% of the time, and at 90% per step it is 35%. Nothing about the model changed; the length did. That is why the productive move is usually a better tool rather than a longer loop, since one tool call that does what three did removes two chances to fail as well as two model calls. The second is cost, and it is the one people get wrong on a whiteboard. Every step resends the whole conversation, so if each step appends T tokens of tool output and reasoning, step i costs roughly iT input tokens and the run totals about 21​TN2. Put numbers through it: T=1,000 and N=10 gives around 55,000 input tokens for a single task, against the 10,000 you would guess from multiplying. Double the budget to 20 and it is roughly 210,000 — four times the tokens for twice the steps. Prompt caching flattens the stable prefix and helps a great deal here, but the growing tail is new on every call and is never cached. Hence 5 to 10 as a hard cap, 2 to 3 retries per tool, and a latency tolerance of 5 to 15 seconds interactive or 30 seconds and up for batch.

The loop is four lines; the guardrails are the rest

state = load_checkpoint(run_id) or State(step=0, msgs=[system, task], seen=set())

while state.step < MAX_STEPS:                      # 5-10. non-negotiable.
    msg = llm(state.msgs, tools=TOOLS)             # THINK - the model picks
    if msg.tool_calls is None:                     # no explicit finish = a bug
        return escalate("no final_answer tool call", state)
    call = msg.tool_calls[0]
    if call.name == "final_answer":
        return call.args["answer"]                 # DONE is a tool, not a phrase

    key = hash((call.name, canonical(call.args)))
    if key in state.seen:                          # LOOP DETECTION - no new info
        return escalate("repeated action, no progress", state)
    state.seen.add(key)

    out = run_tool(call, idem_key=f"{run_id}:{state.step}")   # retry-safe by key
    state.msgs += [msg, tool_msg(call.id, out)]; state.step += 1
    save_checkpoint(run_id, state)                 # resume HERE, never from step 0
return escalate("step budget exhausted", state)    # budget exit is a real outcome

Where this bites in production

ReAct is Yao et al., ICLR 2023 — interleaving reasoning traces with tool actions, and the ablations show the acting half fixes the hallucinated facts that pure chain-of-thought produces while the reasoning half fixes the flailing that pure acting produces. The other document to know is Anthropic’s “Building effective agents” (December 2024), which separates workflows, where the code paths are predefined, from agents, where the model directs its own process, and says plainly that most production systems should be the former.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the difference between an agent and a chain?
Who decides the next step. A chain has a control flow you authored, so every request takes the same route and you can unit-test it. An agent puts the model inside the control flow: it picks the next tool, reads the observation and picks again, looping until it declares itself finished. That is why an agent needs machinery a chain does not — a step budget, loop detection, an explicit final-answer tool and a resume path — because nobody wrote down how long a request takes or when it is over.
When is an agent the wrong answer?
When the workflow is fixed and known — then write the script. If you can draw the flowchart, code the flowchart: it is cheaper, lower latency, deterministic, testable in CI, and it fails the same way twice so it can actually be fixed. An agent buys you adaptivity you only need when the path depends on what you find, and it costs unbounded steps, compounding step-level failure and a debugging story made of transcripts. Reach for the loop when the branching is genuinely data-dependent, and not to look modern.
Your agent retries a failed booking call and the customer is charged twice. What went wrong?
No idempotency key and no checkpoint, so the retry replayed a side effect. Every tool with consequences takes a caller-generated key derived from the run id and step index, and the provider deduplicates on it, so a retry of the same logical action is a no-op rather than a second charge. Then checkpoint after every step, so a crashed run resumes at the last completed step instead of replaying from the top. Separate read tools, retryable freely, from write tools, which need keys, audit records and a human gate when irreversible.

Say this back tomorrow

a chain follows your path  ·  an agent picks its own, so you supply the budget and the exit
  • ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting; plan-and-execute plans up front and replans only on failure
  • Termination is engineering: 5-10 step cap, loop detection on tool plus arguments, an explicit final-answer tool
  • Side-effecting tools need idempotency keys and checkpointed state, or a retry charges the card twice

Agent Memory

Chat history is one of four kinds, and it is the one that runs out first.

There are four different things people mean by an agent remembering. The first is the conversation itself, sitting in the window the model reads on every call — exact, immediate, and strictly limited in size. The second is the record of past interactions, stored elsewhere and fetched back by similarity when something similar comes up again. The third is settled facts about the user, kept in an ordinary database and looked up exactly, because a shipping address is not something you want retrieved approximately. The fourth is learned habit: the instructions, the worked examples, the saved recipes for using a tool, or the weights themselves after training. Naming only the first is the standard weak answer. The second question follows immediately, because anything written automatically will eventually have rubbish written into it, and the day your agent runs out of room is the day it discovers what it should never have dropped.

Think of a colleague back from two weeks away. What is on their desk is one thing. What they can look up in last month’s emails is another. What is in the address book is a third, and it had better be exact. And the way they run a stand-up without being told is a fourth — not a memory they retrieve, a habit they acquired.

Four kinds, and the interview wants all four named. In-context memory is the window itself — system prompt, tool schemas, recent turns, retrieved chunks — exact and fast and bounded, and it is not persistence, because it dies with the request. Episodic memory is past interactions written to a vector store and retrieved by similarity at the start of a turn: good for “we have handled this before”, unreliable for facts. Semantic memory is structured facts in an ordinary database or key-value store — plan tier, timezone, address, entitlements — queried exactly rather than retrieved approximately, and it is where most teams should keep more than they do, because approximate recall of a shipping address is worse than none. Procedural memory is learned behaviour: the system prompt, few-shot exemplars, saved tool recipes, or the weights after fine-tuning. Write policy, retrieval policy and eviction policy are different for each, and saying so is most of the answer.

Pollution first, because unattended writes rot. Six controls, and they cost nothing to name. A write policy that says what is even eligible — a preference the user stated, yes; an inference you made about the user, no. A confidence threshold on the extraction step so a hedged sentence never becomes a stored fact. Deduplication and merge against existing memories before insert, or the same fact is written thirty times in different words and dominates every retrieval. Provenance on every record: which conversation, which turn, when, and by which extraction prompt version. TTL and decay, because an address from two years ago is not a fact and a preference from a one-off task should not follow someone forever. Conflict resolution, usually newest wins with the old value kept for audit. Then the seventh, which is a product requirement as much as an engineering one: the user can see everything stored about them and delete any of it. Now the run-time problem, which is asked as its own question. Your agent hits the limit on turn 30 and the reflex answer, truncate the oldest messages, is wrong in a specific way: the oldest messages are the system prompt, the tool schemas and the early tool results that everything since has been reasoning from, so you delete the contract and keep the chatter. Compaction is the answer. Pin the system prompt and tool schemas at the front, pin the last few turns at the back, and spend one model call rewriting everything in between into a compact running state — decisions taken, facts established, what is still outstanding. Keep large tool outputs out of the window entirely by storing them and passing identifiers the model can fetch again. Do it at a turn boundary and do it rarely, because rewriting the middle invalidates the prompt cache from that point on, and a cached prefix is roughly 90% cheaper to read than a fresh one.

You reach for it when

  • A long-running assistant that has to survive past its context limit
  • Deciding whether a fact belongs in a vector store or in Postgres
  • Stored preferences that are stale, duplicated or simply invented
  • A support agent that must recall a user across sessions, exactly

The trap

Answering “memory” with chat history and stopping. That is one of four kinds and the only one that does not survive the request; the interviewer is listening for episodic, semantic and procedural, and for which one you would put a shipping address in. The second trap is handling overflow by truncating the oldest messages, which deletes the system prompt, the tool schemas and the early tool results that all the later reasoning depends on.

The math what you pin, and what you allow to shrink

S+T+Σ+∑i=n−r+1n​mi​≤L  ·  truncation drops S first  ·  compaction shrinks Σ onlyRead the budget as four terms that are not interchangeable. S is the system prompt and T the tool schemas, and both are pinned: they are the contract, they sit at position zero, and they are also the stable prefix your prompt cache keys on, so moving them costs correctness and money at the same time. Σ is the running summary of everything old, and it is the only term allowed to shrink — that is what compaction means, one model call that rewrites turns 1 to n−r into a few hundred tokens of state. The last term is the most recent r turns, pinned verbatim, because a summary of what someone said forty seconds ago is a lossy answer to a question they are still in the middle of asking. L is the usable limit, which is not the advertised one: retrieval quality inside a long window degrades well before the number on the model card, and material in the middle of a very long context is attended to less reliably than material at either end, which is a second reason the ends are the things you pin. Two operational notes. Compact at a turn boundary and with headroom to spare rather than at the instant of overflow, because compaction is itself a model call and it needs room to run. And every compaction invalidates the cached prefix from the first changed token onwards, so doing it every turn turns an 80 to 95% prompt-cache hit rate into a bill; cached input reads are roughly 90% cheaper, so this is a real number, not a rounding error.

Pin the ends, summarise the middle, gate the writes

PINNED_HEAD = 2          # system prompt + tool schemas. never evicted.
PINNED_TAIL = 6          # last N turns, verbatim.

def compact(msgs, limit):
    if count_tokens(msgs) < 0.75 * limit:        # act EARLY, with headroom
        return msgs
    head, middle, tail = msgs[:PINNED_HEAD], msgs[PINNED_HEAD:-PINNED_TAIL], msgs[-PINNED_TAIL:]
    state = llm(SUMMARISE, middle)               # decisions, facts, open threads
    return head + [{"role": "user", "content": f"[state so far]\n{state}"}] + tail

def remember(fact, conf):                        # the WRITE POLICY, not a dump
    if conf < 0.8 or not fact.stated_by_user:    # inferences are not facts
        return
    if store.near_duplicate(fact, threshold=0.92):
        return store.merge(fact)                 # dedupe, or one fact wins forever
    store.put(fact, ttl_days=180, source=turn_id, visible_to_user=True)
# large tool outputs never enter the window: store them, pass the id back.

Where this bites in production

MemGPT, now Letta (Packer et al., 2023), is the named system to reach for: it treats the context window as main memory and everything else as disk, and has the model call functions to page facts in and out — an operating-system framing that maps cleanly onto in-context versus episodic and semantic stores. For the pollution half, ChatGPT’s memory is the deployed example everyone has seen: extraction is gated, the stored items are listed in settings, and the user can delete any of them individually.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What kinds of memory does an agent have?
Four: in-context, episodic, semantic and procedural. In-context is the window itself — exact, fast, bounded, and gone when the request ends. Episodic is past interactions in a vector store, fetched by similarity. Semantic is structured facts in a real database, queried exactly, which is where a shipping address or an entitlement belongs because approximate recall of those is worse than none. Procedural is learned behaviour: the system prompt, few-shot exemplars, saved tool recipes, or the weights after fine-tuning. Each has its own write, retrieval and eviction policy.
How do you stop long-term memory getting polluted?
Treat writes as the dangerous operation and govern them. A write policy that admits stated preferences and rejects inferences, a confidence threshold on the extraction step, deduplication and merge before insert so one fact does not get written thirty ways, provenance on every record, TTL and decay so stale facts expire, and newest-wins conflict resolution with the old value kept for audit. Then the control that is also a product feature: the user can see everything stored about them and delete any of it, individually.
Your agent hits the context limit on turn 30. What now?
Compact, do not truncate — the oldest messages are the system contract. Truncating from the front deletes the system prompt, the tool schemas and the early tool results the later reasoning depends on, and keeps the small talk. Pin the head and the last few turns, spend one model call rewriting the middle into a short running state of decisions, established facts and open threads, and keep bulky tool outputs out of the window by storing them and passing identifiers. Compact early at a turn boundary, since rewriting the middle invalidates the prompt cache.

  • Long-term memory needs a write policy, dedupe, TTL, provenance and a user-visible delete
  • Truncating the oldest messages deletes the contract; compaction with pinned ends is the answer

Multi-Agent Systems & MCP

The right number of agents is usually one. And MCP is not an API standard — it is a statement about who is allowed to decide.

Splitting a job across several models sounds like an obvious improvement and usually is not. Every hand-off is a chance to lose something, every extra participant carries its own instructions and its own copy of the conversation, and when the result is wrong you are reading a transcript of machines talking to each other rather than a stack trace. Three situations genuinely justify it: the work really does split into parts that can run at the same time, the parts need different permissions so one of them must not be trusted with the dangerous tools, or you need a reviewer whose judgement is not contaminated by having written the thing. Then the second half of this card, which is a protocol for connecting models to outside systems. The thing to remember about it is not the wire format. It is that its three building blocks are told apart by who is in charge of each one: the model, the application, or the person.

Like adding people to a project. Two really can work in parallel, and a second pair of eyes catches what the writer cannot see. Five means a meeting, a document nobody owns, and a mistake in the first hand-off that everyone downstream builds on faithfully. Nobody adds four people to a task one person can finish before lunch.

Three reasons that survive scrutiny. Genuinely separable subtasks that run in parallel, where the wall-clock win is real — twenty sources researched at once. Different tool permissions, where a read-only researcher and a write-capable executor should not be the same principal holding the same credentials. And independence, where a reviewer must not see the writer’s reasoning, because a critic that read the justification tends to agree with it. Everything else is one agent with better tools. The costs are specific. Errors cascade: five sequential agents at 90% each is a 59% pipeline, and the first hand-off’s mistake is treated downstream as fact. Tokens multiply, because every agent re-sends its own system prompt and tool schemas and every hand-off is paid twice, once as output and again as input. And debugging turns into reading a conversation instead of a trace, with no single frame where the failure lives. The structure that helps is a supervisor with typed hand-offs rather than agents chatting freely.

Then MCP, and the answer they are grading is that it is a control model, not a data model. It gives a host application a uniform way to talk to servers that expose context and capability over JSON-RPC, and it has three primitives which are told apart by who decides they enter the conversation. Tools are model-controlled: the model chooses to call one mid-run, subject to your approval. Resources are application-controlled: your client decides what to attach before the model gets a turn — a file, a database row, a document. Prompts are user-controlled: a person picks one deliberately, from a menu or a slash command. The reason this framing matters is that the same underlying data can be exposed as any of the three. One order record can be a resource your app attaches, a get_order tool the model calls, or a /triage prompt the user invokes; the data type never decided which, the control did. So an answer that says “resources are files and tools are functions” has described the examples and missed the protocol. And one honest line on frameworks, because it comes up unprompted: LangChain now draws critical follow-ups, and engaging with the criticism scores better than defending it. What interviewers are listening for is LangGraph’s explicit state machine — nodes, edges, a typed state object and checkpointing — because that is what gives you the resumability and the inspectable state that this card’s other half needs. Naming the abstraction you would actually debug at three in the morning is the point.

You reach for it when

  • Someone proposes a five-agent architecture for a one-prompt problem
  • Subtasks need different credentials, or a reviewer must stay independent
  • Asked to explain the difference between tools, resources and prompts
  • Choosing a framework and expecting the LangChain follow-up

The trap

Proposing five agents for a problem one prompt would solve, with no account of what it costs: hand-offs that lose information, a first-step error everything downstream treats as fact, duplicated system prompts and tool schemas on every call, and a debugging story made of transcripts. The MCP half of the trap is defining the primitives by data type — resources are files, tools are functions. They are defined by who controls them: the model, the application, the user.

The math the two prices of an extra agent, before it does any work

ppipeline​=∏i=1n​pi​  ·  0.955≈0.77, 0.905≈0.59, 0.805≈0.33  ·  tokens ≈n(S+T)+2HThe first expression is why restraint is the senior answer. Chain n agents in sequence and end-to-end success is the product of their individual reliabilities, so a five-stage pipeline of agents that are each right 90% of the time is right 59% of the time, and at 80% each it is 33%. Worse, the failures are not independent in the way this model assumes: an early agent’s confident mistake is passed downstream as an established fact and every later stage reasons faithfully from it, so the realised number is usually below the product. Adding a reviewer helps only if it is genuinely independent — a reviewer shown the writer’s reasoning largely ratifies it, which is the same self-preference bias that makes an unblinded judge unreliable. The second expression is the bill. Each of the n agents carries its own system prompt and tool schemas S+T on every one of its calls, so that overhead is multiplied rather than shared, and every hand-off payload H is paid twice: once as output tokens from the agent that wrote it, once as input tokens to the agent that reads it. A five-agent pipeline is therefore not five times the cost of one agent, it is more, and it is slower too whenever the agents run in sequence — latency only improves in the one case that actually justifies the pattern, which is genuinely parallel subtasks. Price the single-agent version first and make the multi-agent version beat it on a number.

The three primitives, and who owns each

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
mcp = FastMCP("support")

@mcp.tool()                        # MODEL-controlled: it decides to call this
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount_minor: int) -> str:
    ...

@mcp.resource("orders://{order_id}")   # APP-controlled: your client attaches it
def order(order_id: str) -> str:
    ...

@mcp.prompt()                      # USER-controlled: a human picks it from a menu
def triage(order_id: str) -> str:
    ...

# all three touch the SAME order row. the decorator encodes who decides,
# and that is the only thing separating the three primitives.

Where this bites in production

Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024 — JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or streamable HTTP, with a host, clients and servers — and the specification itself uses the control words: tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled. OpenAI adopted it in March 2025 and Google DeepMind followed, which is why it now absorbs the tool-integration question that used to be about bespoke plugin formats.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

When do you actually need more than one agent?
Three cases: genuinely parallel subtasks, different tool permissions, or a reviewer that must be independent. Parallelism has to buy real wall-clock time, not just look tidy. Different permissions means a read-only researcher and a write-capable executor should not be the same principal with the same credentials. Independence means a critic that never saw the writer’s reasoning, because one that did will largely agree with it. Everything else is one agent with better tools, and the interviewer is checking whether you know that.
What does a second agent cost you?
Compounding failure, multiplied tokens and a transcript instead of a stack trace. Five sequential agents at 90% reliability each give a 59% pipeline, and in practice worse, because an early confident error is treated downstream as fact. Every agent re-sends its own system prompt and tool schemas on every call, and each hand-off is paid twice — output tokens to write it, input tokens to read it. And when it fails there is no single frame to look at. Price the one-agent version first and make the split beat it.
What is the difference between tools, resources and prompts in MCP?
Who controls them, not what data they carry. Tools are model-controlled: the model decides to invoke one mid-run, with your application holding the veto. Resources are application-controlled: your client attaches them before the model gets a turn. Prompts are user-controlled: a person picks one deliberately, from a menu or a slash command. The same order record can be all three — a get_order tool, an orders:// resource, a /triage prompt — so defining them by data type describes the examples and misses the protocol.

  • Add an agent only for parallel subtasks, different permissions, or genuine reviewer independence
  • Five agents at 90% each is a 59% pipeline, and every hand-off is paid twice in tokens
  • MCP primitives are model-controlled, application-controlled and user-controlled — same data, different control
